title: Assur Archive 15 (N 1)
name_variants: Assur Archive 15@en | N 1 Archive@en | Assur Archive 15 | N 1 Archive
details: This archive is located in the Aššur temple.
description: In the southwest courtyard and nearby rooms of the Aššur temple, researchers found a library and an archive consisting of at least 301 clay tablets, mostly fragmentary, and possibly several hundred more. These tablets were concentrated in the northwest part of the courtyard, the northwest rooms and the Enpi gate, and some stone tablets and other inscribed objects were also found in this area. Tablets found in other parts of the Aššur temple complex also belong to Assur Archive 15. This includes at least 72 clay tablets, often fragmentary, as well as fragmentary clay prisms and cylinders. These tablets were mostly found in the southern part of the large forecourt, as well as west of the temple complex. The texts included in the library date from the Old Assyrian to the Neo Assyrian period, with a core of Middle Assyrian texts and contained cultic and hymnic texts, myths, omens, incantations, prescriptions, lexical lists, as well as hemerological, mathematical, astronomical and astrological texts. The dating of the archive is similar; it contained lists, decrees, letters and historical texts.

title: Assur Archive 18

Forty clay tablets were found above a sarcophagus, 25 clay tablets were also located nearby and either some or all of them could belong to the first group. Additionally, a clay pot, containing 13 tablets, was found in a door opening of a different house. The texts seem to form a library, except for the tablets in the pot, which formed a separate archive (Assur Archive 51). The library, dating primarily to the 7th century BCE, belonged to a family of scribes and mainly contained documents pertaining to that profession: lexical lists, astronomical and astrological texts, omens, incantations, other literary texts, and drafts or copies of royal inscriptions.

title: Kalhu ziggurat
name_variants: siqqurrat Ninurta@akk | siqqurratu ša Kalhi@akk | siqqurrat Ninurta | siqqurratu ša Kalhi
details: The ziggurat, which was dedicated to the god Ninurta, was constructed by Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) when he made Kalhu his administrative capital. It is clear from in-situ baked bricks bearing Akkadian inscriptions of his son and successor Shalmaneser III (r. 858–824 BC) that construction on the temple-tower remained unfinished at the time of his death. Shalmaneser III completed the imposing temple-tower started by his father. The remains of this multi-staged building still tower over the ruins of the once-grand Assyrian capital, which was mistakenly identified as Nineveh in the mid-nineteenth century. The ziggurat, whose ancient name is not known, had a base measuring approximately 60 x 60 m. The unbaked mudbrick core, which still rises 34 m above the level of the plain, was encased by a six-meter-high ashlar wall and an outer mantel of baked (and inscribed) bricks. Since no completely-intact ziggurat has ever been excavated in Assyria (or Babylonia), it is uncertain what the upper parts of this ziggurat might have looked like or exactly how the upper stages were accessed, although George Smith claims in 1973 to have seen traces of a staircase on the south side of the building. It is now generally thought that the first tier was accessed by an internal staircase within the Ninurta temple, as was the case with other, earlier ziggurats in northern Mesopotamia. At ground level, a large vaulted room measuring 30 m long, 1.8 m wide and 3.6 m in height was discovered. The exact function of this chamber remains a mystery.
description: The temple-tower of the god Ninurta, which was started by the ninth-century-BC Assyrian ruler Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) and completed by his son and successor Shalmaneser III (r. 858–824 BC), is still the most prominent feature of Kalhu (modern Nimrud). This multi-staged ziggurat, whose remains are now a pyramid of eroding mud-brick, was constructed in the northwest corner of the citadel, next to Kalhu's principal sanctuary, the Ninurta temple.

title: Ninurta temple (Kalhu)
name_variants: bīt Ninurta@akk | bīt Enlil u Ninurta@akk | bīt Ninurta | bīt Enlil u Ninurta
details: Akkadian inscriptions of the ninth-century-BC Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) record that that ruler built (or rebuilt) temples to the deities Adad, Damkina, Ea-šarru, Enlil, Gula, Nabû, Ninurta, Sîn, Šala, and Šarrat-niphi, as well as to the Sebetti and Kidmuri; for example, see RIAo Ashurnasirpal II 030 lines 53–78a. Of those, only four have been positively identified during nineteenth- and twentieth-century excavations: the Kidmuri temple , the Nabû temple , the Ninurta temple, and the Šarrat-niphi temple . The Ninurta temple, whose Sumerian ceremonial name is not yet attested in Assyrian texts, was the most important religious building at Kalhu since it was dedicated to the city’s tutelary deity. The temple, the remains of which are still visible today in the northwestern corner of the citadel (located in the southwest corner of the city), abutted the ziggurat (which was also consecrated to Ninurta) and Ashurnasirpal’s palace (the Northwest palace ). According to some Akkadian inscriptions (for example, RIAo Ashurnasirpal II 028 v 7b–13a), this temple was not only dedicated to Ninurta, but also to the god Enlil, which is a bit of an oddity. Various proposals have been made about where the Enlil temple was located (for example, Room 1, Room 5, and Room 6), but none of the suggestions so far are deemed (from a modern point of view) to have been sufficient enough to have been a temple of one of Assyria’s most important gods. For further details, see Reade 2002 . The temple complex has been partially excavated.
description: When Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud) became the principal administrative center of the Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC, king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) built (or rebuilt) numerous temples. The most important of those was dedicated to the god Ninurta, the patron deity of city, which Ashurnasirpal had constructed between his palace and the ziggurat, a building also consecrated to Ninurta.

title: Wilson's Arch
description: Stone archway constructed as part of the expansion of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem during the early Roman period.

title: Great Lemhill Farm Roman villa
description: A Roman villa north-east of Great Lemhill Farm rediscovered in 1937. It remains mostly unexcavated.

title: Paleochristian Church, Lin
description: A paleochristian church located in Lin, Korçë County, Albania, with fourth- and fifth-century mosaics.

title: Agios Nikolaos (island)
description: An island that is part of the Nikasiai islands (Naxos).

title: Kudachurt
description: Burial site in the Northern Caucusus containing 130 burials dated to the Middle-Late Bronze Age (2200-1650 BCE).

title: Upper Agora at Akragas/Agrigentum
description: The Upper Agora at Akragas at Poggetto di San Nicola is the site of the ekklesiasterion, the so-called "Oratory of Phalaris", and the bouleuterion.

title: Agade
name_variants: Agade@akk | Akkade@akk | Akkad@akk | Akkadu@akk | Agade | Akkade | Akkad | Akkadu
description: Agade was the capital of the Akkadian state, which was the dominant military and political force in southern Mesopotamia ca. 2334-2113 B.C. Agade (also known as Akkad and Akkade) is mentioned in cuneiform texts from the late third millennium B.C. to the Neo-Babylonian period. The exact location is still unknown and debated among scholars, many of whom place it along or east of the Tigris River, between Samarra and Baghdad.

title: Roman Arch of Pheradi Majus
description: A triumphal arch located in the civic forum.

title: Red House Roman Camp
name_variants: Red House Roman Camp@en | Red House Roman Camp
description: The site of a Roman camp located in Newbrough, Northumberland, England, United Kingdom.

title: Roman theater at Malaca
description: The remains of the first century B.C. Roman theater are located adjacent to the Alcazaba of Málaga. The theater is not completely excavated, although epigraphic data places it in the Augustan period. Its abandonment came in the third century.

title: Conímbriga amphitheatre
description: The Roman amphitheater at Conímbriga.

title: Delphinion (Miletos)
description: The Hellenistic- and Roman-period sanctuary of Apollo Delphinios is located northeast of the North Market at Miletos.

title: Koreion (Teithras)
description: A sanctuary of Kore / Persephone in the Athenian deme of Teithras, known from inscriptions.

title: Villa Romana di Caselette
description: A Roman villa of the first century CE located near Farchetto, Italy.

title: Roman Villa of San Giovanni Del Palco
description: The remains of a Roman villa located adjacent to the Convent of San Giovanni del Palco in Taurano, Italy. The convent, founded in 1383 at the Niccolò Orsini, utilizes elements of the villa's structural remains in its foundations.

title: Bouleuterion
description: A Bouleuterion complex at Nicopolis in Epirus.

title: Bagnacavallo
description: Bagnacavallo is the site of a Roman pagus located east of the centuriated area of Faventia.

title: Qaṣr-i Abūnaṣr
description: Small mound with Achaemenian remains.

title: Aiano-Torraccia di Chiusi Roman villa
name_variants: Aiano-Torraccia di Chiusi Roman villa@it | Aiano-Torraccia di Chiusi Roman villa
description: The Villa Romana di Aiano-Torraccia di Chiusi, located near San Gimignano, is notable for a tri-apsidal courtyard.

title: Abbey of Monte Cassino
name_variants: Abbazia di Montecassino@it | Abbazia di Montecassino
details: The Abbey of Monte Cassino is a multi-period site. The Lombards destroyed the original Benedictine abbey (ca. 529/530 CE) ca. 570. Little is known of this original phase. A second architectural phase is attributed to Petronax of Brescia ca. 718, with the support of the Lombard Duke Romuald II of Benevento. Saracens sacked this monastery in 883, and the monks relocated, first to Teano and then to Capua from 914. In 949, the abbey was again rebuilt. In the thirteenth century, the monastery began to decline. Serious earthquake damage occurred in 1349. In 1799, the site was sacked by French soldiers, and in 1866, the Italian government dispersed the monks. The Battle of Monte Cassino during the Second World War (1944) destroyed the site once more, and it was rebuilt in the post-war period.
description: A multi-period hilltop settlement with evidence for ancient terrace construction that now supports an abbey of the Benedictine order.

title: Grandford
details: Aerial photographs published in 2000 led to the conclusion that the site preserves the remains of two superimposed forts. The larger of the two measures approximately 140 by 100 meters. The earlier fort, perhaps corresponding to the account of Tacitus, may date ca. 47 CE while the later fort is post-Boudiccan in date.
description: The remains of a Romano-British settlement at Grandford, Cambridgeshire, were identified by aerial photography. The site lies northwest of the modern town of March and likely lay along the Roman road conventionally known as the Fen Causeway that began at the Roman fort of Longthorpe. The site's extent may have been on the order of 40 acres.

title: Awlad Azzaz Site
description: Late 18th Dynasty tomb site near the towns of Nag ed Deir and Awlad Azzaz in Egypt.

title: Sette Sale
description: Cisterns of the imperial period on the Oppian Hill that once supplied the Baths of Trajan.

title: tribus Papiria
details: The name of the tribus Papiria derives from the Roman gens Papiria . The tribe presumably was located in the territory of Labicum (or Labici) and in the fourth century B.C. Tusculum was enfranchised in this tribe.
description: The tribus Papiria is one of the earliest rural tribes of Rome.

title: Doric temple at Kaulonia
description: The Doric Temple at Caulonia has been dated ca. 420 B.C.

title: Temple of Artemis at Sardis
name_variants: Temple of Artemis at Sardis@en | Temple of Artemis at Sardis
description: A large temple dedicated to Artemis at the city of Sardis in western Asia Minor. A sanctuary to Artemis was constructed on the site during the Persian Era (ca. 547-334 BCE), and construction on a new temple on the site began during the third century BCE. The temple was never fully completed. A small church was built on part of the site in the 5th century CE, but the structure declined from the 7th century onwards, and many of its stones were reused or burned.

title: Flacciana
description: A place in Africa Proconsularis, according to the Peutinger map.

title: Roman theater at Sufetula
description: The Roman theater at Sufetula.

title: Tell Imlihiye
description: Tell in the Hamrin Basin with a small Kassite settlement. The area was flooded by the creation of the Hamrin Dam in the late 1970s.

title: Hiera Orgas
description: The Hiera Orgas or ‘sacred meadow’ was a tract of land sacred to Demeter and Persephone. It featured in at least two conflicts between Athens and Megara. It was likely located to the north of the Iapis River on the Megarian side of the Athens-Megara border.

title: Forum of Col. Augusta Raurica
description: The Forum of Augusta Raurica.

title: Blatades Monastery
description: A fourteenth century monastery.

title: Via Aemilia
name_variants: Via Aemilia, Uia Aemilia@la | ἡ Αἰμιλία ὁδός@grc | Via Aemilia | Aemilia odos | ἡ Αἰμιλία ὁδός | Via Aemilia, Uia Aemilia
description: The Via Aemilia was a major Roman trunk road of northern Italy and connected Placentia and Ariminum. Its construction began in 187 BC under M. Aemilius Lepidus.

title: Ponte Romano di Viale Roma
description: The ruins of a Roman bridge located in the Viale Roma, Santa Marinella, Italy.

title: Villa Mattonara
description: A coastal villa and associated necropolis.

title: Episcopal complex of Eio-el Tolmo de Minateda (Héllín, Albacete, Spain)
name_variants: Episcopal complex of Eio-el Tolmo de Minateda@en | Episcopal complex of Eio-el Tolmo de Minateda
description: The episcopal complex of Eio at El Tolmo de Minateda dates to the terminal sixth century CE and was in use during the following two centuries. Its construction may have been directed by Visigothic officials in Toletum.

title: Castellar
name_variants: Castellar@fr | Castellar de Cadenet@fr | Castellar | Castellar de Cadenet
description: A Gallic oppidum and sanctuary to the god Dexiva in the Vaucluse départment.

title: tribus Velina
details: The tribus Velina was organised when Curius Dentatus was censor. Its name derives from the Lacus Velinus, but its location was most likely on the Adriatic coast, presumably in the territory of the Praetuttii .
description: The tribus Velina was one of the later rural tribes which was established in Rome in 241 B.C.

title: House of the Skeleton
name_variants: Casa dello Scheletro@it | Casa dello Scheletro
description: The so-called "The House of the Skeleton" at Herculaneum is a Roman domus that owes its name to the discovery of a human skeleton during excavations. Carlo Bonucci initially explored it between 1830 and 1831. Amedeo Maiuri completed the excavation in 1927.

title: Valencihuela
description: A Spanish village located in the east of the province of Córdoba, near Jaén, that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X. Today it is known as Valenzuela.

title: Stari Ras
description: Stari Ras, the first capital of Serbia, is the site of an impressive group of medieval monuments consisting of fortresses, churches and monasteries listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

title: Tulūl al-Khāldiyah
description: Find place for cuneiform inscription.

title: Pons Fabricius
name_variants: Ponte dei Quattro Capi@it | Pons Fabricius@la | Ponte dei Quattro Capi | Pons Fabricius | Pons Fabricius
description: The Pons Fabricius (sometimes referred to as the Ponte dei Quattro Capi) is a first-century BC bridge in Rome that spans part of the Tiber River from the area of the Circus Flaminius to the Tiber Island.

title: Lycian League
description: Perhaps formed to protest the annexation of Lycia by Rhodes, by 168–7 BCE the league appears to have gained quasi-autonomy under the domination of Rome. Although the league was a party to a treaty with Iulius Caesar in 46 BCE, by 43 CE the region was annexed by Claudius into the province of Lycia; the league survived and had authority over some local customs and legal matters.

title: Monte Sant’Angelo (Tarracina)
description: A hill at Tarracina where, in Roman times, the sanctuary complex of Jupiter Anxur was built. In the medieval period, it was occupied by a monastery. Secondary deposits displaced by Roman and medieval construction indicate that Monte Sant’Angelo was the site of significant human activity from prehistory through at least the 5th century BCE.

title: Mahalliba
name_variants: Khirbet al-Mahalib@ar | Mahalliba@akk | Mahallab@akk | Khirbet al-Mahalib | Mahalliba | Mahallab
description: A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources; the modern site is Maḥālib.

title: Teatro romano, Aquino
description: The Roman theater of Aquinum.

title: Sacred Grove near Mount Pontinos
description: According to Pausanias, there was a grove of plane trees, with temples and dedications to Aphrodite, Demeter, and Dionysos that stretched from the foot of Mount Pontinus (near Lerna) "to the sea." Its precise location cannot be determined today.

title: Villa dei Quattro Venti
name_variants: Villa dei Quattro Venti@it | Villa dei Quattro Venti
description: A monumental villa complex that is known as the “Villa dei Quattro Venti” is situated on a south-eastern offshoot of the Circeo promontory, approximately 100 meters southeast of the historic center of S. Felice Circeo.

title: Khirbet Kūfīn
name_variants: خربة كڢفين@arb | Khirbet Kūfīn | Khirbat Kūfīn | Khirbet Koufin | Kusin
description: Necropolis in the West Bank near the modern village of Beit Ummar dated to the Middle Bronze Age.

title: Roman theater at Casinum
description: The Roman theater at Casinum dates to the Augustan period.

title: Antro delle Sorti
description: The "Cave of the Fates" at Praeneste is a sanctuary at the base of the city's terraced sanctuary of Fortuna. It was said to contain wooden oracular tablets.

title: Capo di Bove
description: An archaeological site located at the fourth milestone of the Via Appia Antica.

title: Grotta Corbeddu
description: A cave near Oliena, Sardinia, where evidence for the earliest human occupation of the island of Sardinia has been recovered.

title: West Coker
description: The site of a third to fourth century Romano-British villa. This is also the findspot of a bronze statuette of Mars and an bronze ansate plate inscribed with a dedication to Mar Rigisamus (RIB 187).

title: Circus Varianus
description: A circus that was part of the Sessorium palace next to the Amphitheatrum Castrense. The obelisk currently situated on the Pincian Hill was discovered on the site in the sixteenth century. It had been moved to the spina of the circus during the reign of Elagabalus.

title: Temple of Amphiaraus
name_variants: Temple of Amphiaraos@en | Temple of Amphiaraus
details: Normal 0 false false false EN-US JA X-NONE /* Style Definitions */ table.MsoNormalTable {mso-style-name:"Table Normal"; mso-tstyle-rowband-size:0; mso-tstyle-colband-size:0; mso-style-noshow:yes; mso-style-priority:99; mso-style-parent:""; mso-padding-alt:0in 5.4pt 0in 5.4pt; mso-para-margin:0in; mso-para-margin-bottom:.0001pt; mso-pagination:widow-orphan; font-size:12.0pt; font-family:"Times New Roman";} The Temple of Amphiaraus is the temple that stands in the Amphiareion, an oracular sanctuary dedicated to the god/hero Amphiaraus. The temple was constructed during the Late Classical or early Hellenistic period. The temple has no external colonnade, but within the cella it has two rows of columns, perhaps Ionic in order. There is a porch in front of the cella and an adyton at the rear. It functioned to support the role of the Amphiareion as a sacred place for healing, incubation and sacrifice to the gods.
description: The Temple of Amphiaraus is an oracular temple dedicated to the hero/god Amphiaraus, located within the sanctuary of the Amphiareion. The site was believed to have healing powers and was particularly important in the Late Classical and Hellenistic periods (fifth to third centuries BCE).

title: Temple of Hathor Miskar
description: A Punic temple founded in the first century B.C.

title: Nuraghe di Sant'Itroxia
description: A Middle Bronze age nuragic site with evidence of a giant's tomb and a nuragic tower.

title: Tomb of Marcus Tullius
description: The schola-type tomb of one Marcus Tullius is located outside the Porta Stabia of Pompeii. The decedent is thought to have been the patron of the Aedes For­tunae Augustae and was three times duovir and tribunus militum a populo.

title: Luxor Temple
description: An ancient Egyptian temple that was initially built ca. 1400 BCE.

title: Tatev Monastery
description: Armenian monastery located in Syunik Province, Armenia. Constructed beginning in 848, the monastery complex was expanded several times from the 10th-13th century.

title: Temple F at Selinus
description: Temple F at Selinus is a Doric temple located on the site's so-called "East Hill". Dedicated either to Athena or Dionysus, the temple dates to the middle of the sixth century B.C. The non-canonical ground plan of 6 x 14 columns gives the temple an elongated aspect.

title: Ninurta temple (Khorsabad)
details: Six inscribed paving slabs were found in a wing of Sargon II’s palace that was mistakenly identified as a harem and those in-situ texts helped identify that part of the building as the palace’s religious quarter. The temple sector of Dūr-Šarrukīn (modern Khorsabad) comprised temples dedicated to the deities Adad, Ea (Ninšiku), Ningal, Ninurta, Sîn, and Šamaš. The single-room temple of the god Ninurta, which was accessed from Courtyard XXVII, was identified from the eight-line Akkadian inscription (Frame, RINAP 2 online Sargon II 16 ) discovered in the doorway of Room 173. The ancient name of the temple is not known.
description: As part of the palatial complex of Dūr-Šarrukīn (modern Khorsabad), the eighth-century-BC Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) constructed six temples, including one to the god Ninurta.

title: Aşağı Anzaf
description: A fortress located close to the Urartian capital Tushpa.

title: Temple of Juno Caelestis
description: Juno Caelestis, a successor divinity of the Punic Tanit, is celebrated by a sanctuary built at Dougga ca. 222-235 CE, and sponsored by Q. Gabinius Rufus Felix.

title: Antipolis
description: According to Pliny the Elder, Antipolis was a settlement opposite the site of Rome that later became the Ianiculum.

title: Mura Greche
name_variants: Le mura greche@it | Le mura greche
description: The so-called "Mura Greche" are remains of the later third-century B.C. fortifications of Neapolis.

title: Temenos castle
description: The Castle of Temenos dates to the tenth century. It is located in the in Heraklion Municipality of Crete.

title: Forum Holitorium
name_variants: forum olitorium@la | Forum holitorium@la | Foro Olitorio@it | forum olitorium | Forum holitorium | Foro Olitorio | forum olitorium | Forum holitorium
description: The Forum Holitorium was the vegetable market of ancient Rome, situated outside the Porta Carmentalis in the southern Campus Martius. This area was bounded by the Forum Boarium and the Circus Flaminius.

title: Tumulus of Marcinelle
details: A Gallo-Roman villa is to be found in the vicinity of the tumulus.
description: A Gallo-Roman tumulus located nesr Marcinelle Charleroi in Belgium.

title: Castello di Mussomeli
name_variants: Castello di Mussomeli@it | Castello Manfredonico@it | Castello di Mussomeli | Castello Manfredonico
description: A 14th-century fortification, built on a hill called Monte Raffe, which is located east of the modern Sicilian town of Mussomeli. The hill was previously the site of a long-lived fortified settlement, dating back at least to the early iron age.

title: Ekklesiasterion at Poseidonia/Paestum
description: The seat of the popular assembly of Poseidonia/Paestum, the Ekklesiasterion was built ca. 480-470 B.C. and could accommodate, at most, 1,700 persons. The structure retained its function after the Lucanian conquest but was abandoned, buried, and built over after the Roman conquest.

title: "Basilica" of San Vitale
name_variants: Basilica of San Vitale@en | Basilica of San Vitale
details: Apse contains famous mosaics portraits of Justinian I and Theodora. The basilica was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996. Coordinates verified in Google Earth at an eye altitude of 219m.
description: A church (but not a basilica) in Ravenna, Italy, established by Bishop Ecclesius in 526 AD and consecrated ca. 547 AD.

title: Mullissu Gate
details: The Mullissu Gate is the second of Dūr-Šarrukīn’s two north-facing ( meḫret ištāni ) gates. Because ‘north’ (Akkadian ištānu ) can refer to both northeast and northwest in Akkadian sources, it is uncertain if the Mullissu Gate was located on the city’s northeast or northwest wall and, therefore, it is uncertain if that entranceway to Sargon II’s newly-constructed capital should be identified as Khorsabad Gate 1 , Gate 2 , Gate 7 , or a hitherto undiscovered (postern) gate on the northwest or southwest side of the citadel. Since one expects a plain gate to be dedicated to Mullissu (when compared to Šamaš, Enlil, and Ištar), the most plausible suggested location for the Mullissu Gate might be a hitherto undiscovered (postern) gate, probably located on the northwest side of the citadel (as suggested by Laura Battini) ; Gate 1 is a grand, decorated entrance, Gate 2 was probably is Adad Gate , and Gate 7 was very likely the Anu Gate , the first of the two west-facing entrances (since that portal actually faces 'west,' not 'north'). With regard to the location of the undiscovered (postern) gate, Battini places the Mullissu Gate on the northwest side of the citadel terrace, just east of the northwest corner. Her proposed placement is based on the fact that that location is 1380 m from Gate 6 ( Ištar Gate ), which is the same distance to Gate 3 ( Šamaš Gate ) on the southeast wall, and 1665 m from Gate 2 ( Adad Gate ), which is equidistance to Gate 5 ( Ea Gate ) on the southwest wall .
description: The Mullissu Gate, which was given the Akkadian ceremonial name Mullissu-muddišat-ḫiṣbi ("The Goddess Mullissu Is the One Who Restores Abundance"), is the fourth of the eight city gates of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon") listed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) in inscriptions recording the construction of his new capital. This gate is the second of the north-facing entrances to the city.

title: Anu Gate
details: The Anu Gate is the first of Dūr-Šarrukīn’s two west-facing ( meḫret amurri ) gates. Because ‘west’ (Akkadian amurru ) can refer to both northwest and southwest in Akkadian sources, it is uncertain if the Anu Gate was located on the city’s northwest or southwest wall and, therefore, it is uncertain if that entranceway to Sargon II’s newly-constructed capital should be identified as Khorsabad Gate 6 , Gate 7 , or Citadel Gate B . Since one expects a plain gate to be dedicated to Anu, Gate 7 seems to be the most plausible suggested location for the Anu Gate; Gate 6 and Citadel Gate B are both grand, decorated entrances and, thus, seem unlikely to have been named after Anu.
description: The Anu Gate, which was given the Akkadian ceremonial name Anu-mušallim-epšēt-qātīya ("The God Anu Is the One Who Makes My Undertakings Successful"), is the fifth of the eight city gates of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon") listed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) in inscriptions recording the construction of his new capital. This gate is the first of the west-facing entrances to the city.

title: Sanctuary of Apollo
details: The statue is thought to have been erected in the seventh or early sixth century BC, with the throne/temple complex being created in the later sixth century. The only remaining part of the throne is the foundation, measuring four meters long and one meter high.
description: The Sanctuary of Apollo near Amyklai is a stoa-like building that enclosed a colossal statue of Apollo on three sides and was decorated with reliefs. The tomb of Hyacinthus is used as a statue base, combining the two local deities together.

title: Tell el-Ajjul
details: Significant amounts of volcanic pumice have been discovered at the site. These deposits may result from the Bronze Age eruption of the Thera (Santorini) volcano. Archaeological excavation at the site occurred in 1930-1934 under Sir Flinders Petrie. Excavations resumed in 1999 and 2000 but were then interrupted by Second Intifada.
description: Tell el-Ajjul was a fortified Bronze Age settlement located in what is now Gaza. Evidence from the site indicates economic interaction with ancient Egypt.

title: Ḥaḳala
description: A village in today's Amasya, Turkey. According to Mehmed Neşrî (Vol. 1, pp. 374-9 (1949)), Kara Devletşah, a commander in the Timurid Sultanate, stayed in this village and was defeated here or nearby by Bayezid I.

title: Tanda
description: 16th-century city of Bengal in South Asia

title: "The Great Basilica" at Butrint
details: Coordinates obtained by eye in Google Earth in September 2012 at an eye altitude of 94m. Dates follow www.butrint.org
description: The so-called "Great Basilica" is an early Christian basilica dating to the sixth century.

title: Church of St. Nicholas Orphanos
description: A fourteenth-century A.D. church in Thessalonica.

title: Cáparra amphitheater
description: The Roman amphitheater at Cáparra (Oliva de Plasencia, Spain).

title: Arco Augusteo di Siracusa
description: The remains of a Roman arch at Syracuse dated soon after the deduction of the Roman colony of 21 BCE.

title: Sirsukh
description: Sirsukh is a ruined urban center that forms part of the archaeological landscape at ancient Taxila (Punjab, Pakistan). This urban center may have been founded during the Kushan era at the end of the first century CE and represents the last of the ancient cities of Taxila.

title: Labyrinth of Knossos
name_variants: λαβύρινθον@grc | Labyrinthus@la | Labyrinthos | Labyrinthus | λαβύρινθον | Labyrinthus
description: Legendary, mythological labyrinth in the palace of Knossos built by mythic figure Daedalus to house the monster Minotaur.

title: Temple of Laodike
description: A temple dedicated to Laodike III, wife of the Seleucid king Antiochos III, at Laodike / Nemavand in Media, which is known from epigraphic evidence. The structure has not been decisively located, but individual archaeological finds suggest that it was located in the northwest of modern Nahavand in the Dokhaharan suburb (between Kucheh Derazeh, Pa Qaleh Square, and Hosseinieh Dokhaharan)

title: Forum of Segobriga
description: The Forum of Segobriga is traditionally dated to the early Iulio-Claudian period when Segobriga became a municipium.

title: Firronanus Saltus
name_variants: salt(us) Firronani@la | Firronanus Saltus | salt(us) Firronani
details: Transpadana (Regio XI)
description: The pontifex Lucius Coelius Baro is recorded as the curator of the Firronanus Saltus located in regio XI.

title: Via Labicana
name_variants: via Labicana@la | Via lauicana@la | via Labicana | uia Labicana | Labicana (via) | Labicana (uia) | Via Lavicana | via Labicana | Via lauicana
description: An ancient Roman road connecting Rome and Labicum.

title: Megali Koryfi
description: Megali Koryfi, an archaeological site on the island of Aegina in proximity to the Christian chapel of Ag. Antonios that is noted for the presence of substantial remains of drystone fortifications dating to the Mycenaean period.

title: Çayönü
description: Çayönü was a Neolithic settlement located in southern Turkey. Its remains date ca. 7200 to 6600 BC. The site spans the entire Pre-pottery Neolithic sequence and recent investigations suggest that Çayönü may be the site of the first domestication of the pig (Sus scrofa).

title: Ancient theater of Eretria
description: The Ancient Greek theater of Eretria is located inside the so-called West Gate of the city walls in the northwest sector of the city. It dates from ca. 400 B.C. to ca. 150 B.C.

title: Regio VI (Alta Semita)
description: The sixth administrative regio of Augustan Rome, Regio VI (Alta Semita) derives its name from the street that crossed over the Quirinal Hill. This is a large district that includes the Viminal Hill, the lower slopes of the Pincian Hill, in addition to the valleys between these hills. The region also contained 17 aediculae (shrines), 146 domūs (patrician houses), 18 horrea (warehouses), 75 bath houses, and 73 fountains.

title: Hagar Qin Megalithic Temple Complex (Malta)
description: Ħaġar Qim is a megalithic temple complex (ca. 3600-3200 BC), included in the UNESCO World Heritage List.

title: Esiskur
description: The New Year's (Akītu) temple of the god Marduk outside Babylon. The Sumerian ceremonial name Esiskur means "House of the Sacrifice."

title: Enunmah
details: The temple was rebuilt by the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus.
description: The ḫilṣu-building of the goddess Ningal inside the Egišnugal temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Enunmah means "House of the Exalted Prince."

title: Minor Acropolis, Norba
details: The "Tempio Maggiore" is only preserved at the platform level. This platform, executed in polygonal masonry, measures 22.8 by 12.9 meters. The plan was likely distyle. The "Tempio Minore" is also a rectangular platform temple and measures 16.5 by 8.16 meters.
description: The so-called Minor Acropolis is located on the hill to the south of the Porta Maggiore. This area is surrounded by the urban enclosure wall and is terraced in polygonal masonry. Two platform temples of unknown assignation are to be found here.

details: The Great Temple of Hera (or Polycrates temple) is the third temple to Hera at the Samian Heraion. Constructed by the tyrant Polycrates between 540 and 530 BCE, the temple measured 55.16 m x 108.63 m. The Ionic temple was built in a peristyle of at least 155, 20 m columns, which makes it one of the largest Greek temples built. The temple served as the hub for the cult of the Samian Hera and housed the xoanon — wooden cult statue — of Hera. During the Byzantine period, the temple was extensively quarried.

The region's name is derived from the Baloch people, who have inhabited the region since at least the ninth century CE. In antiquity, the southern part of the region, along the coast of the Arabian Sea, was known as Maka in the Achaemenid period and Gedrosia in the Hellenistic period.

title: Davti-blur
description: Davti-blur is the Armenian name of an Urartian settlement situated on a natural hill near the modern village Nor-Armavir. Just like the settlement on the immediately adjacent hill, Armavir, which in Urartian was called Argištihinili ("city of Argišti"), it was founded by Argišti I, son of Minua (8th century BCE). In Davti-Blur, a column base with an inscription of Argišti I was found, which reports the construction of a building. Furthermore, several inscriptions on clay pithoi by Argišti have been found there, which attest to the administrative activity at this place. A stone block of the Urartian king Sarduri II, son of Argišti I (8th century BCE), reveals that the place was further developed and extended by Sarduri II.

description: In a fill from various rooms of a private house (in area eA8V), excavators discovered an archive of 75 texts, belonging to Duri-Aššur and his business partners. The archive consists of letters, purchase and loan documents, divisions of inheritance, and other legal documents, as well as administrative lists. Most of these texts are concerned with trade. The available datings suggest that Duri-Aššur and his business partners were active in the trade north of Assur from 651 to the destruction of the city in 614 BC. Notably, some documents exemplify the financial independency of Egyptian women in Assur.

details: According to a text that might have been drawn up as an aide-memoire for Nebuchadnezzar II, the Babylonian king who completed the outer eastern wall of Babylon, the Madānu Canal Gate is the second of the five gates. The “ City Walls of Babylon C ” text records that there were twenty-six towers between it and the Šuhi Canal Gate (to the north) and twenty-nine between it and the Giššu Gate (to the south).
description: The Neo-Babylonian kings Nabopolassar (r. 625–605 BC) and Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–562 BC) constructed an outer wall around the eastern side of Babylon. That mudbrick wall is reported to have had 120 towers and 5 entrances, including the Madānu Canal Gate. This access point to the city was probably located on the eastern stretch of the wall.

It is not considered a member of the canonical grouping of Rome's hills, but it did lie within the line of the walls built by Aurelian. In the early Imperial period, it is known as a zone of elaborate gardens, hence the moniker "collis hortulorum".

details: The Odeon is located in the modern French city of Lyon, known during the Roman era as Lugdunum. Archaeologists believe it was built during the reign of Trajan or Hadrian around 100 CE. It is a small theater with about a 3,000 person capacity and was often confused with the amphitheater of the Three Gauls which archaeologists were attempting to find. The Odeon was excavated and restored multiple times, once between 1941 and 1946, and again from 1953 to 1958, and surveys were completed around it in 1991, 1994, and 2002. It is built of several different materials, including colored stones and granite imported from Egypt and several different shades of marble.
description: The Odeon is a small theater in modern day Lyon, France built specifically for musical performances around the beginning of the 2nd century CE.

title: Tuba
details: Tuba is the southern district of the eastern part of the western half of the inner city of Babylon. It is bounded by the Arahtu River on the east, by the Kumar district on the north, by the nu-x-ù district on the west, and by the walls Imgur-Enlil and Nēmetti-Enlil (with access in and out of the inner city by the Šamaš Gate ) on the south. According to Tintir = Babylon IV (lines 41–43), the temples Ekitušgarza, Esabad, and Ešiddukišara were located in this part of Babylon. According to Tintir = Babylon V (line 102), the southern and eastern limits of Tuba were the Šamaš Gate and the Arahtu River.
description: According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, Tuba was one of the four city districts of the western half of the inner city of Babylon and it contained three temples.

details: The gate is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib dating to 697-691 B.C. Some texts state that it was the first gate of the western stretch of wall, while others report that it was the fourth gate of the ten north- and west-facing gates. The position of the gate is known and it was excavated/restored in 1968-75. Around April 13, 2016, ISIS/ISIL demolished the Mašqû Gate.
description: Nineveh's western wall had seven (or eight) gates: the Mašqû Gate was the northernmost one. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it and gave it the Akkadian ceremonial name Ea-mušēšir-kuppīya, which means "The God Ea Is the One Who Properly Directs (Water Flow into) My Cisterns."

In that text, the Step Gate of the Palace is the second gate of the western stretch of wall; the gates are listed from north to south.
description: Nineveh's western wall had seven (or eight) gates: the Step Gate of the Palace was the second gate from the northern city wall. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it sometime between 694 and 691 B.C. and he gave it the Akkadian ceremonial name Libūr-ēpissa, which means "May Its Builder Endure." The gate is still unlocated, but, based on its everyday name Akkadian name mušlālum ša ēkalli ("Step Gate of the Palace"), it must have led up to Sennacherib's Palace on the citadel, perhaps up to the harem or its northern section.

description: An ancient Sumerian and Akkadian city in the Diyala Valley (modern Tell Asmar in Diyala Province, Iraq).

title: Santuario nuragico di Santa Vittoria
name_variants: Nuragic sanctuary of Santa Vittoria@en | Nuragic sanctuary of Santa Vittoria
description: A nuragic site near Serri, Sardinia, with a later phase of Christian re-use.

title: Cape Nara
description: Cape Nara or Nara Burnu is a headland on the Anatolian side of the Dardanelles Straits, north of Çanakkale, Turkey.

title: Benalúa
description: A late antique harbour site that is linked to the abandonment of the site of Lucentum.

title: Ribaniš
details: An inscription of Šamaš-reša-uṣur of Suhu mentions the city/town Ribaniš together with Alu-eššu, Baqa, and Qaqqar-aradātu. It is also mentioned in several inscriptions of Šamaš-reša-uṣur's successor Ninurta-kudurrī-uṣur.
description: An unlocated city/town in the kingdom of Suhu, probably not far from Alu-eššu, Baqa, and Qaqqar-aradātu.

title: Tholos of Athens
name_variants: Θόλος@grc | Tholos of Athens@en | ἡ Σκιάς@grc | Tholos | Tholos of Athens | hē Skiás | Θόλος | ἡ Σκιάς
description: The so-called "Tholos" located on the west side of the Athenian Agora was a circular civic building that took the place of archaic-period buildings associated with the Peisistratid tyrants. The Classical tholos served as a civic dining hall for the prytany council.

title: Little Farningham Roman iron production site
description: A Romano-British iron working site located in the East Sussex Weald.

title: Oppius Mons
description: The Oppian Hill is the southern spur of Rome's Esquiline Hill.

title: Banbhore
details: The submission for consideration for UNESCO World Heritage Site status notes: "... the site’s surface remains represent the best preserved early Islamic urban form in South Asia and the region’s best preserved mediaeval port."
description: Banbhore is located 65 km east of Karachi. Its sequence of occupation stretches from the first century BC to the thirteenth century AD.

title: "Ponte Sanguinario" at Spoletium
details: The remains of a Roman bridge lying beneath the pavement of the Piazza della Vittoria in Spoleto.
description: The "Ponte Sanguinario" at Spoleto is a late republican to early imperial Roman bridge. The remains of the bridge are now below street level in the Piazza della Vittoria, not far from the Porta San Gregorio.

title: Asklepieion at Eleusis
description: A sanctuary of Asklepios at Eleusis, established in the late 5th century BC and active through the Imperial era. It is known from finds of inscriptions and sculpture to have been located somewhere north of the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore, but the exact site is lost.

title: Yukarı Anzaf
description: Site for Urartian palace and citadel.

title: Stadium at Anazarbos
description: A stadium south of the city proper at Anazarbos (modern Dilekkaya in Turkey)

title: Tepeköy Höyük
description: Settlement in eastern Turkey containing signs of inhabitation dated to the Early Bronze Age. Rescue excavations were conducted at the site prior to its inundation by the Alpaslan-2 Reservoir in 2021.

title: Unnamed Gate of the Themistoklean Wall
description: A gate of the Themistoklean city wall of Athens, whose existence is inferred from a break in the moat to the east.

title: Pentrich
description: A Roman fortlet with a small rectangular earthwork lying within a larger enclosure.

title: Stadium Domitiani
name_variants: Stadium@la | Stadium of Domitian@en | Piazza Navona@it | Stadium | Stadium of Domitian | Piazza Navona | Stadium
description: Domitian built the Stadium Domitiani in the Campus Martius at Rome.

title: Tavoliere delle Puglie
name_variants: Tavoliere di Puglia@it | Tavoliere delle Puglie@it | Tavoliere di Puglia | Tavoliere delle Puglie
description: A plain of northern Apulia, the Tavoliere delle Puglie covers some 3,000 square kilometers. It is particularly noted as a landscape in which both settlement and ritual activity took place during the Neolithic period.

title: Funerary temple of Seti I
name_variants: Funerary temple of Seti I@en | Temple of a million years of Seti I@en | Temple funéraire de Séthi I@fr | Temple des millions d'années de Séthi Ier@fr | Funerary temple of Seti I | Temple of a million years of Seti I | Temple funéraire de Séthi I | Temple des millions d'années de Séthi Ier
description: Temple dedicated to the cult of King Seti I located on the west bank of Thebes.

title: Bāṣ
name_variants: Bāṣ@akk | Āl-Bāṣi@akk | Ša-Bāṣi@akk | Āl-Baṣṣi@akk | Ša-Baṣṣi@akk | Bāṣ | Āl-Bāṣi | Ša-Bāṣi | Āl-Baṣṣi | Ša-Baṣṣi
description: The unlocated Babylonian city is mentioned in cuneiform documents of the second and first millennia B.C. Information provided the texts seem to indicate that Baṣ, whose name might derive from the Akkadian word for sand, might be located somewhere near Sippar, perhaps close to the Euphrates River.

title: Kecharis
name_variants: Կեչառիսի վանական համալիր@hy | Kech’arrisi vanakan hamalir
description: Armenian monastery dated to the 11th-13th centuries CE.

title: Yrokastro castle
description: A ruined Medieval fortification on the island of Naxos.

title: Hermupolis
description: A place in Carmania, known only from literary sources.

title: Apesokari Tholos tomb A
description: Minoan tomb in the Mesara Plain in south-central Crete dated to the Early Minoan II period (ca. 2200-2050 BCE) and in use until the Middle Minoan III period (ca. 1750-1675 BCE).

title: Via Latina
name_variants: Via Latina@la | Λατινὴ ὁδός, ἡ@grc | Via Latina | Latine hodos | Λατινὴ ὁδός, ἡ | Via Latina
details: The road likely predates the construction of the Via Appia.
description: A Roman road running southeast from Rome toward Campania.

title: Stoke Hill
description: The site of a possible Roman signal station.

title: Delos Main Harbor
description: Recent geophysical investigation and analysis have led to a new reconstruction of the main harbor of Delos ca. 100 BCE that identifies a shallow-draft (1-2m) harbor with broad beach area significantly different from the modern situation. Infill of wetland areas for construction in antiquity, combined with contemporary and subsequent sea level rise, dredging, and modern interventions have all contributed to the coastline change.

title: Harappa
details: The archaeological site of Harappa was entered on the 'tentative' list by the UNESCO World Heritage Center in 2004.
description: A Bronze Age fortified city located on the Ravi River, inhabited from the fourth through the second millennia BCE, Harappa was one of the most important settlements of the Indus Valley Civilization.

title: Ponte Brabaciera
name_variants: Ponte Romano di Rio Brabaciera@it | Ponte Romano di Rio Brabaciera
description: A second-century Roman bridge on the Riu Brabaciera.

title: Matzanni
description: A sanctuary that includes a Punic temple built in white limestone, a nuraghe, and a sacred well.

title: Franchthi Cave
description: The Franchthi Cave is located on the Argolic Gulf in southeastern Argolis. The cave and the area outside its entrance (known as the Paralia) were occupied from the Paleolithic (ca. 20,000 BC) through to the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods, ultimately being abandoned ca. 3000 BC. The cave shows continuous human occupation for more than 20,000 years.

title: Adro Vello
details: Recent fieldwork has determined that during the third century CE, European sardines ( Sardina pilchardus ) were being used in the production of garum at the site.
description: The remains of a Roman villa and necropolis.

title: 'Awām
description: The ruins of the Sabaean temple dedicated to Almaqah and its associated burial ground are located near the town of Mārib, Yemen.

title: Roman amphitheater at Santa Maria Capua Vetere
description: Sometimes referred to as the "Anfiteatro Campano", the Roman amphitheater at Santa Maria Capua Vetere is the second largest in the Roman world. Begun under Augustus, it was further renovated under Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.

title: Grotto of the Sibyl
name_variants: L'antro della Sibilla@it | L'antro della Sibilla
description: A cave discovered by Amedeo Maiuri in 1932 and connected in the historical tradition with the Cumaean Sibyl. The site features in the sixth book of Virgil's Aeneid.

title: paleochristian basilica of Lugdunum Convenarum
description: The paleochristian basilica of Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges.

title: Valdonega Roman villa
description: The Roman villa of Valdonega near Verona dates to the first century A.D.

title: Filitosa
description: Filitosa is a megalithic site in southern Corsica that was in use from the Neolithic period until Roman times. A number of menhirs have been discovered at the site.

title: Araghju
description: A prehistoric site of the Torrean civilization in Corsica.

title: Sauve Pre-Roman oppidum
name_variants: Oppidum de Sauve@fr | Oppidum de Mus@fr | Mus à Sauve@fr | Oppidum de Sauve | Oppidum de Mus | Mus à Sauve
description: A pre-Roman and Gallo-Roman oppidum in the territory of the Volcae Arecomici.

title: Roman amphitheater at Egnatia/Gnathia
description: The so-called Roman amphitheater at Egnatia/Gnathia dates to the Iulio-Claudian period. It is an elliptical structure with walls in opus Africanum that were revetted with painted plaster.

title: Roman Town House, Dorchester
description: A Romano-British house located within Colliton Park, Dorchester, Dorset.

title: Roman amphitheater at Durno(no)varia
details: A Neolithic henge monument that was repurposed as a Roman amphitheater ca. AD 100.
description: The Neolithic henge known as Maumbury Rings was adapted for use as an amphitheater space during the Roman period.

title: Tert-Aba
description: Mound site in Khakassia containing burials associated with the Bronze Age Karasuk culture.

title: Tomb of Annedia and Lucius Caesius
description: The Tomb of Annedia and Lucius Caesius is an aedicula tomb in the Porta Nocera necropolis.

title: Temple of Vespasian
name_variants: Temple of Vespasian@en | Tempio di Romolo o di Quirino@it | Tempio di Mercurio@it | Tempio del Genio di Nerone@it | Augusteum@la | Templum or Aedes of the Genius Augusti@en | Templum of Vespasianus@en | VII.9.2@en | Temple of Vespasian | Tempio di Romolo o di Quirino | Tempio di Mercurio | Tempio del Genio di Nerone | Augusteum | Templum or Aedes of the Genius Augusti | Templum of Vespasianus | VII.9.2
description: The "Temple of Vespasian" (VII, 9, 2), also referred to as Aedes Genii Augusti, is situated between the Temple of the Lares Publici and the Building of Eumachia on the eastern side of the forum of Pompeii. Its precise attribution is still a matter of debate.

title: Castle Acre Castle
description: Medieval fortifications in Castle Acre, Norfolk, England.

title: Castle Rising Castle
name_variants: Castle Rising Castle@en | Castle Rising Castle
description: Castle Rising Castle is a ruined medieval castle located in Castle Rising, Norfolk, England. It was established by William d'Aubigny II ca. 1138.

title: Gremoulias ancient sanctuary
name_variants: Γκρεμουλάς@el | Γκρεμουλιάς@el | Gkremoulas | Gkremoulás | Gremoulás | Gremoulas | Gremoulias | Gkremoulias
description: A sanctuary -- with remains of at least two successive temples (6th C BCE and 4th C BCE), a great altar, and votive deposits -- located on the modern Gremoulias saddle, 3.5km SE of Kalavryta in the northern Peloponnese. The site is not known from ancient literature. Scholars speculate that the deity worshiped may have been Artemis and the site may have been an extra-urban sanctuary of nearby Kynaitha.

title: Doric Temple at Kardaki
description: An Archaic Greek temple at Corfu built in the Doric order ca. 500 B.C.

title: Dionysopolis
description: Attalos II and Eumenes II founded this city, and although its precise location is unknown today, it was located somewhere on the north bank of the Maeander River, near Çal Dag and the Çal Ova.

title: Tell Abu en-Ni'aj
description: Archaeological site in the Jordan Valley containing the remains of a village dated to the Early Bronze Age IV (ca. 2500-1900 BCE).

title: Norton Camp
description: The Iron Age Hillfort at Norton Camp is located near Taunton. It covers roughly 13 acres.

title: Bayon at Angkor Thom
description: A temple in the Khmer capital of Angkor Thom, constructed in the late 12th or early 13th century CE.

title: Divorum
description: A porticus constructed by Domitian in A.D. 80 on the eastern Campus Martius on the site of the Villa Publica, whose northern entry—a triumphal arch—was flanked by two small temples in honor of Titus and Vespasian.

title: Erimi Laonin tou Porakou
description: Settlement in the Kouris Valley (southwestern Cyprus) dated to the Middle Bronze Age (ca. 2500-1670 BCE).

title: Kerameikos
description: A district of ancient Athens located northwest of the Acropolis, the Kerameikos takes its name from the potters' workshops in the area; the portion of the district lying outside the Dipylon Gate served as a necropolis.

title: Pyramids of Meroe
name_variants: Pyramids of Meroe@en | Pyramids of Meroe
description: The pyramid tombs of the kings of the Kushite kingdom.

title: Atlit Yam
description: Atlit Yam is the site of an ancient submerged Neolithic village off the coast of Atlit, Israel, occupied during the final Pre-Pottery Neolithic B period.

title: Ǧidda
name_variants: Ǧidda@arb | Djedda@en | Cidde@ota | Ǧidda | Jidda | Jiddah | Jedda | Jeddah | Jadda | Jaddah | Djidda | Djiddah | Djedda | Djeddah | Cidde
details: GANE OBJECT 21537
description: A place from the TAVO Index

title: Roman forum of Iulium Carnicum
description: The Roman forum and civic basilica at Iulium Carnicum (modern Zuglio)

title: Grabbau 79 (Tuna el-Gebel)
description: A monumental burial structure in the so-called "Petosiris-Nekropole" at Tuna el-Gebel, excavated in 2021. Immediately north of the tomb, in the street area, stone basins supporting undisturbed lead coffins, as well as other associated burials, were found in situ.

title: Khentiamentiu, Temple of
description: An unexcavated Old Kingdom temple, attested by epigraphic finds at Abydos in Egypt. Its remains are presumed to underlie later Osiris sanctuary structures and part of the modern town.

title: Metroon at Olympia
description: Temple at Olympia constructed in the late 4th or early 3rd century BCE

title: antrum Cyclopis
description: A curious toponym that comes from the Regionary Catalogues for Regio I, the antrum (or atrium) Cyclopis is thought to have been a cave or grotto, perhaps in the flank of the Viminal Hill. It seems to lend its name to the vicus Cyclopis (CIL 6, 2226) that ran south and west to join the via Appia.

title: Tomb of Marcus Servilius Quartus
description: A Roman tomb on the Via Appia dating ca. A.D. 100.

title: Torre Maggiore
description: A place located at the 21st km of the via Ardeatina, Torre Maggiore is likely built on the site of a domusculta and is connected to key Roman families, including the Savelli, Altieri, Capodiferro, Serlupi, and Maddaleni families. The tower has a square plan and rises to 34 meters.

title: So-called 'Tomb of Cicero' at Formiae
description: A 24-meter tall tower tomb on the Via Appia at Formiae is traditionally considered as a possible location of the Tomb of Cicero.

title: Sarantaporo ancient settlement
description: Located just east of modern Sarantaporo in the Elassona municipality (Larisa, Greece), this ancient settlement was excavated in the late 20th century. Its excavators proposed an identification with ancient Doliche, which previously had been only provisionally located. It may represent the original seat of Doliche. The late-antique fortified site at Kastri Livadiou (q.v.) seems to have made use of spoliated material including an inscription that names Doliche as a polis.

title: Punta della Vipera Etruscan temple
details: Mario Torelli conducted excavations at the site from 1964 to 1967. The votive deposits from the site are of particular importance. The temple, measuring 7.80 by 11.8 meters, is oriented to the southwest and was sacred to Minerva. The site was abandoned by the first century B.C.
description: A coastal Etruscan sanctuary that dates ca. 540-530 B.C. with additional architectural phases dating to the fourth through second centuries B.C.

title: Column of Julian
description: The Column of Julianus, ca. 362 CE, honors the military exploits of the Roman Emperor Julian.

title: Stary Sad
name_variants: Старый Сад@ru | Stary Sad | Staryĭ Sad
description: Bronze and Iron Age burial ground in the Baraba forest-steppe containing 75 burials of the Pakhomovka culture (late second millennium BCE), plus additional burials from the Andronovo culture (ca. 2200-900 BCE) and Sargat culture (ca. 500-250 BCE).

title: House of Leda and the Swan
name_variants: House of Leda and the Swan@en | House of Leda and the Swan
description: The so-called House of Leda and the Swan at Pompeii (Regio V 6,12) is located along the street referred to as Via del Vesuvio. The domus is well-appointed with Fourth Style wall paintings.

title: Baqa
details: An inscription of Šamaš-reša-uṣur of Suhu mentions the city/town Baqa together with Alu-eššu, Qaqqar-aradātu, and Ribaniš.
description: An unlocated city/town in the kingdom of Suhu, probably not far from Alu-eššu, Qaqqar-aradātu, and Ribaniš.

title: Woodhenge
description: Woodhenge is the site of a "Neolithic Class II henge and timber circle monument" located within the Stonehenge UNESCO World Heritage Site in Wiltshire, England. It is located approximately 2 miles (3.2 km) northeast of Stonehenge (Durrington parish).

title: Durrington Walls
description: Durrington Walls is an archaeological site located 2 miles (3.2 km) north-east of Stonehenge (parish of Durrington, Amesbury,Wiltshire). A large Neolithic settlement and a later henge enclosure were located at Durrington Walls and used in the later third millennium BCE. This site is considered to be part of the Stonehenge World Heritage Site in England.

title: Meluhha
description: A Middle Bronze Age trading partner of Sumer, perhaps located in the Indus valley.

title: Catacombs of Commodilla
name_variants: Catacombe di Commodilla@it | Catacombe di Commodilla
description: A catacomb along the Via Ostiensis that contains, among other wall paintings, the earliest depiction of a bearded Jesus Christ.

title: Yibna Bridge
description: The Mamluk arched bridge dating to the 1270s crosses the river Nahal Sorek near modern Yibna, Israel.

title: Mahalibeh Castle
description: Mahalibeh Castle in Syria dates to the 11th century. The castle was surrendered to al-Zahir Ghazi, the son of Saladin, by 1194.

title: Torcularium villa
name_variants: Villa romana del Torcularium@it | Villa romana del Torcularium
description: A Roman villa of the early second century BCE, constructed in opus incertum and so named because of the presence of a torcularium.

title: Temple of Fortuna Augusta
name_variants: Tempio della Fortuna@it | Temple of Victory@en | Aedes of Fortuna Augusta@en | Temple of Serapis@en | VII.4.1@la | Tempio della Fortuna | Temple of Victory | Aedes of Fortuna Augusta | Temple of Serapis | VII.4.1 | VII.4.1
details: The temple was dedicated by the duumvir , Marcus Tullius. Sanctuaries dedicated to Fortuna Redux were built in Rome and other Italian cities following Augustus's return from his expeditions of 19-13 BC.
description: A Corinthian order temple in Pompeii dedicated to Fortuna Redux and likely dating to the late first century BC (VII, 4, 1).

title: Penydarren Roman fort
description: A Roman fort built ca. 74-78 CE and occupied no later than the first third of the second century, now built over by a sports stadium.

title: Pons Neronianus
description: A bridge across the Tiber river built either by Caius or Nero in order to connect the western part of the Campus Martius with the Campus Vaticanus.

title: Srah Srang
description: Large baray or reservoir at Angkor constructed in the 10th century CE.

title: Purṭir
details: Purṭir is mentioned together with Anduarsalla, Anmurru, Kiaka, and Luhsu in royal inscriptions of Sargon II. E. Forrer ( Die Provinzeinteilung des assyrischen Reiches [1920] 75 and Map 2) identifies Purṭir with Puteyrlu, a place ca. 7 km southwest of classical Zimara.
description: A fortress in the vicinity of Til-garimmu fortified by the Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721-705 BC) against Urarṭu.

title: Knaresborough
description: The Knaresborough hoard was discovered in 1864. It contained the largest hoard of Romano-British copper-alloy vessels discovered to date in Roman Britain.

title: Ehulhul
description: The temple of the god Sîn at Harran. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ehulhul means "House which Gives Joy."

title: Egipar
description: The Giparu-House at Ur was the temple of the high-priestess of the moon-god.

title: Charterhouse Warren Farm Shaft
description: The Charterhouse Warren Farm Shaft is a vertical shaft (approximately 20 meters deep) in the Carboniferous limestone plateau of the Mendip Hills, Somerset, southwest England. Originally identified as a swallet, this cave feature was the site of archaeological excavations in 1972-6 and again in 1983-6. The site has produced evidence of several stratigraphic horizons and, notably, a number of disarticulated human and faunal remains. The human remains come from at least 37 Bronze Age individuals and their demise seems to have been the result of deliberate violence.

title: Agora Mint
name_variants: Mint@en | Agora Mint@en | Mint | Agora Mint
description: A building in the southeast corner of the Agora of Athens, built in the late fifth century BC, which was used for minting bronze coinage from the third century BC until it was abandoned in the first century BC.

title: Arch of Lucius Neratius Priscus
description: An arch dedicated to Lucius Neratius Priscus, suffect consul of A.D. 97 and governor of Germania Inferior.

title: Arch of Trajan
description: An arch dedicated to Trajan on the Via Flaminia at Carsulae, also known as the Arco di San Damiano.

title: Gymnasium at Corinth
name_variants: ἀρχαῖον γυμνάσιον (τὸ)@grc | arkaion gymnasion (to) | ἀρχαῖον γυμνάσιον (τὸ)
description: The Gymnasium of the Roman period at Corinth was excavated by the University of Texas and the American School of Classical Studies beginning in 1965. It is possible that Hellenistic and Classical phases preceded the Roman phase, although evidence is scanty.

title: Sintashta
description: Bronze Age archaeological site east of the Ural Mountains. The type site of the Sintashta Culture, it was inhabited from approximately 2800-1600 BCE.

title: Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum
name_variants: Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum@la | Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum
description: The Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum is a place in ancient Rome that is mentioned only in the Regionary Catalogue for Regio III. It was likely located between the lacus Pastorum and the Baths of Titus. While the name and place remain obscure, related epigraphic evidence attests to collegia of caplatores, men who pressed olive oil.

title: Ostia Synagogue
description: The ancient synagogue located in Ostia Antica is one of the oldest known synagogues in the world. The structure's earliest phase dates to the reign of Claudius and it continued in use until the fifth century.

title: Roman theater of Catania
description: The Roman theater of Catania was built in the second century CE and remained in use until the fifth or sixth century. It could accommodate approximately 7,000 spectators.

title: Theater at Heraclea Minoa
description: The Theater at Heraclea Minoa dates to the late fourth century B.C.

title: Currapho
description: Currapho, a place in Mesopotamia included on the Peutinger map.

title: Theater at Bodrum
description: The Theater at Bodrum is dedicated to Ares.

title: Alba Fucens Aqueduct
name_variants: Acquedotto romano di Alba Fucens@it | Acquedotto romano di Alba Fucens
description: The Alba Fucens Aqueduct is a Roman aqueduct dating from the later first century BCE.

title: Puente Melchor Roman villa
details: The mosaic assemblage includes a significant pavement depicting Bacchus / Dionysus.
description: A Roman villa with mosaic decoration located in an archaeological area of Puente Melchor, in Puerto Real, Cádiz, Spain.

title: El Gallinero
description: The remains of a Roman ceramic workshop and manufactory.

title: Fonte Coberta
description: A Roman dam

title: Monte Novo do Castelinho
description: A Roman earthen embankment dam of ca. 56 m length.

title: Roman amphitheater of Venusia
description: A Roman amphitheater dating to the first and second centuries.

title: Kraneion Early Christian Basilica
description: An Early Christian Basilica located near the grove of Kraneion that dates to the sixth century CE.

title: Talianki
description: Talianki or Talianky is an archaeological site of the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture located near the village of the same name in Cherkasy Oblast, Ukraine. The large settlement dates ca. 3850–3700 BCE.

title: Susegana bridge
details: The remains of three Roman bridges on the river Piave about 29 km north of Treviso along the line of the Via Claudia Augusta. These bridges are evident at Colfosco.
description: A Roman bridge along the Via Claudia Augusta.

title: Arx of Cosa
details: The first American excavations of the Arx (1948-1950) conducted by Frank Edward Brown eventually revealed the remains of three sanctuaries, including the monumental Capitolium temple of the colonial town. In addition to these shrines, Brown excavated a ritual pit that he identified as the mundus of the colony.
description: The citadel of the ancient city and location of its Capitolium.

title: Comitium of Poseidonia/Paestum
description: The comitium is a component of a monumental forum complex constructed at Paestum after the city became a Latin colony in 273 B.C.

title: Mithraeum of Lucretius Menander
name_variants: Mithraeum of Lucretius Menander@en | Mitreo di Lucrezio Menandro@it | Mithraeum of Lucretius Menander | Mitreo di Lucrezio Menandro
description: The Mithraeum of Lucretius Menander located in ancient Ostia dates to the third century CE.

title: Alaybeyi Höyük
description: Settlement in eastern Anatolia containing signs of habitation from the Chalcolithic age (ca. 4700 BCE) to the Iron Age (ca. 400 BCE), including a large number of remains associated with the Kura-Araxes Culture.

title: Sacred Area of S. Omobono
name_variants: Area Sacra di Sant'Omobono@it | Area Sacra di Sant'Omobono
description: An archaeological area in the Forum Boarium comprising an ancient ritual precinct with twin temples ranging in date from the Archaic period through the time of the Roman Empire. The Medieval church dedicated to S. Omobono stands atop the remains of one of the two ancient temples.

title: Brusdorciani
description: An ancient people whose territory was located in Thrace on the Hebros near Adrianople.

title: Darsa
description: An ancient city in Pisidia.

title: Costedt Roman Cemetery
description: A Roman cemetery was excavated in the late 20th century at modern Costedt in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

title: Ancient Stadium of Rhodes
details: The ancient stadium of the city of Rhodes was constructed during the 2nd century BC. It is located on the acropolis adjacent to an odeon and near a gymnasium, a theater, and the sanctuary of Apollo Pythios. The stadium, which is one stadion (600ft or 200m) long, was used for sporting events like the footrace, and probably for other entertainments as well. The stadium was excavated and restored by an Italian team during the early 20th century, but very little archaeological work has been done on this site since then. Currently, the only original parts of the stadium which are preserved are the sphendone (rounded end with turning post), the proedries (seats of honor), and a few rows of seats in the auditorium.
description: The Hellenistic Stadium on the Acropolis of Rhodes.

title: Wiveliscombe Auxiliary Fort
description: A Roman auxiliary fort located near Nunnington Park, Wiveliscombe.

title: Scratchbury Camp
details: As with many Iron Age sites, the chronology of Scratchbury Camp has been debated. Multi-period reuse of hill forts often makes precise dating difficult, if not impossible. Some Pre-Roman Iron Age sites in Britannia saw re-use following the Roman conquest.
description: Scratchbury Camp, Wiltshire, England, is the site of a 15 hectare hill fort.

title: Temple of Zeus at Cyrene
details: The Temple of Zeus at Cyrene is located on the northeastern hill of the city, near the modern village of Shahhat. Perhaps because of the bulk of its collapsed remains, this Temple has remained one of the least studied of all the great temples of the Hellenic world. The date of the building's construction is highly disputed, with some scholars arguing that the temple was built at some point in the 5th century, while others view its Archaic Doric design and style as an indicator that the Temple was in fact built in the 6th century. Jewish rebels destroyed the Temple in 115 AD, undercutting and overturning the columns of the surrounding peristasis, which were never re-erected. The temple is most notable for its size and complexity. Measuring 70 by 32 meters, it was larger than the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, and its cella was surrounded by two rows of columns, with 8 columns in each row at the front and back and 17 along the sides. The temple also displays Doric refinements: for example, the Greek architects constructed the columns to lean slightly inwards, correcting some of the effects of perspective.
description: The Doric Temple of Zeus at Cyrene.

title: Aetolian League
description: Based in Aetolia in central Greece, the Aetolian League was founded in the Hellenistic period to counter the power of Macedon and the Achaean League. It was allied with Rome in the First Macedonian War (215-205 BCE), but later was opposed to the republic in Rome's war against Antiochos (192–188 BCE). After Rome's victory in 188, the Aetolian League was fully subordinate to Rome.

title: Achaean League (Second)
description: Established in 280 BCE, the second Achaean League was centered in the northern and central Peloponnese. Allied to Rome in the Second Macedonian War (200-196 BCE), the league extended its control over all of the Peloponnese. In the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BCE), the League's relationship with Rome deteriorated; in ca. 146 BCE, this led to open warfare, which resulted in the defeat and dissolution of the league.

title: Empulum
details: Empulum was an outlying town connected to Tibur. The Romans captured it ca. 355 B.C. It may have been a fortified site. Both Gell and Nibby discussed the site, connecting it with the locality of Ampiglione, along the road to Ciciliano in Lazio, some 35 km east of Rome. The nineteenth-century commentators remark that this fortified site has evidence of "polygonal work", i.e., polygonal masonry, executed in tuff, something that even Smith (1854) remarks upon as being unusual since polygonal masonry is typically executed in calcareous stone, notably limestone. Giovenale (1900, fig. 6) describes these walls as "polyhedric megalithic" and notes that they employ a lithoid tuff as would be expected for this part of Latium.

title: Carzield

Fragments of clay tablets and inscribed prisms in these niches suggest that a temple library was located here. The empty niches might be a result of the move of the capital to Nineveh under Sennacherib (704–681 BC) or of the use of perishable writing materials.

title: Achutrajpur

title: Roman quarry of Antas

title: Dur-Bel-Harran-belu-uṣur
name_variants: Tell Abtah@ar | Dūr-Bēl-Harrān-bēlu-uṣur@akk | تل عبطة@ar | Tell Abtah | Dūr-Bēl-Harrān-bēlu-uṣur | Tall ‘Abṭah

The creation of the city took place during Shalmaneser IV's reign.

title: Madonna del Parto

title: Stoidis (island)

title: Solucar Albayda

title: Munychia

title: Sanctuary of Apollo Ismenios, Thebes
details: The establishment of the cult is dated to the 8th century BC, while the ruins that are visible today are dated to the 4th century BC. Only the west end of the krepis foundations is still visible. The sanctuary of Apollo Ismenios, on the namesake hill, was an important oracle. Divinations were given by observing the flame, smoke, and ash of the sacrifices. In its heyday, many devotees consulted the oracle, among them King Kroisos (Lat. Croesus) of Lydia. Pindar refers to a treasury of gold tripods, emphasising the wealth of the votive offerings. A boy with two living parents served annually as priest and led the procession of the Daphnephoria festival from the city to the temple, holding a laurel branch. Orientation: The temple is oriented approximately east–west at 98°±1° (skyline altitude is 4° on a nearby horizon). To the west, at 278°±1°, Mount Helicon is well visible.
description: At Thebes, the foundations of a Doric temple dating to the Archaic and Classical periods were excavated by the American School of Classical Studies in 2015-6.

name_variants: Eʾesirkalama@sux | bīt Pisangunuk@akk | Eʾesirkalama | bīt Pisangunuk
