title: Holme Roman temporary camp
description: A Roman marching camp covering 9.3 ha.

title: Pasas (island)
description: A small island that is part of the Oinoussai island group, located between Chios and the Ionian peninsula. Its ancient name is unknown.

title: Maltepe Tumulus
description: The Maltepe Tumulus is located in Manole, Bulgaria. The tumulus measures 125 – 130 m in diameter and some 21 m in height.

title: Seleukeia on the Euphrates and the Royal Canal
description: A city in Babylonia on the Euphrates, mentioned in Babylonian texts of the third century BC and possibly to be identified with Sippar.

title: Mettet
description: A Gallo-Roman villa located in the vicinity of Bauselenne.

title: Dereüstü
name_variants: Dereüstü@tr | Anzav@ku | Dereüstü | Anzav | Anzaf | Anzak
description: Find spot for fragmentary stele with Urartian inscription.

title: Roman theater at Salamis/Konstantia
description: Salamis remained an important city of Cyprus during the Roman period and the theater is one part of a complex of monumental architecture there.

title: Sam'al
name_variants: Samʾalla@akk | Zincirli Hüyük@tr | Samʾal@akk | Samʾallāja@akk | Samʾalāja@akk | Samʾalla | Zincirli Huyuk | Samʾal | Samʾallāja | Samʾallāya | Samʾalāja | Samʾalāya
description: A Hittite and Aramaean city located at Zincirli Höyük in the Anti-Taurus mountains. The site appears in Neo-Assyrian sources as Samʾalla and Aramaic texts as šmʿl (also yʾdy). It is identified with the modern site of Zincirli.

title: Royal Stoa
name_variants: Royal Stoa@en | Stoa Basileios@en | στοὰ βασίλειος@grc | Royal Stoa | Stoa Basileios | stoa basileios | στοὰ βασίλειος
description: The Stoa Basileios or Royal Stoa was an important Doric-order stoa originating in the sixth century BCE and located at the northwest corner of the Athenian Agora. It was the administrative seat of the magistrate known as the archon basileus ("king archon").

title: Temple of Magna Mater
name_variants: Temple of Cybele (Palatine)@en | Magna Mater@la | Temple of Cybele (Palatine) | Magna Mater | aedes
description: The Temple of Magna Mater, also known as the Temple of Cybele, was dedicated near the Clivus Victoriae on the Palatine Hill on 11 April 191 BCE. The original temple was destroyed by fire in 111 BCE. Following another series of destructive fires, Augustus restored the temple, as he records in his Res Gestae Divi Augusti.

title: Bidoni
name_variants: Bidoni, Tempio di Giove@it | Bidoni | Tempio di Giove
description: A monumental sanctuary (26 x 20 m) dedicated to Iuppiter.

title: Burmarina
name_variants: تل الشيوخ فوقاني@ar | Tall al-Shiyūkh Fūqānī
description: Minor settlement in Upper Syrian Euphrates.

title: Barç
description: A hilltop archaeological site in southeastern Albania, presently named after the adjacent modern village, that lies less than 2km northeast of modern Korça. Its precise nature is not yet known, but earlier suggestions that it was a burial mound have been refuted by the discovery of significant stone walls and small finds datable to the Iron Age and possibly the Hellenistic period.

title: Temple of Vespasian and Titus
name_variants: Templum divi Vespasiani@la | Templum divi Vespasiani
description: A temple in the Roman Forum dedicated to the deified Vespasian that was begun by Titus and completed under Domitian.

title: Ma’allanate Archive 1
description: An archive, sold on the antiquities market, can be located at Ma’allanate. The site has not been precisely identified, but two suggestions have been made regarding its location. The first situates it in the upper Balikh valley, northern Syria, while the other places it further east, on the Habur River between Tell Halaf/Guzana and Al-Hasakah. Recent opinion favours the first location. 49 cuneiform tablets have been attributed to Ma’allanate. These are mostly written in Assyrian, but three use Babylonian script and dialect. In addition to these texts, 24 documents are written in Aramaic. The archive belonged to Ḫandi, who had the title “steward of the palace“and was active from 700 to 665 BC, his son Ḫarranayu, who was active from 661 to 644 BC, and Ser-nuri, active from 652 to 622 BC. The relationship between Ser-nuri and the father and son is unclear. The archive contains loan documents of silver and barley, payments of loans, purchase documents of slaves and land, and other documents.

title: Byzantine Bath
description: A thirteenth/fourteenth century Byzantine bath at Thessalonica; listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

title: Roman theater of Suasa
description: The Roman theater of Suasa was discovered in 2003 during excavations near the amphitheater. The semicircular structure measures ca. 55 meters in diameter and dates to the first century A.D.

title: Kizkapanli
description: A modern village near the Pazarcik dam in Turkey. The Pazarcik Stele, which bears inscriptions of the Assyrian kings Adad-nerari III and Shalmaneser IV, was discovered here.

title: Afas Lupeici
name_variants: Afas Lvpeici@la | Afas Lupeici | Afas Lvpeici
description: Afas Lupeici is a place included on the Tabula Peutingeriana. It was situated roughly 10 miles to the south of Martae and 5 miles to the north of Augarmi.

title: Spolverino, Alberese
description: An archaeological site of the Roman period connected with the fluvial harbor of Rusellae.

title: Caselle in Pittari
name_variants: Caselle in Pittari@it | Caselle in Pittari
description: An ancient Lucanian settlement located within the territory of the comune of Caselle in Pittari has been explored via archaeological excavation since 2014. This site occupies parts of a large plateau. Evidence for an axial road running north-south and several large structures has been documented.

title: Anavyssos
description: Anavyssos, Greece, is the findspot of the kouros of Kroisos, a fallen warrior. The kouros dates ca. 530–520 B.C. and is housed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens (inv. no. 3851). The kouros was discovered in 1936.

title: Palea Kameni
description: Palea Kameni is the smaller of the two volcanogenic islands in the centre of the Santorini caldera, formed over the last two millennia. It was most likely formed before or during the major period of volcanic activity in A.D. 1866-1870.

title: Zas Cave
name_variants: Cave of Zas (Naxos)@en | Cave of Zas (Naxos)
description: A sacred cave located on Mt. Zas on the island of Naxos, Zas Cave preserves evidence of human occupation ranging from the Late Neolithic period to the Early Cycladic III period. Local tradition holds that the sky god Zeus hid from Cronus in the cave. Rock cuttings in the area refer to "Zeus Melosios".

title: Tavşan Tepe Tümülüsü
name_variants: Tavsan Tepe Tumulus@en | Tavsan Tepe Tumulus
description: The Tavşan Tepe Tümülüsü is a tumulus at Pergamon included in the UNESCO World Heritage site "Pergamon and its Multi-Layered Cultural Landscape".

title: Capitolium Vetus
description: The Capitolium Vetus was located on the Quirinal Hill and was an earlier shrine to the triad of Iuppiter, Juno, and Minerva than the famous Capitoline Temple. It was likely perched on the northern edge of the Quirinal.

title: Pyramid of Cestius
name_variants: Piramide di Caio Cestio@it | Piramide di Caio Cestio
description: An ancient pyramid-shaped tomb built for Caius Cestius (ca. 18-12 BC), a magistrate and member of the Septemviri Epulonum. The tomb stands at the fork of the ancient Via Ostiensis and was later incorporated into the city's fortifications.

title: Andalucía (region)
description: The region of Andalucía (Andalusia in English), located in the south of Spain, is the second largest and the most populous region of modern Spain. At one time it belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X. Much of the modern region is coincident with the extent of ancient Baetica.

title: *Atuna (kingdom)
name_variants: Tunāja@akk | Atunāja@akk | Tunāja | Tunāya | Atunāja | Atunāya
details: The name in Assyrian inscriptions is known only from ethnic names. The capital of this kingdom in Tabal was also called *Atuna, a city often identified as classical Tynna . The identification of * Atuna is not entirely certain and it has been suggested that the city was in the vicinity of Bohça, at Kızılırmak-Bogen, ca. 40 km west of Kayseri, since a Luwian inscription of Kurtis was discovered there; Kurtis might be the Kurtî of *Atuna mentioned in inscriptions of Sargon II (r. 721-705 BC).
description: A kingdom in Tabal mentioned in royal inscriptions of the Assyrian kings Tiglath-pileser III (r. 744-727 BC) and Sargon II (r. 721-705 BC).

title: *Atuna
name_variants: Atunāja@akk | Tunāja@akk | Atunāja | Atunāya | Tunāja | Tunāya
details: The city is mentioned in royal inscriptions of the Assyrian kings Tiglath-pileser III (r. 744-727 BC) and Sargon II (r. 721-705). Two locations have been suggested for the city *Atuna: (1) in the vicinity of Bozça (Boh ça) , on the Kızılırmak river, ca. 40 km west of Kayseri; and (2) in the vicinity of Porsuk/Zeyve Hüyük. The latter is based on the proposed location of classical Tynna, a city that might be identified with *Atuna. For further details, see the Place Resource for T ynna/Dana? .
description: *Atuna is the capital of the kingdom *Atuna in Tabal.

title: Crocifisso del Tufo necropolis
name_variants: Necropoli di Crocifisso del Tufo@it | Necropoli di Crocifisso del Tufo

title: Unnamed Roman bridge
description: A Roman bridge crossing the Rio Mannu stream in Sardinia.

title: Abu Sir

description: A small but tall settlement mound located in the Jordan Valley with archaeological remains from the eighth-fourth centuries BCE.

name_variants: Monastère de la Vierge Kosmosoteira@fr | Θεοτόκος η Κοσμοσώτειρα@el | Μονή Παναγίας Κοσμοσώτειρας@el | Thometor Kosmosoteira@grc | Monastère de la Vierge Kosmosoteira | Theotokos i Kosmosoteira | Moní Panagías Kosmosóteiras | Thometor Kosmosoteira

title: Al-Aqsa Mosque
name_variants: Beyt-i Maḳdis@ota | Mescid-i Aksa Camii@tr | Al-Aqsa Mosque@en | Beyt-i Maḳdis | Beyt-i Maqdis | Mescid-i Aksa Camii | Al-Aqsa Mosque

title: Spera

title: Aloquaz
description: A Spanish village located in the south of the province of Sevilla, between Sevilla and Cádiz, that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X. It is now known as Torres de Alocaz.

title: 'Ein Gedi
description: A Ghassulian public building dating ca. 3500 B.C. near the oasis of Ein Gedi on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

title: Unnamed Roman bridge
description: A Roman bridge on the Rio Murtazzolu near Birori, Sardinia.

title: Tell Abu Hafur
name_variants: Tell Abu Hafur@en | Tell Abu Hafur
description: Tell Abu Hafur is an archaeological site located in the Khabur River basin of Syria. Salvage excavations in 1988–1990 documented the site, which had two main tells. These mounds and the evidence for human activity there ranged in date from the Early Dynastic period to the Mitanni period to the Neo-Assyrian period, with later Hellenistic, Parthian-Roman, and early Islamic activity.

title: Fosso Saina
description: A minor tributary of the Anio river in the vicinity of Guidonia.

title: Litana Silva
details: According to Smith, the forest was likely located between Bononia and Placentia, although its precise position cannot be determined today. Peyre places it between Parma and Reggio.

title: Via Egnatia

title: Bougon

title: Tomba dei Leoni Ruggenti
name_variants: Tomba dei Leoni Ruggenti@it | Tomba dei Leoni Ruggenti

title: Unnamed fortification

title: Īzah
description: Central mound of the modern town of Īzah where artifacts of Elamite date were found in excavations 1976.

title: Tomb of Caecilia Agathia
details: The tomb's inscription reads "Caecilia Agathia and Caecilius Dioscurides Caecilia Agathia, freedwoman of Lucius, in her lifetime constructed this for herself and for Lucius Caecilius Dioscurides, freedman of Lucius, her husband". AE 1990 (1993), 177a.

title: Cayla

title: Castellammare della Bruca
name_variants: Castellammare della Bruca@it | Castellum Velie@akk | Castellammare della Bruca | Castellum Velie
description: A fortified medieval settlement that succeeds the acropolis of ancient Velia.

title: Villa romana de Salar
description: A villa with polychrome mosaics, dating from the first to the fifth centuries. It is located at modern Salar, in the Spanish province of Granada.

title: Yığma Tepe Tumulus
name_variants: Yigma Tepe Tumulus@en | Yigma Tepe Tumulus
description: The Yığma Tepe Tumulus is the largest ancient tumulus in the vicinity of Pergamon.

title: Chughā Sabz
name_variants: چغا سبز@fa | Chughā Sabz | Chigha Sabz
description: A mound where a cuneiform inscription has been found.

title: Tall Dāmiyā
description: Iron Age site in the Central Jordan Valley, sometimes identified with the historical place Adama.

title: Bani Walid
name_variants: بني وليد@ar | Bani Walid | Beni Ulid
description: A modern city in Libya's Misratah province on the western edge of which Roman milestones and funerary inscriptions have been found removed from their original positions as part of modern agricultural activity. The local museum holds artistic and architectural artifacts from a number of nearby locations.

title: Old Oswestry
description: Old Oswestry is an Iron Age hill fort located in northwest Shropshire, England.

title: Temple complex at Kommos
description: Multi-phase temple site in the city of Kommos in southern Crete. Temple A was constructed by the late 11th century CE. A larger structure, Temple B, was built over it in the 9th century CE. The temple complex reached its maximum extent when Temple C was built over the site and its surroundings in the 7th century CE.

title: al-Jazirah (region)
name_variants: الجزيرة@arb | ܓܙܪܬܐ@syr | Al-Jazīrah | al-Jazira | al-Djazirah | al-Djezirah | Gāzarta | Gāzarāta | Gozarto
description: The northern portion of the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers is known today as Upper Mesopotamia. The area, extending from the mountains of eastern Anatolia in the north to the Tharthar Depression (northwest of Baghdad) in the south, is an alluvial plain that formed an important crossroads region in the ancient and medieval periods. Major settlements of the region in the early Islamic period include Ar-Raqqah and Edessa.

title: Acropolis of Selinus
description: The fortified Acropolis of Selinus in Rough Cilicia.

title: Avenches Roman amphitheater
name_variants: Amphithéatre d'Avenches, Amphitheatre d'Avenches@fr | Amphithéatre d'Avenches
description: The Avenches Roman amphitheater.

title: Roman Theater of Side
description: The Roman Theater of Side dates to the second century CE.

title: Temple of Apollo (Side)
description: A Roman temple at Side dating to the reign of Antoninus Pius.

title: Nea Kameni
description: In the present-day caldera, Nea Kameni is the larger of the two volcanogenic islands formed over the last two millennia. It is a geological successor of Cameini, and was likely formed before, or during, the major period of volcanic activity in 1866-1870.

title: Roman theater of Privernum
description: The Roman theater of Privernum is attested mainly by means of epigraphic evidence.

title: Lio Piccolo Roman Villa
description: A probable Roman villa site at Lio Piccolo in the Venice lagoon, with a well-preserved, first-century oyster tank made of brick and wood.

title: Quarries at Aquae Albulae
description: Travertine quarries in the vicinity of Tibur and Aquae Albulae.

title: Triconch Palace at Butrint
description: The so-called Triconch Palace.

title: Achilleion

title: Ancient harbour (submerged) at Aegina
description: Archaeological remains of Aegina's military harbor.

title: Ancient sanctuary at Marion
description: An Iron Age sanctuary located at Peristeries in Polis Chrysochous, Cyprus, dedicated to the female goddess of Cyprus that was in use for half a millennium, from ca. 950 to ca. 450 BCE.

title: Turlu Höyük
description: Tell Turlu (Turlu Höyük) is ca. 7 km northwest of Nizip (Gaziantep Province, Turkey), near the modern village Turlu. In 2003, a basalt stele of the Assyrian official Bēl-iddin (reign of Sargon II; r. 721–705 BC) was discovered there. The ancient name of this large site, which was occupied in the Neolithic Period, is not known.

title: Sant'Andrea Catabarbara
description: Sant'Andrea Catabarbara was a church located in Rome; it was dedicated to Saint Andrew. It likely succeeds the fourth-century CE civil basilica known as the Basilica of Iunius Bassus, via the patronage of the Goth general Valila. Its remains were demolished in 1930 and its site is now occupied by the Pontifical Oriental Institute on Via Napoleone III, in the Esquilino district.

title: Castellaccio Europarco
description: A villa and a number of burials located along the Via Laurentina, dating from the fourth century BC to the second century AD.

title: Torre Dell'Angelo
description: A Roman columbarium tomb located on the Via Latina.

title: Fut / Quosenum?/ Kousa? fl.

details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Tensift MOR
description: A river in central Morocco that flows from the eastern High Atlas to the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Tomb of Thutmes I and Hatshepsut (KV20)
description: KV20 may be the earliest tomb cut in the Valley of the Kings. It was first the tomb of Thutmose I, although he was later re-interred in KV38. KV20 was adapted to accommodate both her and her father.

title: Gutium
name_variants: Gutium@akk | Gutî@akk | Qutî@akk | Gutium | Gutî | Qutî
details: With the fall of Agade, “kingship” passed to Gutium according to the Sumerian King List (which lists twenty-one of its rulers). During the Sargonic and Ur III Periods, Gutium was a region in the Iranian highlands or in the valleys of the Zagros Mountains.
description: Gutium is a designation appearing in cuneiform texts of the third, second, and first millennia B.C. for the land of the Gutians (Akkadian Gutî or Qutî), a people responsible for bringing an end to the Akkadian empire. In first millennium B.C. sources, the name is used as an archaic designation for the region northeast of Babylonia, near and in the Zagros Mountains.

title: Girsu Bridge
description: The archaeological site of the Girsu Bridge, located in modern Iraq's Dhi Qar governorate, was identified in 1920 and has been dated to the third millennium BCE.

title: Tor Tignosa
description: Tor Tignosa, mapped and listed in the 17th century Catasto Alessandrino as a landed estate, is a ruined stone structure located some 8 km northeast of Lavinium. Multiple votive inscriptions were found in the vicinity, providing evidence for an ancient sanctuary dating to between the fifth and second centuries BCE.

title: Villa of the Lillies (Amnisos)
details: S. Marinatos excavated the Villa of the Lillies in 1932; it takes its name from the 1.8-meter-high lily fresco discovered in situ . The villa was destroyed by fire ca. 1450 BC.
description: A Bronze Age house at Amnisos, Crete.

title: Dağönü
description: Once known as İririn or Érérin and now known as Dağönü, this modern Turkish village located in the Van Province of eastern Turkey at the eastern coast of Lake Van lies ca. 10 km north of Ayanis. Here a stela with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) has been found (CTU I A 5-18).

title: Attalenses
description: An ancient people of Galatia.

title: Hyctanis (river)
description: A river in Carmania mentioned by both Pliny and Strabo.

title: Perorsi
description: Ancient population on the Atlantic coast of Africa, mentioned by Pliny and located in the vicinity of the River Salsum.

title: Funerary chapel of Amenirdis I
name_variants: Funerary chapel of Amenirdis I@en | Chapelle funéraire d'Aménirdis I@fr | Funerary chapel of Amenirdis I | Chapelle funéraire d'Aménirdis I
description: Funerary chapel of the Divine Adoratrice of Amun Amenirdis I, daughter of King Kashta.

title: Imgur-Enlil
description: The great, inner wall of Babylon was called by the ceremonial Akkadian name Imgur-Enlil, which means "The God Enlil Showed Favor." According to the text Tintir = Babylon, Imgur-Enlil had eight city gates, four on the eastern side of the Euphrates and four on the western side of the river. The Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal and the Babylonian kings Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II, and Nebonidus all undertook construction on Babylon’s great wall. Imgur-Enlil is one of the seven wonders of the ancient according to some classical sources.

title: Sumer
name_variants: Šumeru@akk | Šumerum@akk | Kiengir@sux | Šumeru | Šumerum | Kiengir
description: Sumer (Akkadian Šumeru; Sumerian Kiengir) is the name of a historical region of southern Mesopotamia, now modern-day southern Iraq. It is home to one of the world’s earliest civilizations and one of the places where writing was first developed. Eridu, Girsu, Lagash, Shuruppak, Umma, Ur, and Uruk are among its most well-known urban centers.

title: Castalian spring
name_variants: Κασταλία@grc | Castalia@la | fons Castalius@la | Κασταλία πηγή@el | Kastalia | Castalia | fons Castalius | Kastalía pigí | Κασταλία | Castalia | fons Castalius
description: A spring in the ravine between the Phaedriades cliffs (on the lower southern slope of Mt. Parnassos) at Delphi.

title: Ermine Street
description: The Ermine Street was a major Roman road of Britain, running from Londinium to Colonia Lindum and Eburacum.

title: San Gimignano
description: San Gimignano, which originated as an Etruscan settlement, is best known as a Medieval town renowned for its fortified towers.

title: Pyramid of Amenemhat I
description: The Pyramid of Amenemhat I is an ancient Egyptian pyramid located at Lisht. It was built for Pharaoh Amenemhat I, the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt.

title: Standing Stones of Stenness
name_variants: Standing Stones of Stenness@en | Standing Stones of Stenness
description: The Standing Stones of Stenness is a Neolithic monument on the mainland of Orkney, Scotland, generally dated to the third millennium BC.

title: Barnhouse Settlement
description: The Barnhouse Settlement is a Neolithic village of approximately 15 houses located adjacent to the Loch of Harray, Orkney Mainland, Scotland.

title: Oenoanda bridge
description: An Ottoman bridge at Oinoanda on the Xanthos river. A Latin inscription found nearby suggests an earlier Roman bridge existed at the site.

title: Ayrarat
description: Province of the ancient kingdom of Armenia centered around the upper Araxes River.

title: Diodori insula
name_variants: Διοδώρου νῆσος@grc | Perim Island@en | بريم,@ar | جزيرة ميون@ar | insula Diodori@la | Diodorou nēsos | Perim Island | Barīm | Mayyun | insula Diodori | Diodori (insula) | Διοδώρου νῆσος | insula Diodori
description: A volcanic island located in the Strait of Mandeb at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

title: Horti Aciliorum
description: An urban villa in ancient Rome of the second century CE located on the Pincian Hill between what is now the Porta Pinciana and the Spanish Steps.

title: Centocamere at Lokroi Epizephyrioi
description: The so-called "Centocamere" is an urban complex within the city walls dating to the fourth and third centuries B.C. This complex is laid out a organized city blocks separated by planned streets.

title: Nubian Lion Temple at Naqa
description: The Temple of Apedemak, also known as the Lion Temple, is located to the west of the temple of Amun.

title: Room W9 in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona
name_variants: Room W9, Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona, Dura-Europos@en | Room W9 | Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona | Dura-Europos
description: Pronaos in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona, Dura-Europos, also known as the salle aux gradins or stepped room. The steps of Room W9 carry inscriptions on them.

title: Vounous Cemetery (Cyprus)
description: Cemetery site in northern Cyprus near Kyrenia with Bronze Age remains.

title: Theater of Tios
description: The ancient theater of Tios.

title: Psamathe
description: A spring in Boeotia.

title: Nisāya / Nisaian plain
name_variants: Nisāya@peo | Nu-iš-šá-ya@elx | Ni-is-sa-a-a@akk | Νησαῖον πεδίον@grc | Nisāya | Nu-iš-šá-ya | Ni-is-sa-a-a | Nḗsaion pedíon | Νησαῖον πεδίον
description: A plain in Media, not far from Behistun, famous in the Achaemenid and Hellenistic periods for the quality of its horses.

title: Pnyx
description: The gathering place of the Athenian Assembly in the Classical Period.

title: House of Julia Felix
name_variants: House of Julia Felix@en | Complesso di Giulia Felice@it | II.4.3@en | Praedia di Giulia Felice@it | House of Julia Felix | Julia Felix (House of) | Complesso di Giulia Felice | Giulia Felice (Complesso di) | II.4.3 | Praedia di Giulia Felice | Giulia Felice (Praedia di)
details: The site was excavated first 1754-1757 and again in 1952-1953.
description: The so-called House of Iulia Felix (II, 4, 3) is situated on the south side of the Via dell'Abbondanza, near the Palaestra and the Amphitheater. The estate was formed from two complete insulae that were merged. About one-third of the area was occupied by the house, the remainder by a large garden. Following the AD 62 earthquake the proprietress seems to have leased out portions of the property.

title: Martini-Marescotti Tomb
name_variants: Tomba Martini Marescotti@it | Tomba Martini Marescotti
description: The so-called Martini-Marescotti Tomb is an Etruscan tomb located in the Monte Abatone necropolis of ancient Caere. The tomb was built in the late sixth or early fifth century BCE and is composed of a dromos and three funereal chambers covered by a tumulus. The tomb contained a substantial funereal deposit that included painted Attic wares.

title: Fosso del Manganello
name_variants: Fosso del Manganello@it | Fosso del Manganello
description: The stream known as the Fosso del Manganello is a stream that delimits the northern part of the tuff plateau upon which the Etruscan metropolis of Caere developed.

title: Cairn de Barnénez
description: A megalithic monument of the Neolithic period (ca. 4500 BCE) located near Plouezoc'h, on the Kernéléhen peninsula, in northern Finistère, Brittany

title: Torre del Pascolaro
description: The ruins of a Medieval tower in South Etruria.

title: Vouga River
name_variants: Vouga River@en | Rio Vouga@pt | flumen Vagia@la | Ὀυάκου@grc | Ὀυακούα@grc | Vouga River | Rio Vouga | flumen Vagia | Ouakou | Ouakoua | Ὀυάκου | Ὀυακούα | flumen Vagia
description: Pliny the Elder includes the Vagia in his description of the rivers of Lusitania. The river is now known as the Vouga River, and it flows through Portugal's Centro Region from the Chafariz da Lapa to the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Isthmia Fortress
description: A Byzantine fortress erected in the fifth century CE that includes three gates and 21 towers.

title: Alu-eššu
details: Several Akkadian inscriptions from Suhu mention the city/town Alu-eššu.
description: An unlocated city/town in the kingdom of Suhu, probably not far from Baqa, Qaqqar-aradātu, and Ribaniš.

title: Surb Stepanos Vank
name_variants: Սուրբ Ստեփանոս վանք@hy | Surb Step’anos vank’
details: In 2008 the St. Stephanos monastery was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site as part of the "The Armenian Monastic Ensembles of Iran". Located in the north-west of the country, this heritage listing consists of three monastic ensembles of the Armenian Christian faith: St Thaddeus and St Stepanos and the Chapel of Dzordzor.
description: Armenian monastery in East Azarabaijan province, Iran. The first church was constructed on the site in 62 CE. A monastery was constructed there in the 7th century, and the structure was expanded in the 10th century.

title: tribus Collina
details: The tribus Collina was one of the four, large, urban tribes of Rome ( Palatina , Collina , Esquilina , Suburana ), which corresponded to the four urban regions that Servius Tullius created.
description: An early urban tribe of the city of Rome, reportedly established by Servius Tullius.

title: Forum Boarium (at Rome)
name_variants: Forum Boarium@la | Foro Boario@it | forum bovarium@la | Forum Boarium | Foro Boario | forum bovarium | Forum Boarium | forum bovarium
description: Rome's so-called "cattle market", the Forum Boarium is a key area of commercial and ritual activity on the east bank of the river Tiber. It is flanked by the Capitoline, Palatine, and Aventine hills.

title: Ara Maxima Herculis
name_variants: ara magna Herculis@la | Ara Maxima@la | ara magna Herculis | Ara Maxima
description: An early cult center connected with Herakles located in Rome's Forum Boarium.

title: Monte Solaro
description: Monte Solaro is the tallest mountain on the island of Capri with an elevation of 589 meters.

title: Yacimiento arqueologico de Doña Blanca
description: An archaeological site with multiple settlement horizons.

title: Beyoba tumulus
description: Tumulus located approximately 13km southeast of Parion. The tomb contained two burials dated to 350-300 BCE.

title: Bouleuterion
name_variants: Bouleuterion in Priene@en | Bouleuterion in Priene
description: The bouleuterion at Priene, located northeast of the agora, dates ca. 200 BCE.

title: Abbazia di San Vincenzo al Volturno
name_variants: San Vincenzo al Volturno@it | San Vincenzo al Volturno
details: The Chronicon Vulturnense , names three noblemen from Benevento - Paldo, Tato, and Taso - as those responsible for founding the abbey in 731.
description: An historic Benedictine monastery located in the Province of Isernia, near the source of the river Volturno.

title: Foro Romano
name_variants: Foro romano di Aquileia@it | Foro romano di Aquileia
description: The Roman forum of Aquileia.

title: Late Antique domus
description: The structure that now stands at Via in Selci no. 82 in the city of Rome rests on the structural remains of a late Roman building that likely date to the fourth or fifth century. These structural remains are likely those of the basilical hall that often was part of a Late Antique domus.

title: Alta Semita
description: The Alta Semita was an urban street running along the spine of the Quirinal Hill. The Alta Semita also lent its name to the sixth Augustan region of the city.

title: Sorpara
description: A place in Cappadocia included on the Peutinger map.

title: Tracias
description: A place included on the Peutinger map.

title: Sacriportus
description: Sacriportus is an ancient site of Latium located between Signia and Praeneste, although its precise location is no longer known. It was the site of a decisive battle between Caius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Sulla.

title: Dede Harabeleri
description: Late Antique rural settlement located in Gaziantep Province, Turkey, less than 2km southeast of the tell at Tilbaşar Kalesi. Salvage excavations were carried out on the site in 2016-2018 prior to the construction of the Doğanpınar Dam.

title: Unnamed group of bridges over R. Zadorra, north of Bele(g)ia
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Trespuentes over R. Zadorra, N Bele(g)ia
description: An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 25 C3 unnamed bridge group (Trespuentes over R. Zadorra, N Bele(g)ia)

title: Ponte Manlio
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: on Via Flaminia (20) Ashby notes that the modern toponym results from a "fictitious inscription" related to a supposed restoration of the bridge.

title: Ishān Khālifa
description: Group of mounds where cuneiform inscriptions have been found.

title: Skopje aqueduct
description: A Roman aqueduct in Macedonia.

title: KS-04
name_variants: چغادوسر@fa | Chogha Do Sar | Chegha Dowsar
description: Archaeological site designation of a settlement inhabited in the 6th-4th millennia BCE, locally known as Chogha Do Sar.

title: KS-108
description: Archaeological site in Khuzestan with signs of habitaiton during the 4th millennium BCE; locally known as Chogha Kabira or Tepe Kirub.

title: Ebabbar
description: The temple of the god Šamaš at Sippar. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ebabbar means "Shining House."

title: Terento
description: Terento is a place included on the Peutinger map, lying between Aeliae and Aqvas Regias. It is also mentioned by the Ravenna Cosmographer.

title: Mieza theater
description: The theater at Mieza dates from the second century BCE.

title: Nemyriv Hillfort
name_variants: Городище Немиров@ru | Немирівське городище@uk | Gorodishche Nemirov | Nemyrivs'ke Horodyshche
description: Scythian hillfort site located on the Southern Bug River near the modern town of Nemyriv. The site was primarily inhabited in the early Iron Age (8th-6th centuries BCE), with additional deposits from the Chalcolithic Age, the Bronze Age, the La Tene period, the Chernyakov Culture, and the Middle Ages.

title: Creissels
description: Evidence for human activity stretching from the Late Bronze Age to the sixth century A.D. was discovered in the cave of Boundoulaou in 1962.

title: Corre
details: According to L. Lerat writing in PECS , a number of fine sculptures were discovered at the site. They are displayed in the museum at Vesoul.
description: A Gallo-Roman site located near the junction of the Saône and Coney rivers.

title: Concarneau
description: Site of a Gallo-Roman villa discovered in 1964 in the village of Le Questel near Concarneau. The villa dates from the middle of the first century BCE to the fourth century CE.

title: Colleville
description: An unusual Gallo-Roman dwelling was excavated during the 1960s. Its main periods of occupation corresponded to the reign of Augustus and then the second century A.D.

title: Roecliffe Fort
description: The site of a Roman fort and an adjacent settlement is located on a terrace south of the River Ure to the west of Boroughbridge. The Roman fort was identified via geophysical survey and test excavations.

title: Forum of Carsulae
description: The Forum of Carsulae is supported by terraces and it includes the basilica and a twin sanctuary, in addition to tabernae.

title: Mangadu Megalithic Site
description: An archaeological site with Iron Age funerary megaliths located in the vicinity of the modern Moonamkutty-Mangad Road in the northeastern portion of India's Kollam municipality. The site was damaged by cashewnut tree farming and is now not visible due to habitation on the site.

title: Atrium Libertatis
description: Built first in the late third century BCE, the Atrium Libertatis was the headquarters of the censors, as well as an archive and public library. Asinius Pollio expanded the complex in 39 BCE.

title: Church at Trimithis
description: A structure at the city of Trimithis (Amheida) in the Dakhleh Oasis, identified as a church and dated to the 4th century CE.

title: Baths at Cremna
description: Public baths at Cremna.

title: Kumtepe (Troad)
details: Four occupational horizons have been identified at Kumtepe (Kumtepe IA, IB, IC and II). The initial settlement was established ca. 4800 B.C. but then abandoned ca. 4500 B.C. The site was re-settled around 3700 B.C. This "Kumtepe B" culture used large houses that had multiple rooms and they practiced both animal husbandry and cultivation. There may be connections between Kumtepe and the settlement of Yassıtepe and Hisarlık (Troy) around 3000 B.C.
description: The oldest permanent settlement in the Troad.

title: Stadium of Delos
description: Stadium in the settlement of Delos, constructed in the early 3rd century BCE.

title: Church of the Nativity
name_variants: Church of the Nativity@en | Church of the Nativity
description: A church that many claim marks the birthplace of Jesus Christ is located in Bethlehem, now in the State of Palestine in the West Bank. The original church built on the site was commissioned by Constantine I and dedicated in May 339 CE. The church was destroyed by fire, likely in 529, and replaced by Justinian I.

title: North Palace at Babylon
name_variants: North Palace@en | Nordburg@de | ēkallu eššu@akk | New Palace@en | North Palace | Nordburg | ēkallu eššu | New Palace
details: The North Palace (Nordburg) was excavated by Robert Koldewey in 1899–1900 and in 1913–14, as well as by Iraqi archaeologists in 1958 and the early 1980s. This palace was less extensively excavated than the South Palace , the traditional palace at Babylon. This might have been because this royal residence built upon a complicated terraced structure. The plan, as far as it is preserved, is identical to the western wing of the South Palace and the Summer Palace . In an Akkadian inscription written on large stone tablets, Nebuchadnezzar II records the following about the construction of his new palace: “In Babylon, the private chambers of my residence were not decorous enough for my status as king. Because worshiping the god Marduk, my lord, was present in my heart, in order to widen the residence of my royal majesty, in Babylon, the city (under) his (Marduk’s) protection, I did not change its street(s), displace its dais(es), nor block up its canal(s). I searched far and wide for (the site of a new) kummu -building and, so that no arrow (during) battle can come close to Imgur-Enlil, the wall of Babylon, 490 cubits distance outside of Nēmetti-Enlil, the outer wall of Babylon, I built two strong embankments with bitumen and baked brick (and) a wall like a mountain. I fashioned a baked brick structure between them and, on top of it, I built a large kummu -building as the residence of my royal majesty with bitumen and baked brick to a great height. I added (it) to the palace of my father and in a favorable month, on an auspicious day, I secured its foundation on the surface (lit. “breast”) of the netherworld and raised its superstructure as high as a mountain. I completed its construction in (just) fifteen days and made the seat of my lordly majesty resplendent. I had (beams of) hard cedar originating from the holy mountain (Lebanon), thick pine, and the best selection of cypress stretched (over it) as its roof. At each of its gates, I fixed doors (made) of musukkannu -wood, cedar, cypress, ebony, and ivory with mounting(s) of silver (and) gold and a facing of bronze, (and) threshold(s) and nukuššû -fittings of cast copper. I surrounded its summit with parapets (colored with) blue glaze. I surrounded it with a fortified wall of bitumen and baked brick like a mountain. Beside the wall of baked brick, I built a great wall using strong stone(s) (and) large (slabs) quarried from the mountains and (then) I raised its superstructure like a mountain. I had that building built to be an object of wonder and I filled it with splendor for all of the people to see. Dignity, anger, reverence, (and) brilliance of kingship surround it so that criminals (and) the unrighteous cannot enter inside it. As for the merciless, evil doer in the outskirts of the wall of Ka-dingirra, I drove away his arrows by reinforcing the wall of Babylon like a mountain.” In another text inscribed on clay cylinders, this Babylonian king states: “At that time, I constantly stove (to do things) to strengthen the protection [of] Esagil and Babylon. Beside Nēmetti-Enlil, the outer wall of Babylon, from the bank of the Euphrates River up to the lower enclosure Nēmetti-Enlil, which faces East, (at) a distance of 335 cubits from the outskirts of Nēmetti-Enlil, I built with bitumen and baked brick [o]ne embankment (whose width was) thirty-two baked bricks (and) a second embankment (whose width was) twenty-three baked bricks, [two] strong embankments, one in front of the other. I secured their foundation(s) directly on the apsû , [i]n the water table far below and raised their superstructure(s) as high as mountain(s). I fashion[ed] a baked brick structure between them [and, on t]op of them, I built a kummu -building, a large sacred building, to a great height. I skillfully the strengthen (Esagil’s and Babylon’s) protection and established the city of Babylon as a fortress.”
description: The Neo-Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–562 BC) constructed a new royal residence for himself at Babylon. This grand palace was constructed north of the so-called “South Palace,” the traditional royal residence of the kings of Babylon. The building, which is referred to as the “new palace” (ēkallu eššu) in Achaemenid-period texts, is generally called the “North Palace,” “Nordburg,” and “New Palace.”

description: Tell Leilan is situated near the Wadi Jarrah, in the Khabur River basin in Al-Hasakah Governorate, northeastern Syria. The ancient names of the site are Shekhna and Shubat-Enlil.

title: Adad Gate
name_variants: Adad Gate@en | Abul-Adad@akk | Adad-napišti-ummāni-uṣur@akk | Adad Gate | Abul-Adad | Adad-napišti-ummāni-uṣur
details: The German excavators of Babylon did not excavate any of the city gates west of the Euphrates; the Adad Gate was one of four unexcavated gates of the inner city.
description: The Adad Gate is one of Babylon's eight city gates and it is situated on the western side of the inner city, directly west of the nu-x-ù quarter. King Nebuchadnezzar II built the gate ca. 575 B.C.

title: Garden Houses
description: A large residential complex, built in ca. 128 CE as part of the Hadrianic remodeling of Ostia. Its central area was occupied by two blocks, each comprising four houses, surrounded by a garden furnished with six fountains.

title: Malkata
description: Site located south of the Theban Necropolis containing a New Kingdom palace complex constructed by Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty.

title: House of the Fishes
name_variants: Domus dei Pesci@it | Domus dei Pesci
description: A domus in Ostia Antica, whose two building phases have been dated, respectively, to the middle and last quarter of the third century CE.

title: Kaims Castle
description: Kaims Castle is a Roman fortlet located between the forts of Ardoch and Strageath.

title: Appleby-in-Westmorland
description: A Roman signal station of the "Gask ridge" type was located 1.5 miles southeast of Appleby-in-Westmorland.

title: Corinthian League
name_variants: League of Corinth@en | League of Corinth
description: The League of Corinth was a federation of Greek states that was created by Philip II of Macedon in 338–337 BC.

title: Vessagiriya
description: Vessagiriya is the site of an ancient Buddhist forest monastery in Sri Lanka. It is considered part of the ruined site of Anuradhapura. The monastery was initially built in the middle of the third century BCE and was expanded in the late fifth century CE. A Roman bronze coin, as well as punch-marked coins and/or ingots, were excavated at Vessagiriya in the first decade of the 20th century.

title: House of the Triclinium at Italica
description: House of the Triclinium is located in the area southeast of the House of Hylas.

title: Roman theater at Antium
description: The Roman theater at Antium is most likely built in the second half of the first century.

title: Southeastern Cluster
details: This group includes Biete Amanuel (House of Emmanuel), Biete Qeddus Mercoreus (House of St Mercoreos/House of St Mark), Biete Abba Libanos (House of Abbot Libanos), Biete Gabriel-Rufael (House of the angels Gabriel, and Raphael), and Biete Lehem (House of Holy Bread).
description: The Southeastern Cluster of rock-cut churches at Lalibela.

title: Church of St. George
description: One of a group of eleven rock-hewn monolithic churches located in Lalibela, a city in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia. The church likely dates to the twelfth or thirteenth century.

title: Cadbury Camp Hill Fort
description: A 2.8 ha hill fort near Tickenham, Somerset, England, in use from the Bronze Age to the Anglo-Saxon period.

title: Lagaba
description: Unlocated city in Mesopotamia. Though its location is unknown, approximately 400 illicitly excavated cuneiform tablets are believed to have originated there. It is believed to have been located approximately 15 km north of Babylon on the western bank of the Euphrates.

title: Necropolis of San Germano
name_variants: Necropoli etrusca di San Germano (Gavorrano, GR)@it | Necropoli etrusca di San Germano (Gavorrano | GR)
description: Burial ground containing 28 burials dated to the Etruscan period.

title: Arch of Gordian III at Musti
description: A Roman arch monument located at Musti (Tunisia) that is dedicated to the Roman emperor Gordian III. Parra-Pérez et al. (2024) argue that the arch was dedicated in 240 CE based on its inscription.

title: Umbilicus urbis Romae
name_variants: Umbilicus urbis Romae@la | Umbilicus urbis Romae
description: The remains of a monument marking the symbolic navel of the city of Rome that dates to the reign of Septimius Severus.

title: Nuraghe Gibe Truttiri
description: A nuraghe located near the beach of Cala Marina.

title: Roman theater at Gortyna
description: The Roman theater at Gortyna dates to the second century.

title: Roman amphitheater at Rusellae
description: The Roman amphitheater at Rusellae dates to the first century.

title: Temple of Roma and Augustus (Athens)
name_variants: ὁ ἐν ἀκροπ]όλει βωμὸς [τῶν] Σεβαστῶν@grc | Temple of Rome and Augustus@en | ho en Akropolei bōmos tōn Sebastōn | Temple of Rome and Augustus | ὁ ἐν ἀκροπ]όλει βωμὸς [τῶν] Σεβαστῶν
description: The Temple or Altar of Roma and Augustus on the Acropolis of Athens was erected shortly after 27 BC near the east front of the Periklean Parthenon.

title: Nuraghe di Tanca Manna
description: A monopteral nuraghe located near Nuoro, Sardinia.

title: Hypogeum of Clepsina
name_variants: Hypogeum of Clepsina@en | Ipogeo di Clepsina@it | Hypogeum of Clepsina | Ipogeo di Clepsina
description: A late eighth to early seventh century B.C. hypogeum tomb on the main plateau of ancient Caere.

title: Sep. Eurysacis
name_variants: Tomb of Eurysaces@en | Tomb of Eurysaces
description: The tomb of a baker, M. Vergilius Eurysaces, built at the point where the via Labicana and the via Praenestina exit from Rome's walls to the east. The tomb dates to the later Republican period (ca. 50-20 B.C.).

title: Paliopyrgos tower
description: The foundations of a tower dating to the fourth century BCE located southwest of Nemea.

title: Lamā Cemetery
description: Cemetery site near Lama village, Iran with almost 60 graves dating to the late 2nd-early 1st millennium CE. Most of the graves were destroyed by bulldozing in the area for a road in December 1999.

title: Ayn Braq Aqueduct
description: An aqueduct that supplied Petra with water drawn from the Ayn Braq spring, where a large sanctuary had been built.

title: Archaeological Site at Plasi of Marathon
description: The excavations at Plasi, Marathon, have revealed evidence across a broad chronological spectrum, including evidence of an archaic sanctuary.

title: Kalhu Archive 11
details: This archive is located in the Northwest Palace.
description: Most documents found in the Northwest Palace, built by the Assyrian king Ashurnarsipal II (883–859 BC), predate the move of the new Assyrian capital to Dur-Šarrukin under Sargon II (721–705 BC). The archive found in Rooms ZT 13–17 was written between 687 BC and 614 BC, thus postdating this move. This repository contained about sixty clay tablets, specifically loan documents, the sale of slaves and land, juridical texts, marriage contracts, and administrative lists.

title: Sarugu
details: According to an Akkadian inscription of Ninurta-kudurrī-uṣur of Suhu, the Sarugu, together with other Aramean tribal groups, attacked the land Lāqê. The Sarugu and their allies were defeated by Ninurta-kudurrī-uṣur.
description: The name of a nomadic Aramean tribal group that was in the middle Euphrates region during the early part of the first millennium B.C.

title: Haṭallu
details: According to an Akkadian inscription of Ninurta-kudurrī-uṣur of Suhu, the Haṭallu, together with other Aramean tribal groups, attacked the land Lāqê. The Haṭallu and their allies were defeated by Ninurta-kudurrī-uṣur. The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III also fought with them during his first regnal year.
description: The name of a nomadic Aramean tribal group that was active in the middle Euphrates region during the early part of the first millennium B.C. and in Babylonia in the middle of the eighth century B.C.

title: Hither Province (Pylos)
name_variants: Hither Province@en | 𐀆𐀸𐀫𐁁𐀒𐀨𐀂𐀊, 𐀆𐀸𐀫𐁁𐀒𐀨@grc-Linb | Hither Province | de-we-ro-a3-ko-ra-i-ja | de-we-ro-a3-ko-ra | 𐀆𐀸𐀫𐁁𐀒𐀨𐀂𐀊, 𐀆𐀸𐀫𐁁𐀒𐀨
details: The place-names of the Hither Province settlements run north to south along the west coast of Messenia. Likely geography of the Hither Province: (see Bennet 2011 p. 152 and Cosmopoulos 2006 p. 205-6) North boundary: either the River Neda or the Kyparissia valley. South boundary: Cape Akritas, somewhere north of modern Koroni. West boundary: the coast of Messenia. East boundary: Mount Aigaleon.
description: The Hither Province of Mycenaean Pylos, containing nine settlements as recorded in the Linear B tablets.

title: Roman aqueduct
description: The Roman aqueduct of San Giovanni.

title: Roman amphitheater at Viminacium
description: The Roman amphitheater at Viminacium could accommodate roughly 12,000 spectators.

title: Poggio Civitella
description: The hill of Poggio Civitella near Montalcino, Italy, rises to a height of 661 meters above sea level. Beginning in 1993, excavation campaigns revealed a series of settlement horizons dating to the first millennium BCE, ranging from the archaic to the Hellenistic periods. The hilltop was fortified during this period.

title: Sam'alla (province)
details: The province is first attested in an administrative records of Sargon II (r. 721-705 BC); it is also mentioned in a text dating to the reign of Ashurbanipal (r. 668-ca. 631 BC). The governor of Sam’al held the post of eponym in the year 681 BC.
description: The eighth-century-BC Assyrian king Shalmaneser V (r. 726-722 BC) conquered Sam'al and its territory and established the city as the administrative capital of an Assyrian province named after it.

title: Rujm al-Ḥenū
name_variants: رجم الحنو@ar | Rujm al-Ḥenū | rajm alhanu | Rujm el Ḥinū; Rujm al Hinu
description: Two stone buildings (west and east) located 30 m apart were excavated at modern Rujm al-Ḥenū in Jordan. The pottery found has been dated largely to Iron Age IIc.

title: Sebetti temple (Kalhu)
details: Akkadian inscriptions of the ninth-century-BC Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) record that that ruler built (or rebuilt) temples to the deities Adad, Damkina, Ea-šarru, Enlil, Gula, Nabû, Ninurta, Sîn, Šala, and Šarrat-niphi, as well as to the Sebetti and Kidmuri; for example, see RIAo Ashurnasirpal II 030 lines 53–78a. Of those, only four have been positively identified during nineteenth- and twentieth-century excavations: the Kidmuri temple , the Nabû temple , the Ninurta temple , and the Šarrat-niphi temple . The location of the Sebetti temple at Kalhu is not known. Julian Reade (2002: 194–195) suggests the following: " The House of the Sibitti is mentioned in Ashurnasirpal's final text and therefore presumably lay outside the temples already discussed, though perhaps not far from the House of Kidmuri, since texts link Sibitti and Kidmuri shrines, probably both at Dūr-Šarrukēn ( Parpola 1987: 94) and at Nineveh (Kataja and Whiting 1995: 83-4)." T his proposal cannot be confirmed from in-situ inscriptions and, therefore, must remain conjectural.
description: When Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud) became the principal administrative center of the Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC, king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) built (or rebuilt) numerous temples. One of those was dedicated to the divine Sebetti. The location of this building is not known.

title: Temple of Augustus and Rome (Ankara)
description: The Temple of Augustus and Roma at Ankara likely dates ca. 20 BCE. It is also known as the "Monumentum Ancyranum", highlighting the structure's role in preserving the most complete copy of the inscription known as the "Res Gestae Divi Augusti", which was promulgated in both ancient Greek and Latin following the death of emperor Augustus in 14 CE.

title: Uronarti
description: An ancient settlement located on an island in the Nile just south of the Second Cataract, now in the north of Sudan. An ancient fortress dating to the reigns of the Middle Kingdom pharaohs (19th century BC), Senusret I and Senusret III, is found there.

title: Tell Um Hammad al-Gharbi
description: Archaeological site on the banks of the Zerqa River with signs of habitation in the Early Bronze Age I-II and IV. The eastern portion of the larger Tell Um Hammad site is called Um Hammad Sharqiya; the western section is Um Hammad al-Gharbi. The two may have been linked as a single village in the Early Bronze Age IV.

title: Qutb Minar
description: The second tallest minar (73 m) in India after Minar-E-Fateh was built by Qutb-ud-din Aibak beginning in AD 1192. The monument is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Civitas Leonina
description: The Civitas Leonina or Leonine City is a portion of the city of Rome on the left bank of the river Tiber around which Pope Leo IV commissioned the construction of the Leonine Wall in the ninth century AD. This followed the Saracen sack of Rome in AD 846.

title: Neolithic Settlement at Knossos
details: Neolithic layers were identified via excavation beneath the footprint of the Central Court of the so-called Palace of Minos beginning in 1997.
description: A neolithic settlement on a hill known today as Kephala, south of Heraklion on the island of Crete. It preceded the Bronze Age (Minoan) palace and settlement on this site.

title: Odéon at Carthage
description: The theater and odéon of Roman Carthage stood in the northeast of the city, some three blocks from the cardo maximus.

title: Panagia tou Politi church (Amorgos)
description: A Christian chapel on the island of Amorgos that succeeds a Classical sanctuary, with architectural elements of the latter in reuse.

title: Via Ciminia
name_variants: Ciminia, Via@la | Via Ciminia | Ciminia Via | Ciminia, Via
details: The Via Ciminia is attested in second century inscriptions dealing with the curatores viarum. Remains of a paved tract running from Sutrium to Lago di Vico has been presumed to be the Via Ciminia. It is then assumed, by Duncan and others, to continue toward Viterbo, rejoining the Via Cassia at Aquae Passeris.
description: The Via Ciminia was a Roman road that left the Via Cassia and continued toward the Ciminian hills. Its course likely ran from Sutrium to near Viterbo.

title: Roman theater of Philippopolis
name_variants: Plovdiv Roman theatre@en | Plovdiv Roman theatre
description: The Roman theater in Plovdiv, Bulgaria.

title: Odeon of Philippopolis
description: The ancient Roman odeon in Plovdiv, Bulgaria.

title: Nuraghe Su Valsu
description: A Middle Bronze Age nuraghe located southwest of Florinas in Sardinia.

title: Tell es-Samarat
description: A multi-period settlement site located in the Jericho Governorate, West Bank.

title: House of the Tiles
name_variants: House of the Tiles@en | House of the Tiles
description: The so-called "House of the Tiles" at Lerna belongs to the Korakou culture in the Early Helladic II period (ca. 2500–2300 BCE). It was a monumental two-story building (12 x 25 meters) and has been interpreted as either a "proto-palace" or administrative center.

title: Peiraic Gate
name_variants: Gate II@en | Πειραϊκὴ πύλη@grc | Gate II | Peiraikḕ púlē | Peiraike pyle | Πειραϊκὴ πύλη
description: A gate in the Themistoklean Walls of Athens, through which the road to Peiraeus ran.

title: Sanctuary at Lucus Feroniae
description: The sanctuary and grove of Feronia located at the site of Lucus Feroniae.

title: Assur Archive 25
name_variants: Assur Archive 25@en | N 10 Archive@en | Assur Archive 25 | N 10 Archive
details: The archive is located in a private house in Assur.
description: In the northern corner, along the northwest town wall of Assur (bD5I, bC/D5II, bC5III), researchers unearthed Houses 67–68 with an archive belonging to a family with the title ḫunduraya, a gentilic meaning "from Ḫundur". Another archive belonging to a related family of ḫunduraya was found nearby (Assur Archive 24). In House 67 and 68, about 48 clay tablets and fragments were found. The tablets mostly date to the second half of the 7th century BC. The archive consists of loans, mostly concerning silver, work contracts, purchase documents and a juridical settlement.

title: Spring at Amphiareion
details: Coordinates taken on 09 July 2013 with a Sony DSC-HX200V GPS camera
description: The spring at the healing sanctuary at Amphiareion and a site of votive deposits in the form of coins. It still flows today.

title: Kadembas/Katepants
description: Kadembas (Katepants) is a modern settlement in the Van Province in the Southeast of Turkey. Here several rock inscriptions of the Urartian king Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) were found which report the construction of the “Canal of Minua” which is still in use today. Furthermore a rock inscription of Tariria, wife of Minua, (9th / 8th century BCE) is located here which attributes a vineyard to her belongings.

title: Kalecik
description: Kalecik (formerly known as Aralesk or Lesk) is a modern village situated ca. 5 km north of Van Kalesi in southeast Turkey. In the village church, a re-used cylindrical stone (presumably a column base) with a building inscription of the Urartian king Išpuini, son of Sarduri I (ninth century BCE), was found. Furthermore, a re-used stone slab with an inscription of the Urartian king Argišti, son of Minua and grandson of Išpuini (eighth century BCE) has also been found here.

title: Pust-i Gau
description: A large, multi-period site in modern Afghanistan. One of its key feature is a large, fortified enclosure with 48 towers.

title: Sra Ghundai, Ghazni
description: Remains of a walled ancient city in the Ghazni province of Afghanistan. Its remains date to various periods according to W. Ball (1982): Late Sassanian and Turki Shahi (sixth–ninth century AD) and Early Islamic (tenth -twelfth century).

title: Acarnanian League
name_variants: τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Ἀκαρνάνων@grc | to koinon tōn Akarnanōn | τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Ἀκαρνάνων
description: The Acarnanian League was a tribal confederation of the Acarnanians that later transformed into a league by the 5th century BCE. The league was incorporated into the Roman province of Achaea following the battle of Actium in 31 BCE.

title: Burgast
description: Area in the Altai region of extreme western Mongolia containing a number of burials and other structures from the Bronze Age (Bulan-Kobin Culture), Turkic, and Medieval periods.

title: Via Campana?
name_variants: Via Campana?@la | Via Campana | Via Campana?
description: A road located on the right bank of the Tiber River leading to the Campus Salinarum romanarum and sharing the first part of its course with the Via Portuensis.

title: Cetona
description: The present town of Cetona grew around the rocca (fortress) of the tenth century A.D., although occupation at the site reaches back to the Paleolithic when a number of caves show evidence for human activity. There are also indications of an Etruscan phase of occupation.

title: Castelliere di Monte Acuto
description: A multi-period site on Monte Acuto with evidence for habitation (Late Bronze Age) and cult activities (mid-first millennium BCE).

title: Ploutonion at Hierapolis
name_variants: Πλουτώνιον@grc | Pluto's Gate@en | Plutonium@la | Ploutonion | Pluto's Gate | Plutonium | Πλουτώνιον
details: The Plutonion at Hierapolis is a walled sanctuary dedicated to Pluto and Kore centered around a small subterranean cave. The cave itself contained poisonous gas, which killed any animal which entered it. Strabo, Pliny the Elder, and Cassius Dio all report this phenomenon. Ammianus Marcellinus (23.6.18) seems to indicate that the cave was no longer extant in his time. Ancient sources report a sort of cistern around the cave and a theater built above it (Dio 68.27.3). Evidence at the site suggests that the cave was sealed in the sixth century CE. Recent excavations (2008-2014) uncovered a theatron set above a wall with an opening in the center, which is the presumed entrance to the ancient cave. The identification of an inscription dedicated to Pluto and Kore over the opening, and the resemblance to ancient descriptions of the site, positively identifies this site as the Plutonion. These excavations were the latest conducted by the Italian Archaeological Mission, which began in 1957.
description: The Ploutonion at Hierapolis is a walled sanctuary dedicated to Pluto and Kore.

title: Maiden Castle, Dorset
name_variants: Maiden Castle@en | Δοὺνιον@grc | Maiden Castle | Dorset | Dunium | Δοὺνιον
description: One of the largest and most complex Iron Age hillforts in Europe, Maiden Castle, in Dorset, was occupied from the Neolithic period through to the fourth century A.D.

title: Romano-British Bath House
description: A bathhouse located at Orpington, Kent was excavated between 1971 and 1975. The site flourished between ca. 270 and 400 CE. Its post-abandonment phase includes Anglo-Saxon graves of the fifth and sixth centuries.

title: Komninon (Macedonian tomb), Stavroupolis
description: Stavroupolis is the site of the largest Macedonian tomb known in Thrace.

title: Baths of the Philosopher
name_variants: Terme del Filosofo@it | Terme del Filosofo
description: The so-called "Baths of the Philosopher" or "Terme del Filosofo" in region V of the ancient city of Ostia take their modern sobriquet from a bust of Plotinus dating to the middle of the third century CE.

title: Shrine of Sabazius
name_variants: Shrine of Sabazius@en | Shrine of Sabazius
description: The Shrine of Sabazius was installed in part of a horreum (V, XII, 2) that was initially built ca. 120-125 CE. The Sabazius shrine likely dates to the early third century. Dante Vaglieri excavated the shrine in 1909.

title: Domus, M. Tullius Cicero
description: The house of the Roman statesman and orator M. Tullius Cicero was located on the north-eastern corner of the Palatine Hill in Rome.

title: Chiesa Ipogea di San Nicola
description: A poorly understood paleochristian site located on the grounds of the Inviolata park in the comune of Guidonia-Montecelio in the greater metropolitan area of Rome. The cave site may originally have functioned as a mithraeum.

title: Stadium at Kibyra
description: The Stadium at Kibyra dates to the second and third centuries CE and could seat about 10,000 people.

title: Torre d'en Galmés
description: Torre d'en Galmés was a Talaiotic settlement of Bronze Age Minorca and was established ca. 1400 BC.

title: Remoria
name_variants: Remurinus ager@la | Ῥεμορία@grc | Remurinus ager | Remoria | Ῥεμορία | Remurinus ager
description: A place, perhaps legendary, connected with Remus, Romulus' twin brother. It may have been located five miles downstream from the Palatine Hill.

title: Poikile Petra
description: Poikile Petra is the name of a road connecting Seleucia ad Calycadnum and Corycus.

title: Roman amphitheater at Thermae Himeraeae
description: Roman amphitheater at Termini Imerese was of modest size and is today poorly preserved.

title: Clepsydra of the Oropos Amphiareion
name_variants: Clepsydra of the Oropos Amphiareion@en | Clepsydra of the Oropos Amphiareion
details: Excavated by the Archaeological Society in Athens in 1884, t he clepsydra (water clock) at the Amphiareion at Oropos is thought to have been built in the 4th century BCE. This particular clepsydra is a rare example of an inflow water clock, meaning time is measured against a constant rate of deposition, rather than the more usual outflow water clocks found in ancient Greece. The clock is located opposite the sacred spring at the Amphiareion, to the southeast of the sanctuary. It is made up of a rectangular tank with a staircase leading down, allowing for an attendant to routinely pull a plug and drain the tank of water. A pipe sourced from the nearby sacred spring was likely used to fill the tank with water. This particular water clock is unusually well-preserved, allowing for a better study of its mechanics and ancient water clocks in general.
description: The Oropos Amphiareion clepsydra is a hydraulic inflow clock serving the Sanctuary of Amphiaraus. Situated on the southeast bank of the sacred spring of Amphiaraus, this inflow hydraulic clock dates to the 4th century BCE.

title: Ocazanes (river)
description: A river that was a tributary of the Cyrus.

title: Oeandenses
description: An ancient people of Galatia.

title: Cellarulo
description: An area in the Contrada Cellarulo of Benevento that is designated as an archaeological area with evidence for the later phases of ancient Benevento's history.

title: Ahramat Branch
description: An ancient, now-vanished, branch of the Nile River. Geophysical research has demonstrated that the Ahramat Branch, no longer visible to the naked eye, was located west of the main Nile River channel and flowed from south of Lisht to the area of the Giza Plateau area. This channel would have bordered on the complexes of more than 30 ancient pyramids ranging in date from the Old Kingdom to Second Intermediate Period (2686−1649 BCE).

title: Pozzuolo necropolis
description: A necropolis of Etruscan Veii.

title: Can Blai
description: A Late Roman fortlet on the island of Formentera.

title: Ponte del Diavolo
description: A bridge in the territory of Blera known as the "Devil's Bridge".

title: Bouleuterion of Onchestos
description: The Bouleuterion of Onchestos has been identified adjacent to the Temple of Poseidon.

title: ager Mutycensis
description: The territory of Motyca in the Roman province of Sicilia that, according to Cicero, supported 187 farmers.

title: Kybele Sanctuary at Kapikaya
name_variants: Sanctuary of Cybele, Pergamon@en | Sanctuary of Cybele | Pergamon
description: The Kybele Sanctuary at Kapikaya is a rock-cut sanctuary sacred to Kybele, approximately 6 km from Pergamon, and is included in the UNESCO World Heritage site "Pergamon and its Multi-Layered Cultural Landscape".

title: Abū Fanduwā
name_variants: ابو فندوا@ar | KS-59@en | Abū Fanduwā | KS-59
description: Settlement inhabited in the 5th-4th milliennia BCE, located in the modern Hoseynabad-e Goruh Rural District of Iran's Kerman province.

title: Roman theater of Neapolis
description: The Roman theater of Neapolis is a structure of the first century B.C. that is built atop the pre-existing fourth century B.C. Greek theater.

title: Arch of Hadrian at Athens
name_variants: Arch of Hadrian at Athens@en | Πύλη του Αδριανού@el | Αψίδα του Αδριανού@el | Πόρτα της Βασιλοπούλας@el | Καμαρόπορτα@el | Arch of Hadrian at Athens | Pyle tou Adrianou | Apsida tou Adrianou | Porta tis Vasilopoulas | Kamaroporta
details: The Arch of Hadrian was built by the city of Athens to celebrate a visit by the Roman Emperor Hadrian in AD 131 or 132. Its structure is similar to that of a Roman triumphal arch with a single opening, but the attic of the arch is occupied by a series of Corinthian columns supporting a triangular pediment in the center and an entablature on each side.
description: The Arch of Hadrian is a monument in the form of a Roman triumphal arch, constructed by the citizens of Athens in AD 131 or 132 to honor the Roman emperor Hadrian.

title: Castello di Agropoli
description: A Medieval castle built atop Byzantine foundations.

title: Roman baths, Carsulae
description: Baths of the early imperial period at Carsulae.

title: Nuraghe Nolza
description: The Nuraghe Nolza consists of a central, quadri-lobate tower. The tower still stands to ca. 13 m and the complex covers 2.5 ha.

title: Son Bou Basilica
description: A three-aisled Paleochristian basilica of the fifth century A.D. located in the village of Son Bou in Menorca, Spain.

title: Domvs Romana
description: A ruined Roman townhouse located on the boundary between Mdina and Rabat, Malta that was discovered in 1881. It dates to the first century B.C.

title: Tumulus of Vissoul
description: A Gallo-Roman burial mound located near Vissoul in Belgium.

title: Jonvelle
description: The ruins of a Gallo-Roman villa with polychrome mosaic pavement.

title: Agora of Magnesia
description: Agora of Magnesia on the Maeander

title: Hadd-Hajar-Clausura
description: Hadd-Hajar-Clausura, a modern appellation for a Roman-era linear barrier that is thought to have been part of the Limes Tripolitanus in the province of Africa Proconsularis.

title: Porticus Octaviae
description: A porticus in the area of the Circus Flaminius, the Porticus Octaviae was dedicated by Augustus sometime after 27 B.C. in honor of his sister, Octavia Minor. The porticus replaced the Porticus Metelli. It was restored twice after major urban fires in A.D. 80 and 203.

title: Church of San Primitivo
details: The Christian church dedicated to a local saint, Primitivus, said to have been beheaded at Gabii. The church was the center of the Late Roman Christian community.

description: The Fontana dell'Acqua Paola or Il Fontanone stands on the Ianiculum near the church of San Pietro in Montorio. It was built in 1612 to mark the end of the Acqua Paola aqueduct after it had been restored by Pope Paul V.

title: Arch of Titus

description: A triumphal arch erected in summa Sacra Via and dedicated to the deified emperor Titus by his brother Domitian, ca. 81 CE.

description: A Roman road of Campania built during the reign of Domitian.

title: Tagisken Plateau
details: The Tagisken plateau contains two burial sites: A larger southern site dated to the early Saka period (7th-5th centuries BCE) and a smaller northern site used throughout the first half of the first millennium BCE (Itina & IAblonskiĭ 2001).
description: A plateau in modern Uzbekistan near the Aral Sea containing two burial sites dating to the first millennium BCE.

name_variants: Sepulcrum Statiliorum@la | Tomb of the Statilii@en | Sepulcrum Statiliorum | Tomb of the Statilii

It was located on the north side of the via Praenestina, ca. 100 m. inside the Porta Maggiore at the south-west side of the modern Viale Principessa Margherita. The tomb's three chambers included a wealth of inscriptions dating from Augustus to Claudius.
description: A columbarium tomb of the slaves and freedmen of the Statilii, and of M. Statilius Taurus, consul in A.D. 44.

title: Roman villa at Verige Bay
description: A Roman villa rustica located in the bay of Verige, dating from the first century B.C. through the sixth century A.D. The villa's ruins lie within Croatia's Brijuni National Park.

title: Άγιος Νικόλαος
description: A paleochristian basilica dating to the fifth and sixth centuries CE, located near the harbor of Limani Khersonesou, Pediada District, northern Crete.

title: Egalgabarinutukua
name_variants: Egalgabarinutukua@akk | Palace of Sargon II@en | Palace That Has No Equal@en | Egalgabarinutukua | Palace of Sargon II | Palace That Has No Equal
description: The palace of the eighth-century-BC Assyrian Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) at Dūr-Šarrukīn (modern Khorsabad), Egalgabarinutukua ("Palace That Has No Equal"), was constructed between 717 BC and 706 BC. This royal residence was constructed on a high, mud-brick terrace located within the city’s citadel, which was located against the northwestern stretch of the city wall. This large, ornately-decorated palace complex consisted of over two hundred rooms (including chapels to the deities Ea, Sîn, Ningal, Adad, Šamaš, and Ninurta) and courtyards, as well as a ziggurat.

title: Nadlesk
description: Nadlesk, Slovenia, was the site of a Roman fortification and associated settlement.

title: Roman villa at Tourmont
description: Remains of a large Roman villa and site of a significant coin hoard of the third century A.D.

title: Šibaniba

description: A settlement mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources, Šibaniba is identified with the modern site of Tell Billa in Iraq. Although excavated in the early 20th century, very little was published about the archaeology of the site (but see now Creamer 2021).

title: Ezida (Kalhu)
name_variants: Ezida@akk | bīt Nabû@akk | Ezida | bīt Nabû
details: The Nabû temple was one of the nine temples that the ninth-century-BC Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II claims to have (re)founded when he made Kalhu his primary royal residence (RIAo Ashurnasirpal II 030 lines 55–60); Ezida, a name that was adopted from this deity’s temple in Borsippa, is situated on the southeast side of the citadel mound. The building plan consists of two large courtyards on the east, the shrines themselves facing onto the inner court; there are also two smaller courtyards, a twin set of shrines, and a reception suite (Throne Room) in the northwest quarter of the building ("South-East Building" or SEB). The entire southern part of the temple was rebuilt by Adad-nārārī III , to whom the seventh-century rulers Ashurbanipal and Sîn-šarru-iškun attribute its foundation (or at least its last rebuilding); see RINAP online Ashurbanipal 007 x 88–90; and Sîn-šarru-iškun Cylinder B . Little is known about Adad-nārārī III’s work on Ezida from the textual record, but inscriptions of his were found on a slab in the main shrine and on colossal statues with folded hands, presumably divine attendants of the god. In addition, Bēl-tarṣi-ilūma, the governor of Kalhu, dedicated two further statues (also attendants) for the life of Adad-nārārī and his mother Sammu-ramat (Semiramis). Adad-nārārī appears to have (re)built the southern wing of the temple, although the original version of the temple (the northern section) was almost certainly 9th century in date (reign of Ashurnasirpal II). The eighth-century-BC king Sargon II made repairs and alterations, as suggested by the upper wall decoration with recesses and rows of engaged columns in the style of the Nabû temple at Dur-Šarrukīn . The seventh-century-BC ruler Ashurbanipal, Assyria's last great king, reports that he rebuilt/restored part of Ezida, most likely the southern part of the temple, the wing worked on by Adad-nārārī III. Fragments of large decagonal clay prisms found in the debris from the collapse of the upper walls, which had fallen into the rooms soon after the fall of Kalhu, or in the rubble left by squatters or 19th century archaeologists who had dug through the fallen and standing mud brick walls, describe work on this temple. Ashurbanipal describes his work as follows: “[At] that time, the temple of the god Nabû which is inside Calah (and) which Adad-nārārī (III), son of Šamšī-Adad (V), king of Assyria, a king prior to me, had built, had become old. I cleared away its dilapidated portion(s) and I mixed beer and wine into (its) kalakku-mortar. Basket carriers moulded bricks while singing. I completely (re)built (this section of Ezida) from top to bottom while there was singing and joyous celebration. I roofed it with long cedar beams (and) [... I] decorated all its copings.” This work took place early in Ashurbanipal’s third decade as king. Aššur-etel-ilāni , Ashurbanipal’s son and immediate successor, made some repairs to the rooms on the east side of the north courtyard, an area that might have served as temple oﬃces. Bricks of this son of Ashurbanipal attest to this. Aššur-etel-ilāni might have also made repairs to the smaller shrines NTS 1 and 2. Sîn-šarru-iškun, another son and successor of Ashurbanipal, also made repairs to Ezida, as attested by fragments of clay cylinders discovered in the ruins of the temple. Unfortunately, the building report of that inscription (Cylinder B lines 30–37) is badly damaged and little can be gleaned about this project of that Assyrian king. Despite this, Sîn-šarru-iškun boasts of laying some of Ezida's foundations and placing the statues of Nabû and Tašmetu back on their daises.
description: When Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud) became the principal administrative center of the Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC, king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) built (or rebuilt) numerous temples. One of those was dedicated to the god Nabû. Unlike most of the religious buildings constructed at Kalhu, the Ezida ("True House") was built in the southeast corner of the Citadel.

title: Hexamilion wall
name_variants: Εξαμίλιον τείχος@grc | Hexamilion tecihos | Εξαμίλιον τείχος

name_variants: Tomb of Hilarus Fuscus@en | Tomb of Hilarus Fuscus
description: The Late Republican tomb of the freedman Hilarus Fuscus along the Via Appia (ca. 30 B.C.).

title: Domus of A. Octavius Primus
name_variants: House of A. Octavius Primus@en | House of A. Octavius Primus
description: The so-called House of A. Octavius Primus was excavated in 1859 and again in 1872.

title: Casa dell'Imperatrice di Russia
name_variants: Casa dell'Imperatrice di Russia@it | Casa della Imperatrice di Russia.@it | Casa dell'Imperatrice di Russia | Casa della Imperatrice di Russia.
description: Dwelling in Pompeii discovered in 1846, likely to have been the house of Inventus.

title: Hot Baths
details: According to La Trobe-Bateman and Niblett, this building was composed of at least seven rooms. One of these had a pillared hypocaust and a geometric mosaic. To the west of the building was a 3m-wide road that led towards the temple precinct.
description: Remains of a large building and baths uncovered between Bilbury Lane and Lower Borough Walls, beneath what is now known as the Gainsborough Spa in Aquae Sulis, modern-day Bath.

title: Theater at Letoon
description: An ancient theater associated with the Letoon, a sanctuary of Leto near the ancient city Xanthos in Lycia. The theater is located on the Roman agora, to the the north of the acropolis.

title: Ménec alignments
description: A complex comprised of 11 rows of megaliths covering an area of 1,165 x 100 meters.

title: Petit-Ménec alignments
description: An alignment of megaliths located east of Kerlescan.

title: Temple of Veiovis
name_variants: Temple of Veiovis@en | Temple of Veiovis

description: The Temple of Veiovis, also attested as Aedes Vediovis, was a temple of ancient Rome located on the Capitoline Hill in a location known as "inter duos lucos", which is interpreted to mean a saddle between the two summits of the hill. The remains of a temple podium were discovered beneath the northwest corner of the Palazzo Senatore in 1938-1939.

title: Mausoleum of Lucius Munatius Plancus
name_variants: Mausoleo di Lucio Munazio Planco@it | Mausoleo di Lucio Munazio Planco
description: A Roman mausoleum that is associated with Lucius Munatius Plancus.

title: Abu Rawash
name_variants: Abu Rawash@en | Abu Roach@en | Abu Roash@en | ابو رواش@arz | ⲁⲃⲣⲱⲟⲩϣⲓ@cop | Abou Rawach@fr | Abou Rawash@fr | Abou Roash@fr | Abu Rawash | Abu Roach | Abu Roash | Abou Rawach | Abou Rawash | Abou Roash

title: Chassenon Roman amphitheater
description: Remains of a Roman amphitheater at Chassenon.

title: Caput Africae

title: Necropoli Romana
description: A Roman necropolis at Brixia dating to the first century CE.

description: Pompeii II, 3, 7 is a garden entrance linked to II, 3, 8 and II, 3,9. II, 3, 8 is identified as a workshop, either the Officina vasaria or caupona of Nicanor. This complex was positioned across the street from the Palaestra.

title: Tor di Mezzavia di Frascati
name_variants: Torre di Mezzavia di Frascati@it | Torre di Mezzavia di Frascati
details: The tower was built in the thirteenth century on the land of the Mardoni family. The tower is of square plan, measuring ca. 7.5 meters per side and standing to a height of 15 meters. It rests on ancient Roman foundations. A structure, now ruinous, built in peperino once surrounded the tower. Its location is strategic in terms of a commanding position along important roads.
description: The Tor di Mezzavia is a Medieval tower located along the modern Via Tuscolana, marking the midway point between Rome and Frascati.

title: Saint-Pierre-d'Aurillac
