description: An Etruscan tomb of the seventh century B.C.

title: (As)Syria (region)
description: The long-lived, ancient region of Assyria, which originated with ancient Aššur and its empire in the early first millennium BCE. Understanding of its extent shifted with time and the perspectives of ancient writers. For Herodotus, Pliny, and Strabo (whose individual understanding seems to have differed), it was a broad region, centered on Mesopotamia. For the Assyrian kings and subsequent imperial powers of the region (as well as Biblical authors), it was confined to a more specific area along the Tigris, corresponding to what is now sometimes referred to as the "Assyrian Homeland". It seems likely that this tighter definition also applied to the ephemeral Roman province of Assyria that is reported to have been established during Trajan's short-lived incursion into Mesopotamia.

title: Minar-i Chakri
description: Minar-i Chakri, located in the Kabul province of Afghanistan, was the site of a Kushan-era pillar dating to the second or third century AD that was destroyed in the later twentieth century by the Soviet army.

title: Peshawar
description: Ancient Peshawar was a capital of the Gandharan kingdom from the second century AD, when it was known as Purushapura.

title: Roman Walls of Le Mans
description: Late-roman fortifications at Le Mans (France).

title: Qaryat ad Dawā’irah, Libya
description: A possible fortified farm site.

title: Zakisovaia Balka
description: An unfortified Hellenized settlement located along the Bug river.

title: Za Rodina
description: A fortified Bosporan site near Temriuk that was founded no later than the fourth century B.C.

title: Tell Hazna I
name_variants: Телль Хазна I@ru | Tell Hazna I@en | Tell' Khazna I | Tell Hazna I
description: Religious and administrative center in Syria with two temple complexes. This site was in use in the Early Dynastic Period and the Uruk and Abaid periods.

title: Sidorovka Burial Ground
description: Burial ground in modern Omsk Oblast, Russia from the Sargat Culture with five burial mounds.

title: Tell Sheikh Hassan
description: Tell in northern Syria first settled in the Early Neolithic, resettled in the Chalcolithic Ubaid period, resettled again in the mid-late Uruk period, and finally resettled again in the Iron Age, from which point the site was continuously inhabited until the early Islamic period. The site was deluged by the creation of Lake Assad in 1974.

title: Vakilabad
description: Hill in Southern Iran with pottery remains from the end of the Bakun period, through the Uruk period, and into the Proto-Elamite period.

title: Villa Fuente Álamo
name_variants: Villa Fuente Álamo@es | Villa Fuente Álamo
description: A Roman villa at Puente Genil in the province of Córdoba in Spain.

title: Palace at Amathous
description: A large-scale building, tentatively identified as a palace, constructed during the 9th century BCE and in use until about 500 CE.

title: Roman macellum at Aeclanum
description: Once hypothetically identified by some scholars as an amphitheater, this structure at Aeclanum is now understood to be a Roman macellum.

title: Temple of Apollo at Corinth
details: Coordinates were determined by eye using Google Earth on 27 October 2011. Imagery date was 8/27/2009 (Image copyright 2011 GeoEye). Eye alt: 210m. The peripteral Doric temple of Apollo at Corinth dates ca. 540 B.C. and replaced an earlier temple of ca. 625 B.C. The temple’s ground plan of 6 x 15 columns grant it the elongated proportion of Archaic Doric temples.
description: The second temple of Apollo at Corinth whose reconstructed remains are visible on the site today. The structure dates ca. 540 B.C.

title: Mithraeum at Vulci
description: A mithraeum was discovered at Vulci in 1975 during excavations of a Roman aristocratic house. The shrine was well preserved with two tauroctony scenes dating to the third century. The site was destroyed in the fourth century A.D.

title: Tsitelbegebi
description: Settlement site between the villages of Takhtidziri and Dvani in the Kareli Municipality of Georgia. The site has late-Achaemenid-Early Hellenistic and Late Hellenistic-Early Roman period cemeteries. This settlement has largely been washed away by flooding of the River Prone.

title: Eganunmah
details: Eganunmah was rebuilt by the following Mesopotamian kings: Kudur-Marduk, Marduk-nādin-ahhē, Nūr-Adad, Sîn-iddinam, and Warad-Sîn.
description: The treasury of the god Nanna/Suen/Sîn in the Ekišnugal temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eganunmah means "House, Exalted Storehouse."

title: Casa di Primigenia
name_variants: House of Primigenia@en | House of Primigenia
description: The House of Primigenia was a townhouse (domus) in Pompeii. It was excavated in 1880.

title: Porticus margaritaria
description: A place located in regio VIII that was connected with jewelers. While the porticus itself is mentioned only in the Regionary Catalogues, numerous extant inscriptions attest to the shops of jewelers in the vicinity of the Sacra Via.

title: Forum Suarium
description: A forum venalium of ancient Rome linked to the sale of pork, the Forum Suarium is mentioned in two inscriptions dating ca. 200 CE. The forum lay near the barracks of the urban cohorts (cohortes urbanae) in the northern portion of the Campus Martius, perhaps near the location of the present Via di Propaganda in metropolitan Rome.

title: Sanctuary of Heracles (Thespiai)
name_variants: ἱερόν Ἡρακλέους@grc | hieron Herakleous | ἱερόν Ἡρακλέους
description: Pausanias describes a Sanctuary of Heracles located at Thespiai with a virginal priestess. This priestess, says Pausanias, was one of the 50 daughters of Thestius. The precise location of the sanctuary is not known today.

title: Khalij al-Masri
description: The Khalij was a canal in Cairo. It was created during the Arab conquest in the seventh century CE, when a Pharaonic, Hellenistic, and Roman canal was rebuilt in order to once again link the Nile River to the Red Sea. It remained in use until the eighth century.

title: Tol-e Sangi (Fars)
description: Neolithic archaeological site in the Fars province of present-day Iran.

title: Roall auxiliary fort
description: A Roman auxiliary fort was identified via cropmarks in Kellington, Selby, England, United Kingdom.

title: Claudia
details: The Claudia tribe was organised in 504 B.C. by the founder of the Claudian house Attius Clausus, later known as Appius Claudius. It was located north of Anio, between Fidenae and Ficulea. Later Claudia adjoined with Clustumina tribe.
description: A Roman rural tribe that was one of the most ancient of Rome's gentes. The gens Claudia traced its history to the earliest days of the Roman Republic. Appius Claudius Sabinus Regillensis, in 495 B.C., was the first of its members to hold the consulship.

title: Ksar Chouline Ancient Quarry
description: An ancient stone quarry, associated with the Roman-era agricultural establishment at modern Ksar Chouline in Tunisia.

title: Abbotsbury Abbey
description: Abbotsbury Abbey is a Benedictine abbey located in Dorset, England. It was founded in ca. 1026 for secular canons, became a monastery of the Benedictine order in 1044, and was dissolved in 1539.

title: Roman amphitheater at Grumentum
name_variants: Grumentum amphitheatre@en | Grumentum amphitheatre | Grumentum amphitheater
description: Grumentum's amphitheater (first century B.C.) is the only known example in Lucania. The arena measures ca. 62.5 by 60 meters.

title: Sikani
name_variants: Tell Fekheriye@ar | Sikāni@akk | تل الفخيرية@ar | Tell Fekheriye | Sikāni | Tall al-Fakhīriyah
details: In earlier cuneiform sources the name appears as Sigan, Uššukani, Waššukkanni, and Wašukana. The name is skn in Aramaic sources.
description: A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources that is generally identified with Tell Fekheriye (Tell Faḫārīya).

title: Villa Prato, Sperlonga
description: A villa rustica excavated by the École française de Rome between 1979 and 1984.

title: Chatal Höyük (Amuq)
details: Not to be confused with Çatalhöyük in Anatolia.
description: Mound site in the Amuq Plain inhabited from the late 4th millennium BCE-mid-1st millennium BCE. In the Late Bronze Age Chatal Höyük was the site of a sizeable town with connections to the Hittite Empire. In the Iron Age the town was within the sphere of the Syro-Hittite state of Unqi, based at Tell Tayinat/Kinaliya. The town gradually declined, but remained inhabited without interruption until at least the fifth century BCE.

title: Vila Mogorjelo
name_variants: Villa rustica "Vila Mogorjelo"@en | Villa rustica Vila Mogorjelo
description: A Roman villa located in Čapljina, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

title: East Stoa at Thermon
description: East stoa fronting the agora at Thermon

title: Minorca (island)
description: Minorca is one of the Balearic Islands of the Mediterranean Sea. Its name likely derives from the Latin 'Insula minor'.

title: Mandra Castellone
name_variants: Fortificazione Sannita di Mandra Castellone@it | Fortificazione Sannita di Mandra Castellone
description: A fortified Oscan center at high altitude (647 meters) located near Capriati al Volturno. The site is difficult to access, and the fortifications measure 80 meters in diameter.

title: Amiternum (Samnium)
details: During the Third Samnite War (293 B.C.), the Roman consul Spurius Carvilius Maximus captured and destroyed Amiternum. The opinion offered by S. Oakley contradicts those of Nissen, Salmon, and La Regina.
description: An ancient city in Samnium, located between Interamna Lirenas and Atina, perhaps corresponding to the modern comune of Sant'Elia Fiumerapido (FR).

title: Pseira (island)
description: Pseira is a small island of the Gulf of Mirabello of the northeastern coast of Crete where the archaeological remains of Bronze Age and later civilizations have been excavated.

title: Monument of Eumenes II/Agrippa
name_variants: Monument of Eumenes II@en | Monument of Agrippa@en | Monument of Eumenes II | Monument of Agrippa
description: A tall plinth next on the left side of the entrance to the Acropolis of Athens, which supported a bronze quadriga. It was probably originally erected for the Attalid king Eumenes II ca. 178 BC, possibly re-dedicated to Marcus Antonius in the 30s BC, and certainly to Agrippa 27-12 BC.

title: Sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia on the Acropolis
name_variants: Ἀρτέμιδος Βραυρωνίας ἱερόν@grc | Sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia@en | Artémidos Braurōnías hierón | Sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia | Ἀρτέμιδος Βραυρωνίας ἱερόν
description: The sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia on the Acropolis of Athens was a branch of the sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron in eastern Attica, perhaps established by Peisistratos or his sons in the second half of the sixth century BC, although the surviving structure probably dates from the 430s BC. It consisted of a Doric stoa with two wings surrounding a court, hosted a giant bronze statue of the Trojan horse by Strongylion, and was probably the site of the Arkteia ritual.

title: Lichades Islands
description: An island group off North Euboea, Greece. Near the Malian Gulf.

title: Grotta Porcina tumulus
description: A rock-cut tumulus of the first half of the sixth century B.C.

title: Ḥorbat 'Uẓa
description: Settlement east of Acre with remains from the Neolithic through the 12th century. The site was destroyed to make a highway in 1991.

title: Castra of Drobeta
description: A Roman castrum dating to the reign of Trajan located on the Danube, at Turnu-Severin, Romania.

title: Villa della Pisanella
name_variants: Villa della Pisanella@it | Villa della Pisanella
description: A Roman villa rustica at Boscoreale that was first discovered in 1868 by Modestino Pulzella. The villa is best known as the findspot of the so-called "Boscoreale Treasure". Following excavation, the remains of the villa were reinterred.

title: Bitwātā
description: The findspot for a cuneiform inscription.

title: Greek theater at Alabanda
description: The Greek theater at Alabanda dates to the Hellenistic period.

title: Paleokastro, Nisyros
description: The classical and Hellenistic period acropolis of the island of Nisyros dates from the sixth to the fourth century BCE.

title: Palace of Tupkish
description: Palace at the Hurrian city Urkesh, constructed by Tupkish in the late third millennium BCE.

title: A'ali Mound Cemetery
description: A large complex of burial mounds located near the town of A'ali in central Bahrain. The burials date to the early Dilmun era, ca. 2050-1700 BCE.

title: House of the West at Baelo
description: Roman domus at Baelo Claudia, also known as House no. 1.

title: Kalatepe
description: A Chalcolithic mound near the village of Büyükgülücek, 15 km. north of Alaca Höyük.

title: Hirbemerdon Tepe
description: A settlement in the upper Tigris River Valley inhabited from the Chalcolithic period through the Iron Age.

title: Tell al-Fakhar
description: Tell al-Fakhar is located in northeastern Iraq. Excavations between 1967 and 1969 two occupation phases dating to the Mitanni/Kassite and Neo-Assyrian periods.

title: Tell Taya
description: Tell Taya is an archaeological site located in Iraq's Nineveh Province. The site was occupied from the third to the first millennia B.C.

title: Serra Orrios
name_variants: Villaggio Nuragico di Serra Orrios@it | Villaggio Nuragico di Serra Orrios
description: An important nuragic complex that includes remains of a megalithic megaron-type structure.

title: Casale dell’Infernaccio
description: A Roman villa located at Magliana Vecchia that dates to the second century A.D.

title: Monte Bibele
description: A massif of the middle Bolognese Apennines rising 617 meters above sea level,

title: Monte Tamburino
description: A peak rising to 594 meters above sea level.

title: Ancient Greek theater at Palazzolo Acreide
description: The theater at ancient Akrai.

title: Bruncu Campulongu Nuraghe
description: A nuragic site.

title: Aramu
description: A general designation for Arameans in Akkadian texts.

title: Edurgina
details: The temple was worked on the the Assyrian king Esarhaddon and the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II.
description: The temple of the god Bēl-Ṣarbi at Bāṣ. The Sumerian ceremonial name Edurgina means "House, Established Abode."

title: I͡Asinovskiĭ III Kurgan
name_variants: Ясиновский III Курган@ru | I͡Asinovskiĭ III kurgan | Iasinovskii III kurgan | Yasinovskiy III kurgan
description: Bronze age burial site near the banks of the Seversky Donets.

title: Tiri Monastery
description: Georgian Orthodox monastery and church in South Ossestia, constructed in the 13th century.

title: Češov
description: The remains of what is likely a Celtic oppidum of the later first millennium BCE, covering some 35 ha and located on the hill known as Češovské valy in the Czech Republic.

title: Cortegana
description: A Spanish village located in the north of the province of Huelva that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.

title: Aroche
description: A Spanish village located in the north of the province of Huelva, near Portugal, that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.

title: Punta Epitaffio nymphaeum
name_variants: Ninfeo di Punta Epitaffio@it | Ninfeo di Punta Epitaffio
description: A now-submerged nymphaeum that dates to the reign of Claudius.

title: Vici Luccei
description: Buildings in the Forum Boarium, mentioned by Cicero, that correspond to a Latin inscription discovered in 1939 and published by Silvio Panciera in 1970.

title: Negrar Roman Villa
description: Remains of a Roman villa with mosaic pavements located near the modern comune of Negrar di Valpolicella were first discovered in 1922.

title: Villa di Casale Ghella
description: A villa complex at the eighth mile of the Via Cassia, to which it was linked by means of a paved diverticulum. The first phase dates to the first century BCE and the villa remained in use until the Late Antique period.

title: Terme Aquae Passeris
name_variants: Terme Aquae Passeris@it | Terme Aquae Passeris
description: A Roman bath located at Aquae Passeris.

title: Unnamed Roman tomb
description: An unnamed Roman tomb that is located near Casale Ghella.

title: So-called Tempio di Venere e Cupido
description: The so-called Temple of Venus and Cupid at Rome is part of the complex of buildings associated with the Sessorian palace. The structure's modern assignation is owed to the discovery of a fragmentary statue of Sallustia Orbiana in the guise of Venus Felix. Sallustia Orbiana was the wife of Alexander Severus. The statue is now held in the Museo Pio Clementino in the Vatican Museums.

title: The House of the Masks
name_variants: The House of the Masks@en | The House of the Masks
details: The House of the Masks, sometimes referred to as House of the Comedians, served as a temporary housing complex for traveling theatrical groups performing at Delos. The house consists of several small rooms connected by a large, central courtyard. It is well known for its intricate mosaics, most notably one depicting Dionysus riding a leopard. Others depict theatrical masks. Built sometime between 150-100 BC, the house saw less frequent use after an attack on Delos by the troops of Mithridates VI of Pontus in 88 BC. By the 2nd century AD, the island was mostly abandoned and the House of Masks fell into ruin.
description: The House of the Masks (also known as the House of the Comedians), built around 150-100 BC, was a luxurious residential complex that may have housed traveling troops of actors performing at the theater in Delos.

title: Temple of Diana
description: The temple in the forum of Augusta Emerita is conventionally known by the misnomer "Temple of Diana", yet was actually dedicated to the Imperial cult.

title: Bakcheion
description: A sanctuary to the west of the Acropolis of Athens, which was the clubhouse for a private religious association called the Iobakchoi, in the 2nd century AD.

title: Eandasaya
name_variants: Eandasaya@sux | bīt Ištar-kakkabī@akk | Eandasaya | bīt Ištar-kakkabī
description: The temple of the goddess Ištar of the Star, Eandasaya (“House Which Rivals Heaven”), was located in the New City district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of two temples in that part of Babylon.

title: Ekitušgirzal
name_variants: Ekitušgirzal@sux | bīt Bēlet-Eanna@akk | Ekitušgirzal | bīt Bēlet-Eanna
details: According to Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV (line 22) and Tablet V (lines 95–96), Ekitušgirzal was located in the New City district of Babylon and was the easternmost landmark of the New City district and the westernmost landmark of the adjoining Kullab district. It is clear that the actual boundary between those two eastern city districts of Babylon was actually a little east of this temple of the goddess Bēlet-Eanna. Ekitušgirzal was located on the bank of the eastern canal.
description: The temple of the goddess Bēlet-Eanna, Ekitušgirzal (“House, Abode of Joy”), was located in the New City district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of two temples in that part of Babylon.

title: Etruscan necropolis of Dometaia
name_variants: Necropoli di Dometaia@it | Necropoli di Dometaia
description: An Etruscan necropolis dating to the sixth century B.C.

title: Findspot of so-called Kabul Hoard
details: Approximate point location as identified on Google Earth base imagery in QGIS 3.x.
description: The approximate location of the fourth century BCE archaeological deposit that is referred to as either the Kabul or Chaman-i Ḥaz̤ūrī Coin Hoard.

title: Italia, Regio IX
description: One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Liguria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.

title: Roman necropolis at Carmo
description: A necropolis of the Roman period wherein most tombs date between the first century BC and the second century AD.

title: Pyramid of Unas
name_variants: Pyramid of Unas@en | Pyramid of Unas
description: A pyramid at Saqqara built for Unas, the final ruler of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty.

title: Künzing Roman amphitheater
description: A Roman timber amphitheater dating from the first to fifth centuries, the Künzing Roman amphitheater measured 46 by 40 meters. The site was discovered during excavations carried out in 2003 and 2004. The archaeological site is no longer visible but a reconstructed evocation of the ancient structure marks the location.

title: Palus Caprae
name_variants: Caprae palus@la | Αἰγὸς ἕλος@grc | Caprae palus | Aigos Helos | Αἰγὸς ἕλος | Caprae palus
description: A site in the Campus Martius of Rome where mytho-historic tradition held that Romulus vanished during a storm, thus marking his apotheosis.

title: Roman theater of Acinipo
description: The Roman theater of Acinipo dates ca. 59-53 B.C.

title: Umm al-Ḥafriyāt
description: Find place for cuneiform inscription.

title: Via Triumphalis necropolis
name_variants: Via Triumphalis necropolis@en | Via Triumphalis necropolis
description: A segment of an imperial necropolis preserved along a portion of a consular road on the Vatican Hill. The Via Triumphalis necropolis was uncovered during the construction of a parking structure in the Via del Pellegrino.

title: Toshbuloq
description: Toshbuloq or Tashbulak was a high-altitude urban center located along the medieval Silk Route (6th–11th century CE).

title: Mes Aynak
description: The site of Mes Aynak in modern Afghanistan flourished between the between the fifth and seventh centuries A.D. More than 400 Buddha statues, stupas, and a 40 ha monastery complex have been documented at the site.

title: Hadrian's Wall (Cumbrian Coast)
description: Line of Roman fortifications along Cumbrian Coast running from western terminus of the stone wall commonly referred to as Hadrian's Wall at Maia (Bowness-on-Solway) in the north to Gabrosentum (Moresby) in the south.

title: Church of the Archangels at Sige
name_variants: Baş Melekler Kilisesi@tr | Taksiyarhon@tr | Baş Melekler Kilisesi | Taksiyarhon
description: Church in the village of Sige (modern Kumyaka) on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara. Constructed under Constantine VI in 780, the structure was restored twice, in 1448 and 1819. It remained in continuous use until it was ultimately abandoned in 1922.

title: Insula Batavorum
name_variants: insula Batavorum@la | Insula Batavorum | insula Batavorum
description: Both Iulius Caesar and Tacitus refer to the "Island of the Batavi", once located at a split in the Rhine and framed by the Waal river on the one hand and the Lower Rhine on the other. This area seems to correspond roughly to the modern Betuwe in the Netherlands.

title: Temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal
description: Large temple dedicated to the Amun located at the base of Jebel Barkal. Designated temple B500, the structure was likely constructed by the Napatan king Piankhi in the 8th century BCE.

title: Wehringen villa rustica
description: A series of villa rustica located along the road to Cambodunum.

title: Knook Castle hill fort
description: Knook Castle is a hill fort located in Wiltshire, England.

title: Treasury of the Massaliots
name_variants: Treasury of the Massaliots@en | Treasury of the Massaliots
description: The Treasury of the Massaliots at Delphi is an in antis building built of Parian marble with Aeolic capitals. It stands in the area of the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia. It dates ca. 510 BCE.

title: Bi'r Minayh
description: Multi-period site surrounding a well in Wadi Minayh, eastern Egypt. The site includes a mining settlement or Christian lavra dated to the 4th-6th centuries CE, an earlier Pharaonic settlement, and numerous inscriptions from the Old, Middle, and New Kingdom periods.

title: Lothal
description: Lothal is among the southernmost cities of the ancient Indus Valley civilisation. The site is located in India, specifically in the Bhal region of the Indian state of Gujarat. The settlement dates ca. 2300 BCE.

title: Nuraghe Arrubiu
description: A Middle Bronze Age nuragic site (ca. 1500 BC) near Cagliari, Sardinia.

title: Basilica di Santa Restituta
name_variants: Basilica di Santa Restituta@it | Basilica di Santa Restituta
description: The Basilica of Santa Restituta is a Christian church in Naples, Italy. It is considered the oldest Christian basilica in the city. Tradition assigns its foundation to Constantine I, and the Liber Pontificalis identifies him as patron in a passage from the life of Pope Sylvester I. The Christian church may have occupied a location that was formerly home to a temple of Apollo.

title: Hospitalet Vell
name_variants: Talayotic town of l'Hospitalet Vell@en | Talayotic town of l'Hospitalet Vell
description: A prehistoric settlement of Mallorca with two phases: a Pre-Talayotic period (ca. 1700/1600 to 1200/1100 BCE) and a Talayotic phase (ca. 1100 to 123 BCE). There is also some evidence of Punic influence.

title: Porta Eburnea
description: The so-called Porta Eburnea or the Arco della Mandorla is an ancient gate of the Etruscan walls of Perusia.

title: Worthy Down
description: A Middle Iron Age-3rd/4th century A.D. settlement complex at Worthy Down, lying 8 km. NNW of Winchester.

title: Alcázar del rey Don Pedro
details: A castle dating to the thirteenth century AD.
description: A fortification at Carmona built by Pedro I of Castile.

title: Villa Romana Baláca
name_variants: Balácapusztai római villagazdaság@hu | Balácapusztai római villagazdaság
description: The site of a Roman villa that was discovered in 1904 in the Balácapuszta field of Vámos village in western Hungary.

title: tribus Stellatina
details: The tribus Stellatina was located to the northeast of Rome, towards the Tiber river. It later became the tribe of Capena.
description: The tribus Stellatina was a later rural tribe of ancient Rome which was established in 387 B.C.

title: Bozköy-Hanaytepe
description: A settlement mound and archaeological site located in the Troad containing evidence of habitation from the Chalcolithic through the Late Bronze Ages.

title: Veranes
description: A Roman villa.

title: Guadalimar
description: The River Guadalimar is a right-bank tributary of the Guadalquivir.

title: Visigothic necropolis, Duratón
description: A Visigothic necropolis at Duratón, Spain, that was discovered in 1929.

title: Aedes Ceres Liber Liberaque
name_variants: Temple of Ceres Liber and Libera@en | Temple of Ceres Liber and Libera
description: The Temple of Ceres, located on the slope of the Aventine Hill in Rome, was originally dedicated by Sp. Cassius in 494/3 B.C.

title: Band-e Kaisar
description: A third century AD Roman bridge located near Shushtar, Iran.

title: Theater at Leuke
description: The theater is located at the north-east end of Kouphonesi. It was a stone-built building that could accommodated ca. 1000 spectators.

title: Cave of Anigrid Nymphs
name_variants: σπήλαιον Ἀνιγρίδων νυμφῶν@grc | spylaion Anigridon nymphon | σπήλαιον Ἀνιγρίδων νυμφῶν
description: A healing sanctuary connected with the river nymphs of the river Anigros. The cave is in proximity to the thermal springs of Lake Kaiafas.

title: Temple of Thelsae
description: A well-preserved Roman period temple located in modern Dmeir, Syria. The sanctuary was later converted into a fortification.

title: Sanctuary of Artemis at Avlonas
description: A sanctuary possibly sacred to Artemis on the island of Lemnos.

title: Philippeion
name_variants: Philippeion@en | Φιλιππείο@el | Φιλιππεῖον@grc | Philippeion | Filippeio | Phlippeion | Φιλιππεῖον
details: The Philippeion was begun by Philip II of Macedon to commemorate his victory at the battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and was completed by Alexander the Great. The circular tholos consisted of small enclosure with eighteen Ionic columns. The structure originally contained five statues by Leochares depicting Philip II, his father, his wife’s father, and Alexander the Great in the middle of the others. It is unclear as to whether Alexander was always meant to be the center of the monument or if this is an emendation of his own. It was probably destroyed along with most of the Sanctuary of Olympia in between 393 - 426 CE.
description: The Philippeion is a tholos at Olympia constructed to celebrate Philip II's victory at Chaeonea in 338 BCE and completed by Alexander the Great.

title: Tell Ischali
description: Tell Ishchali is an archaeological site in Iraq's Diyala province. Its main floruit in antiquity was from ca. 2700–1800 BC, primarily Dynastic through the Isin–Larsa period. The site was part of the city-state of Eshnunna.

title: Shrine of Strenia

title: Theater of Chersonesos
name_variants: Theater of Chersonesos@en | Античный театр (Херсонес)@ru | Theater of Chersonesos | Antichnyy teatr (Khersones)
details: The Greek theater at Chersonesos dates to approximately the 4th or 3rd century BC and represents the cultural vitality of this northern outpost of the Hellenistic world. The theater was constructed in the standard Hellenistic style, featuring a stone cavea (seating area), an orchestra, and a stone stage building. It was built largely of local limestone blocks and is estimated to have accommodated between 1,800 and 2,000 spectators. Its design reflects close ties to the architectural traditions of mainland Greece and the broader Hellenistic world, adapted to the local topography of the coastal site. As in other Greek cities, the theater served multiple civic and religious functions, including dramatic performances, musical and poetry competitions, and public assemblies. The theater remained in active use into the 4th century AD. With the adoption of Christianity in late antiquity, the theater fell out of use and was gradually dismantled. By the 6th century AD, a Christian basilica had been constructed over part of the site, a pattern common across the former Roman and Byzantine world. Archaeological excavations in the 19th and 20th centuries have revealed substantial remains of the theater's foundations, seating, and stage area. The structure is noted among the features listed for Chersonesos on the UNESCO World Heritage list (the site was inscribed in 2013 as the "Ancient City of Tauric Chersonese and its Chora").

title: Palaestra at Olympia
details: The Palaestra at Olympia is a ruin on the west bank of the Kladeos River. Aligned almost perfectly with the cardinal directions, the palaestra takes the form of a large square lined with columns, with a courtyard in the middle. The north side contains the main ephebeum, or exercise room, and a water channel runs through the entire structure. The architecture follows the Corinthian order, but the colonnade around the courtyard is of the Doric order, and other architectural details reflect the Ionic order. It is unclear when this monument was abandoned or destroyed. Towards the end of the third and beginning of the second century BCE, palaestras were used primarily for boxing and wrestling matches, although they also housed social gatherings of other sorts. Every palaestra was equipped with rooms dedicated to powdering, washing, a punching bag, oil storage, youth activities, and intellectual pursuits. In this period, palaestras usually existed only as one element in larger gymnasium complexes. The standardization of the architectural form during this period reflects a set of values and practices shared across the Hellenistic Greek world.

title: Temple of Hera, Olympia

details: The Temple of Hera (or Heraion) at Olympia is a temple dedicated to Hera, the Greek goddess of marriage, the wife of Zeus, and the Queen of the Olympian gods. Built originally out of wood ca. 600-590 BC, the Heraion is the oldest temple at Olympia and one of the earliest examples of the Doric order extant in Greece. As described by the Greek geographer and traveler Pausanias, the wood was gradually replaced with stone over time as the temple was renovated. After being destroyed by an earthquake in the fourth century A.D., however, the temple was not rebuilt. Pausanias, who visited during the second century A.D., described the temple as housing a standing statue of Zeus accompanied by a statue of Hera enthroned, along with numerous other figures of various Greek gods. Pausanias also described the temple's priestesses, known as the Elean women, as having control over the temple's activities, which included organizing the Heraean Games.

title: Governor's Palace at Kalhu
name_variants: Governor's Palace@en | 1949 Building@en | Governor's Palace | 1949 Building
details: This Assyrian palace was excavated by Sir Max Mallowan in 1949 and 1951. Only a 50 x 50 m area of the building has been explored. The audience chambers were decorated with painted, geometric patterns. The building was probably built by Shalmaneser III (r. 858–824 BC) since bricks inscribed with his name were found embedded in the palace's pavements. However, some scholars have proposed that these baked and inscribed bricks were leftover from Shalmaneser's work on Ninurta's ziggurat (located in the northwest corner of the citadel) and that Adad-nārārī III (r. 810–783 BC), the grandson of Shalmaneser, used those bricks to construct the Governor's Palace. Numerous clay tablets discovered in the north wing of the building (Rooms K, M, and S) demonstrate that the building was the office and/or residence of several important individuals in the administration of the Assyrian Empire, perhaps including Kalhu's governor (although this cannot be proved with certainty). These texts, the so-called Governor's Palace Archive , date between 835 and 710 BC and suggest that the principal function of the building was moved elsewhere after Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) transferred the royal court to Dūr-Šarrukīn . Despite this, the building appears to have remained in use until Kalhu was captured and destroyed in 612 BC. Squatters occupied parts of the building after the fall of the Assyrian Empire; some of its inhabitants were buried within the palace. In the Hellenistic Period, the central courtyard was used as a burial ground.
description: This beautifully-decorated Assyrian palace is located just north of the Nabû temple Ezida, in the southeast quarter of the citadel of Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud). The building likely served as the office and/or residence of several important individuals in the administration of the Assyrian Empire, probably including the governor of Kalhu. Numerous cuneiform tablets were discovered in three rooms north of the central courtyard. Because many of those Akkadian texts relate to the activities of several governors, British excavators in the 1950s dubbed the building the "Governor's Palace."

title: Fort Shalmaneser
details: Fort Shalmaneser was the most ambitious building project of Shalmaneser III (r. 858–824 BC). That monumental palatial complex had numerous workshops, treasuries, barracks, private quarters, and grand state apartments built around several large courtyards. Shalmaneser’s grandson Adad-nārārī III (r. 810-783 BC) added to the work of his grandfather, as evident from in-situ inscriptions. When the Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) moved the capital of the Assyrian Empire to Dūr-Šarrukīn , the importance of Fort Shalmaneser, a building whose ancient name is not known, was greatly diminished since Sargon and his successors, especially Sennacherib , constructed their own armories at Dūr-Šarrukīn and Nineveh . Esarhaddon (r. 680–669 BC), according to several inscriptions written in his name, renovated Fort Shalmaneser, a building that he referred to as an ēkal māšarti (‘review palace’). The building was twice destroyed, once in 614 BC and again in 612 BC. After the final sack of Kalhu in 612 BC, locals made hasty repairs to the once-grand palatial complex and lived in it for a significant period of time after the fall of the Assyrian Empire.
description: The ninth-century-BC Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (r. 858–824 BC) constructed an impressive palatial complex in the southeastern corner of the city Kalhu (biblical Calah). This armory, which the seventh-century-BC ruler Esarhaddon (r. 680–669 BC) referred to as an ēkal māšarti (‘review palace’), was completed ca. 846 BC. Fort Shalmaneser, the name of building dubbed by its excavators, remained in use until the very end of the Assyrian Empire (612 BC), although its importance was significantly diminished after the Assyrian court moved away from Kalhu at the end of the eighth century BC, first to Dūr-Šarrukīn and then to Nineveh.

title: West House at Vasiliki
details: The West House is one component of an architectural complex previously known as the “House on the Hilltop” built at Vasiliki in Early Minoan IIB. The other component is the Red House, which served as a residential area. The West House was built as an annex to the Red House, with poorer construction. The West House is believed to have been an area for storage as well as weaving, which is indicated by the presence of loom weights. These buildings are examples of early complex architecture on Crete, showing the development of planning and architectural sophistication at a stage before the appearance of Minoan palaces. The techniques used at Vasiliki were particular to this Minoan settlement alone. The thick walls of the West House were made of mud with wooden beams laid horizontally and transversely to strengthen the walls. The building was destroyed by fire around the end of the EMIIB period.

title: Grave Circle B
name_variants: Grave Circle B@en | Grave Circle B
details: Grave Circle B was a grave complex located outside of the Bronze Age citadel at Mycenae. In use from around 1650-1550 BC, it enclosed 14 shaft graves and 12 cist graves. These graves were used and reused, possibly along family lines. Most of the 35 skeletons found were men; only four were positively identified as female. This, as well as the forensic data showing that the deaths were mostly violent, suggests that these graves were used for an elite warrior class. The site is notable for the extensive presence of grave goods. The quality of goods at the site (which includes weapons and pottery) reveals an increasing differentiation of wealth within Mycenaean society and the rise of an elite class. Some scholars also believe that many of the items were either imported from or influenced by Minoan centers on Crete, which gives insight into the relationship between Crete and mainland Greece at this time. The grave circle was excavated in the early 1950s by a team of archaeologists from Greece.

title: Portara on Naxos
details: The Portara is the entryway to an unfinished temple that was begun by the tyrant Lygdamis of Naxos in the Late Archaic period, around 530 BC. It stands 26 feet high and is located on an islet known as Palatia, which is connected to the north shore of Naxos by a man-made causeway. The islet is believed to be the place where Ariadne was abandoned by Theseus while she slept after she helped Theseus escape the labyrinth and the Minotaur. In local lore, the Portara was thought to have been the entrance to Ariadne's palace. The islet was also traditionally believed to be the place where Dionysus, the god of wine, found the sleeping Ariadne, who would become his bride. This led to the hypothesis, now generally rejected, that the entrance belonged to a temple dedicated to Dionysus. The most recent scholarly interpretation proposes that the temple was dedicated to Apollo because the entrance's unusual westward orientation aligns it with Delos, Apollo's birthplace.
description: The Portara is the 26-foot-tall doorway of an unfinished Ionic temple of the Late Archaic Period on the island of Naxos.

title: Vignale
details: The archaeological site of Vignale was inhabited continuously from the third century B.C. to the fifth century A.D. Until the middle of the first century B.C. While it was probably a small farm, it nevertheless had already some connection with the road network. Around 40 B.C. a villa was established at the site, with a production of wine-carrying amphorae (Dressel 1). During the principate of Augustus, alongside the villa some buildings started to function as a mansio . Only a few decades later, during the reign of Tiberius or Nero, a new owner established a massive production centre for roof-tiles at the site, some of them bearing the maker's stamp M·FULVI·ANT. Some of these stamps were also found in Rome. By the second century A.D., the settlement was no longer an active production centre, but continued to be a dwelling place. In the fifth century, possibly following a short period of abandonment, a small village occupied the ruins, with wooden huts and a large funerary area. The archaeological site has been known since 1831, but regular excavation only began in 2003.

title: Farmhouse 151 in the chora of Chersonesos
name_variants: Farmstead 151@en | Farmhouse 151@en | Site 151@en | Farmstead 151 | Farmhouse 151 | Site 151
details: The remains of the farmhouse at site 151 were excavated in the 1990s by a joint-Ukainian-American team. It was originally built around the 3rd century BC and was occupied throughout the Hellenistic period until the early 1st century BC. The remnants of Hellenistic vineyard planting walls at site 151 provide insight into the agricultural practices of the period. The farmhouse was likely used for wine production and food storage using pithoi (large clay containers). Other finds from the site include storage ware, various types of fineware pottery, and amphorae. Another significant archaeological find was a household shrine in the form of a niche containing a kantharos and a terracotta club; together with some goat bones that seem to represent ritual offerings, these items may represent household cult focused on Dionysus and Heracles. The farmhouse features a fortified tower, which was modified in ways that indicate an increasing concern with defense in the later years of the site's occupation. Site 151 likely went out of use in the early 1st century BC.
description: Site 151 is in the chora (agricultural territory) of the ancient Greek colony of Chersonesos. The farmhouse consists of a modest structure, a fortified tower, and a small household shrine. Modifications over time indicate changes in defensive concerns until its abandonment.

title: Nergal Gate
name_variants: abul Nergal@akk | Nergal Gate@en | Erra-mušamqit-ayyābī@akk | Erra-šāgiš-zāmânīya@akk | abul Nergal | Nergal Gate | Erra-mušamqit-ayyābī | Erra-šāgiš-zāmânīya
details: The gate is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib dating to 697-691 B.C. In those texts, the Nergal Gate is always listed as the second gate of the northern stretch of wall. Unlike Nineveh’s seventeen other gates, this entrance to the city is flanked by colossal stone human-headed winged bulls. The name of the gate is Erra-mušamqit-ayyābī in texts dated to 697-695 and 691 B.C. and Erra-šāgiš-zāmânīya in a text written in 694 B.C. The position of the gate is known and it was excavated in 1846, 1849-51, 1941, 1956, and 1966-67. Like several other gates, the Nergal Gate has been partially reconstructed.
description: The northern city wall of Nineveh had three gates: the Nergal Gate was middle gate. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it and gave it the Akkadian ceremonial names Erra-mušamqit-ayyābī ("The God Erra Is the One Who Cuts Down Enemies") and Erra-šāgiš-zāmânīya ("The God Erra Is the One Who Cuts Down My Enemies").

title: Ušnanis
details: The location of Ušnanis is presently unknown. From the inscriptions of Sargon II, it is certain that it was near another Quean fortress (Harrua), a place that was also taken away from Que by the Phrygians. One text of that Assyrian king mentions Ušnanis and Harrua together with a third fortress: Qumasi. With regard to Harrua, E. Forrer (1920) and P. Naster (1938) tentatively identified it with classical Seleucia ad Calycadnum /Hyria (modern Silifke), in Cilicia Tracheia . That proposed location, however, is well outside the territorial reach of Que (as already noted, e.g., by A. Bagg [2007]) and, therefore, one must look for a location a bit closer to Que ( Cilicia Pedias ), perhaps near the Cilician Gates . Ušnanis is generally thought to have been near Harrua and, thus, possibly also located near the Cilician Gates.
description: Ušnanis is a Quean fortress located on the Cilician plain. In the eighth century BC, perhaps only for a short time, Phrygia controlled the territory in which Ušnanis was located. title: Temple of Hera I (the "Basilica")
name_variants: Tempio di Hera detto la Basilica@it | Tempio di Hera detto la Basilica
details: Normal 0 false false false EN-US JA X-NONE /* Style Definitions */ table.MsoNormalTable {mso-style-name:"Table Normal"; mso-tstyle-rowband-size:0; mso-tstyle-colband-size:0; mso-style-noshow:yes; mso-style-priority:99; mso-style-parent:""; mso-padding-alt:0in 5.4pt 0in 5.4pt; mso-para-margin:0in; mso-para-margin-bottom:.0001pt; mso-pagination:widow-orphan; font-size:12.0pt; font-family:Cambria; mso-ascii-font-family:Cambria; mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-hansi-font-family:Cambria; mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin;} The Temple of Hera I was probably dedicated to the wife of Zeus, goddess of fertility and creativity. Constructed in the Doric order in the middle of the sixth century BC, the temple is peripteral, with nine columns along the east and west facades and eighteen along the north and south. The unusual division of the cella by a colonnade has been attributed to either the structural design or a double dedication to Hera and Zeus, although these explanations are still debated. Several architectural details, such as the prominent entasis of the columns and the curvature of the echinus of their capitals, help date the construction to the Archaic period. Other features reflect an interest in decoration and elaboration unusual for the Doric order, but more common in the West: some of the capitals, for example, have carved floral bands around the base of the echinus. Upon discovery of the temple in the eighteenth century, archaeologists and architects began to argue that Roman architectural developments might have their roots in earlier Greek forms. Although early archaeologists mistakenly identified the Temple as a civic building (the reason it is also known as the "Basilica"), several votives depicting Hera found at the site confirm the religious nature of the building and the goddess to whom it was dedicated. Location based on OpenStreetMap.

title: Odeon at Kom el-Dikka
name_variants: Odeon at Kom el-Dikka@en | Odeum at Kom el-Dikka@en | المدرج الروماني@ar | Theatre of Kom el-Dikka@en | small theatre@en | Odeon at Kom el-Dikka | Odeum at Kom el-Dikka | al-Madraj al-Rumani | Theatre of Kom el-Dikka | small theatre
details: The odeon at Kom el-Dikka was constructed in the fourth century CE and rebuilt in the late fifth to first half of the sixth century CE. Its construction was part of a larger building project in Alexandria that redesigned civic space, including an imperial bath complex and a large portico. In its first phase, the odeon was an open air theater-like structure with 16 to 17 rows of seating. In the second phase, the odeon was reduced to 13 rows of seats and dome added to create a covered space. The vestibule and main room of the odeon were decorated with mosaics and wall-paintings. The odeon initially probably served as a location for staging plays and musical performances, and later, beginning in the 6th century, likely became part of an academic complex which included numerous auditoria , or lecture halls. As part of that complex, it was likely used to host public orations and declamations before an audience. Graffiti indicate that the odeon was a probably also a meeting place for the faction of the Greens. A Polish-Egyptian team has been excavating in the area continuously since 1960. The odeon was reconstructed in 1966-67.
description: The Odeon at Kom el-Dikka, used both for entertainment and academic functions, was built in the center of ancient Alexandria in the fourth century CE and rebuilt between the end of the fifth and beginning of the sixth century CE.

description: A coastal fortified settlement dating to the late Bronze and early Iron Ages, known in modern times as Castro de Cociñadoiro and A Punta de Muros. The site was excavated ahead of its complete destruction in the first decade of the 21st century as part of the development of the Porto Exterior da Coruña at Punta Langosteira.

title: Roman Circus (Bosra)
details: Location of the center of Roman Circus in the Ancient City of Bostra. Coordinates determined by eye in Google Earth in October 2012.
description: The Roman circus of Bosra dates to the third century.

title: Temple of Janus, Autun

title: Turkdean
description: Site of a major Roman villa complex in Gloucestershire, active from late second century CE until the end of the fourth century.

title: Thasarte
description: Now unlocated, Thasarte was a place in Africa Proconsularis that is included on the Peutinger map.

title: Anami
description: Anami was an ancient settlement in Egypt. It is marked on the Peutinger map along the route leading from Panopolis to Chenoboskeion. Anami was not included in the Barrington Atlas. It should be noted that compilers of the Tabula Peutingeriana database at the Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt correlate Anami with a place named Antaiopolis/Tkoou (BAtlas 77 FC) that is a standalone place in the Pleiades gazetteer.

title: Pythionike monument
description: A cenotaph monument in western Attica praised by Pausanias, the Pythionike monument was located along the Sacred Way linking Athens and Eleusis. Stewart (2012) speculates whether Sulla could have plundered statuary from the monument when he marched on Athens.

title: Monte San Giovanni Campano
description: Monte San Giovanni Campano is the site of ancient first millennium BC fortifications, atop which was built the eleventh century fortress, Castello di Monte San Giovanni Campano, where Thomas Aquinas was imprisoned.

title: Aeaea
name_variants: Αιαία@grc | Aeaea@la | Aiaia | Aeaea | Αιαία | Aeaea
description: The mythical, unlocatable island of Circe from the Odyssey, visited by Odysseus. Possibly identified with Cape Circaion on the west coast of Italy

title: Assur Archive 26
name_variants: Assur Archive 26@en | N 11 Archive@en | Assur Archive 26 | N 11 Archive
details: The archive is located near the Adad ziqqurrat in Assur.
description: Southwest of the Adad ziqqurrat in Assur, in dE5V, researchers found 6 clay tablets, some of which had envelopes, in the remains of a destroyed private house. The archive, belonging to Dadaya, dates to the reigns of Aššur-etel-ilāni (ca. 630–627 BC) and Sin-šarru-iškun (ca. 626-612 BC) and mostly contains loan documents.

title: Hathor Temple, Timna Valley

title: Theater at Phoinike

title: Torrione di Micara

title: Montione
description: A large villa platform, perhaps measuring 150 meters square, located near Grottaferrata, southeast of Rome. The earliest phase belonged to the first century B.C.

title: Unnamed place
description: A place marked on the Peutinger map whose label is now illegible. It is positioned between Cisi municipium and Rusuccuru colonia.

title: Myrmeces scopuli
description: Myrmeces scopuli, cliffs or rocks near the mouth of the Hermos River at the point where it debouches into the Gulf of Smyrna. According to Pliny the Elder, they are to be located near Leukai.

title: Kef Kalesi
name_variants: City of the god Haldi in the land Ziuquni@xur | Kef Kalesi@tr | City of the god Haldi in the land Ziuquni | Kef Kalesi
description: Kef Kalesi is an Urartian fortress near Adilcevaz in the area of Lake Van in the southeast of Turkey. According to an Urartian inscription of Rusa, son of Argišti II (7th century BCE), it was built by this very king. The inscription further mentions the foundation of a new city at this site which Rusa named "City of the God Haldi in the Land Ziuquni".

title: Via Praenestina

description: Site for Urartian rock inscription.

title: Berlanga
name_variants: Berlanga de Duero@es | Berlanga de Duero
description: Berlanga de Duero is a Spanish municipality located in the province of Soria, in the autonomous region of Castile and León. An object dubbed the "Berlanga cup" was discovered here. This object is a hemispherical bowl that belongs to a small group of artifacts referred to as "Hadrian's Wall pans", as these vessels depict places and names from sites along the line of Hadrian's Wall.

title: Tomb of the Seven against Thebes at Eleusis
description: According to Pausanias, the Seven against Thebes were buried at Eleusis, at the road to Megara, after the sanctuary of Metaneira. The location of this monument is unknown today.

title: Pozzo sacro di Sa Testa

title: House of the Birds at Italica

title: Ribadiso Roman bridge

title: Sant Amanç de Viladés
description: The archaeological site of Sant Amanç de Viladés includes multi-period remains, stretching from indigenous Iberian remains to those of a Roman villa to Medieval occupation.

title: Guillena

title: Roman theater at Perge
description: The Roman theater at Perge was built ca. 120 AD and renovated ca. 250 AD.

title: balneum Caesaris
description: A bath complex known from the Severan marble plan and perhaps also referred to in the Historia Augusta.

title: Cuccuru Nuraxi
description: A nuragic site near Cagliari, Sardinia.

title: Cattabania (region)
description: A region of pre-Islamic, south-western Arabia centered in the Baihan valley. Strabo notes that this region produces frankincense.

title: House of Aufidia Cornelia Valentinilla
name_variants: domus di Aufidia Cornelia Valentinilla@it | domus di Aufidia Cornelia Valentinilla

title: Domus dei Ritratti

title: Mut el-Kharab

title: Brills Farm

title: Ripatransone
description: In antiquity, Ripatransone was a significant Picene center. It now lies in the Province of Ascoli Piceno, in the Italian region Marche.

title: Amphissa Tholos
name_variants: Amphissa Tholos@en | Θώλος Άμφισσας@el | Tholosgrab von Amfissa@de | Amphissa Tholos | Tholos Ampfissas | Tholosgrab von Amfissa

title: Ince fortlet

description: A double-ditched enclosure site located to the north of the modern village of Ince (Cheshire, England) has been identified as a Roman fortlet. The enclosure covers some 0.48 ha and was first identified via crop marks seen in aerial photographs in 1994.

title: Kirphis (Mountain)

title: Temple of Apollo Pythios
details: The temple of Apollo Pythios was constructed in the second century BC. It stands on the southern part of the Agios Stephanos hill. This Doric-order temple is rather small compared to other Doric temples. Its peripteros consists of 6 Doric columns across the front and fewer than 12 along the sides. It was made of local limestone. After subsequent earthquakes and damage from bombing during WWII, only four columns remain. An Italian crew started excavating the temple in 1914. After the excavation, the Italian excavators re-erected the remaining columns of the East facade. Minimal archaeological work has been done since the initial excavation.
description: The Hellenistic Temple of Apollo Pythios on the Acropolis of the city of Rhodes.

title: House of the Actors
name_variants: Casa degli Attori@it | Casa dei Mimi@it | Casa degli Attori | Casa dei Mimi
description: A Roman domus in in Pompeii overlooking the via Stabiana, with shops on both sides of the entrance. The site was excavated in 1872 and bombed in 1943. Located at I,2,6.

title: Roman amphitheater at Marruvium
description: The Roman amphitheater at Marruvium measures 95 by 75 meters.

title: Temple of Aphrodite (Thessalonica)
description: The remains of a marble temple executed in the Ionic order.

title: Kuruçay Höyük
description: Kuruçay Höyük is a fortified settlement site of the Late Chalcolithic period (ca. 4200–3100 BCE)

title: Graecostadium
description: Located in Regio VIII of the ancient city of Rome, Graecostadium refers to a place that is either an area that is enclosed by walls or a set of buildings. This seems to have been a large area in any case. The Graecostadium is damaged by fire and subsequently restored under Antoninus Pius. Ths place burned again during the reign of Carinus.

title: Old Kandahar citadel

title: London Wall
details: The remains of a third century AD defensive all around Roman Londinium.
description: London's original Roman wall in stone was built ca. A.D. 190 to 225. The wall originally had a length of ca. 4 km (2.5 miles and enclosed an area of ca. 134 hectares. It once included four city gates.

title: Cadira del Bisbe

title: Le Carrozze-Gravetta

title: Freilichtmuseum Römerbad
description: A Roman bath complex located at Rottweil, Germany.

title: Çamlıdere
description: Modern name for an otherwise unnamed ancient settlement. It may have been a possession of the Ptolemies, Rhodes, and the Attalid kingdom, and was at least peripherally involved with Rome's war against Aristonikos as a Roman ally.

title: Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert
description: The abbey of Saint-Guilhem-le-Desert or Abbey Gellone, is Benedictine abbey founded in A.D. 804 by Guillaume Gellone. The abbey is a listed historical monument in France and was listed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1998 .

title: Umbranicia
description: A region in Gaul marked on the Peutinger map.

title: Handere bridge
description: A bridge on the road from to Egin and Harput.

title: Saintes-Marie-de-la-Mer Roman Port
description: A Roman commercial port near the modern French town of Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer is attested by over forty Roman-era shipwrecks discovered in the area since the 1990s, most carrying cargoes of metal. The excavators posit in Roman times a significantly different coastline (generally further south) and an old mouth of the Rhone (Ancien Rhône de Saint-Ferréol), located to the east of Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer (Long 2011, Figure 1).

title: Villa in via Enzo Tortora
name_variants: villa di via Enzo Tortora@it | villa di via Enzo Tortora
description: A villa site that was active from the middle Republican period to the early Middle Ages was investigated in 2009 and 2010 at via Enzo Tortora, no. 79. The site is located about 500 meters east of the line of the ancient Via Flaminia.

title: Capanna dell’Elceto
description: The so-called Capanna dell’Elceto was part of a fortified Protovillanovan settlement located near Monte Rovello, Italy.

title: Parco archeologico Griso-Laboccetta
details: Archaeological evidence on the site includes remains of a sanctuary of Demeter.
description: An Archaic to Hellenistic sanctuary sacred to Demeter.

title: Sol et Luna, Aedes
description: A temple sacred to Sol ("The Sun") and Luna ("The Moon") that likely predated the imperial construction of the Circus Maximus. Given this dating, the preexisting temple came to be incorporated into the cavea of the circus. The temple is iconographically represented in coin issues of the reign of Trajan.

title: Marduk Gate
name_variants: Marduk Gate@en | Abul-Marduk@akk | Šuʾâšu-rēʾi@akk | Marduk Gate | Abul-Marduk | Šuʾâšu-rēʾi
details: The Marduk Gate was one of four gates of the inner city of Babylon excavated by Robert Koldewey at the beginning of the 20th century. The gate is called the Belidan Gate in Herodotus (3.155.6).
description: The Marduk Gate is one of Babylon's eight city gates and it is situated on the eastern side of the inner city, directly east of the Kullab quarter. King Nebuchadnezzar II built the gate ca. 575 B.C.

title: Via Hadriana
description: A Roman road established by Hadrian running from Antinoopolis to Berenice. The road was completed in AD 137.

title: Cento Camerelle (Bacoli)
description: The so-called Cento Camerelle at Bacoli is an archaeological site that dates initially to the late republican period. A multi-story structure with provisions for a water system and cisterns, the building is linked initially to the Roman consul Quintus Hortensius Hortalus and later to Antonia Minor, the mother of the emperor Claudius.

title: Majorca (island)
name_variants: Mallorca@ca | Cezīre-i Mayorḳa@ota | Mallorca | Cezīre-i Mayorḳa
description: Majorca is the largest island in the Balearic Islands archipelago in the western Mediterranean Sea.

title: Tell Djassa
description: Tell Djassa is an archaeological site in the upper Khabur River basin identified by salvage excavations in 1988-1990. Four main phases of human occupation were identified, all belonging to the third millennium BCE. The site was re-settled in the later first millennium BCE as demonstrated by Hellenistic pottery.

title: nu-x-ù
details: The name of this city district in western Babylon is corrupt, damaged, or illegible in all extant and identified copies of Tintir = Babylon V (line 99). Because it did not have any temples, shrines, or daises, it is not mentioned in Tintir = Babylon IV . nu-x-ù/nu-HAR-UD is the westernmost city district and it appears to have been bounded on the south, west, and north by the walls Imgur-Enlil and Nēmetti-Enlil (with access in and out of the inner city by the Adad Gate and probably also the King’s Gate ) and on the west by the Bāb-Lugalerra , Kumar , and Tuba districts. According to Tintir = Babylon V (line 99), the western and eastern limits of nu-x-ù/nu-HAR-UD were the Adad Gate and Akus Gate (which formed part of the former, Old Babylonian city wall).
description: According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, nu-x-ù/nu-HAR-UD (name fragmentary and not reconstructable) was one of the four city districts of the western half of the inner city of Babylon.

title: Kumar
details: Kumar is the central district of the eastern part of the western half of the inner city of Babylon. It is bounded by the Arahtu River on the east, by the Bāb-Lugalerra district on the north, by the nu-x-ù district on the west, and by the Tuba district on the south. According to Tintir = Babylon IV (lines 34–40), the temples Enamtila, Eešmah, Ekadima, Emesikilla, Edikukalama, Eʾesirkalama, Enamhe were located in this part of Babylon. According to Tintir = Babylon V (line 100), the western and eastern limits of Kumar were the Akus Gate and the temple Enamtila, which probably was located close to the western bank of the Arahtu River. The district is first attested in the Old Babylonian Period.
description: According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, Kumar was one of the four city districts of the western half of the inner city of Babylon and it contained seven temples.

title: Bāb-Lugalerra
details: Bāb-Lugalerra is the northern district of the eastern part of the western half of the inner city of Babylon. It is bounded by the Arahtu River on the east, by the Kumar district on the south, by the nu-x-ù district on the west, and by the walls Imgur-Enlil and Nēmetti-Enlil (with access in and out of the inner city by the Enlil Gate ) on the north. According to Tintir = Babylon IV (lines 31–33), the temples Enunmah, Egišhurankia, and Ebursasa were located in this part of Babylon. According to Tintir = Babylon V (line 101), the western and eastern limits of Bāb-Lugalerra were the navel of the bow of the temple of the goddess Bēlet-Ninūa (Egišhurankia) and the bank of the (Arahtu) river. The district is first attested in the Old Babylonian Period.
description: According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, Bāb-Lugalerra was one of the four city districts of the western half of the inner city of Babylon and it contained three temples.

details: An inscription of Šamaš-reša-uṣur of Suhu mentions the city/town Qaqqar-aradāt together with Alu-eššu, Baqa , and Ribaniš.
description: An unlocated city/town in the kingdom of Suhu, probably not far from Alu-eššu, Baqa, and Ribaniš.

description: Hilltop structure in the Mesara Plain in south-central Crete in use during throughout the Minoan period. Two Tholos tombs are located north of the building.

title: Atlantis
name_variants: Atlantis@en | Ἀτλαντὶς νῆσος@grc | Atlantis | Atlantis Nesos | Ἀτλαντὶς νῆσος
description: Atlantis is the mythical island state used by Plato in the Timaeus and Critias as an example of a powerful and hubristic nation. It has been used in later literature, speculation in pseudo-history, and conspiracy theory.

title: Oude Rijn
description: The "Old Rhine" is now a branch of the Rhine River delta in the Dutch provinces of Utrecht and South Holland. In antiquity, this was a part of the main River Rhine, which forked at the Betuwe into a northern branch, the Rhine, and a southern branch, the Waal.

title: Verbovskiĭ Mogil'nik
description: A burial mound dated to the fourth-third centuries BCE located northwest of the city of Stavropol'.

title: House of Mikion and Menon
name_variants: House of Mikion and Menon@en | House of Mikion and Menon

title: New Kalabsha Island
description: New Kalabsha is a promontory located near Aswan. It currently is the site of several ancient temples relocated to avoid the rising waters of Lake Nasser created by the construction of the Aswan High Dam.

title: Nirabu
name_variants: Nayrab@ar | Nīrabu@akk | نيرب@ar | Nayrab | Nīrabu | Naiyrab

title: House of Messius Ampliatus
name_variants: II.2.4@en | House of Messius Ampliatus@en | II.2.4 | House of Messius Ampliatus
description: A Pompeian domus excavated in 1916, 1918, and 1921. (II.2.4).

title: Chancy
description: The fortification located at Chancy dates initially to the reign of Valentinian.

title: Saint-Saphorin
description: A Roman villa located near the shores of Lake Geneva.

title: Roman amphitheater of Carthage
description: A Roman amphitheater built at Carthage.

title: Tophet of Carthage
description: The Tophet of Carthage, also known as tophet de Salammbô, is a hybrid sanctuary-necropolis of Punic Carthage.

title: Nuraghe Cabudbbene
description: Nuraghe Cabudbbene I is a single tower nuraghe built of trachyte.

title: Catacomb of the Nunziatella
name_variants: Catacomb of the Nunziatella@en | Catacomb of the Nunziatella
description: The Catacomb of the Nunziatella or the Catacomb of the Annunziatella is an ancient catacomb located in Rome's Ardeatina neighborhood in the via di Grotta Perfetta. The catacomb was excavated on the site of a large Republican-period necropolis and does not seem to have been connected with any Christian martyrs.

title: House of Hylas at Italica
description: Residence named for a mosaic floor with an emblem showing Hylas carried off by the nymphs. The mosaic has been removed to the Archaeological Museum in Sevilla.

title: Fabrateria Nova amphitheater
description: Remains of a Roman amphitheater at Fabrateria Nova.

title: Porticus Boni Eventus
name_variants: porticus Eventus Boni@la | porticus Eventus Boni
description: A portico built in 374 CE by an urban prefect named Claudius near the temple of the god Bonus Eventus.

title: Tumulus of Avennes
description: The Tumulus of Avennes is a Gallo-Roman burial mound dated to the Flavian period located in Liège Braives, Belgium.

title: Tumulus of Avernas
description: A Gallo-Roman burial mound located near Avernas-le-Bauduin, Belgium.

title: Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor
name_variants: Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor@en | Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor

The villa was partially excavated by Vincenzo De Prisco between July 1899 and March 1902. The villa's exceptional Second Style wall paintings were removed and dispersed among various museums, a move that remains controversial. The villa itself is not well understood overall. It is no longer visible.
description: The Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor was built after the middle of the first century B.C. and was ultimately destroyed by the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius. The villa may have been owned by P. Fannius Synistor and/or L. Herennius Florus.

title: Mura Serviane, Anagni
description: An ancient opus quadratum wall at Anagni referred to as "Mura Serviane" based on its construction technique.

title: Tomb of Aulus Hirtius
name_variants: Sepolcro di Aulo Irzio@it | Sepolcro di Aulo Irzio
description: A tomb located in Rome's Campus Martius. Its remains are now submerged in the channelized waters of the Euripus canal beneath the Palazzo della Cancelleria.

title: Temple B
name_variants: Fortunae huiusce [d]iei in campo@la | Temple B@en | Tempio B@it | aedes Catuli@la | Fortuna Huiusce Diei in Campo | Temple B | Tempio B | aedes Catuli | Fortunae huiusce [d]iei in campo | aedes Catuli

title: Chirik-Rabat
description: City in southern Kazakhstan inhabited from the 14th century BCE-14th century CE. Chirik-Rabat was an important trade center on the Silk Road.

title: Water Eaton Roman camps
description: A series of Roman camps on the River Penk along the line of Watling Street.

title: Market Hall at Aspendos
description: A large, Hellenistic structure at Aspendos subsequently reused as the foundation for a Roman-era basilica that seems to have had a presumably public market and grain storage function.

title: Pen-Llwyn fort
description: A Roman fort was established in the Flavian period and occupied until at least AD 125 and possibly AD 140.

title: Mausoleum of Clesippus Geganius
description: The ruins of a first century B.C. Roman tomb along the Via Appia at Mesa di Pontinia.

title: Civita d'Arlena
name_variants: Civita del Fosso di Arlena@it | Civita d'Arlena@it | Civita del Fosso di Arlena | Civita d'Arlena

It was the site of Etruscan occupation until the third century BCE. Excavations carried out by the École française de Rome (1952 to 1958) revealed parts of a fortification wall and a sacred building, along with evidence for a city plan.

Excavations exposed occupation layers dating from Ubaid 0 (ca. 6500-5400 B.C.) to Ubaid 4. The site was first identified by André Parrot and then excavated by Jean-Louis Huot (1976, 1978, 1981-1989).
description: Tell el-'Oueili is an archaeological site located in the Dhi Qar Governorate of southern Iraq. Occupation at the site predates the occupation levels of Eridu, making Tell el-'Oueili one of the earliest known human settlements of southern Mesopotamia.

title: Ponte dei Saraceni, Adrano
name_variants: Ponte dei Saraceni, Adrano@it | Ponte dei Saraceni | Adrano
description: A bridge over the Simeto River with ancient origins, the so-called Ponte dei Saraceni has been rebuilt several times, including after the 1693 Sicily earthquake.

title: Hannibal's Bridge (Rapallo)
description: A ruined bridge at Rapallo, Italy, that the local toponymastic tradition links to the third-century BCE military operations of the Carthaginian commander Hannibal.

title: Haut Bécherel
description: Haut Bécherel is the site of a major Gallo-Roman sanctuary sacred to Mars.

title: Capitol Baths
description: A bath complex dating to the later second century that were subsequently repurposed as a Christian basilica.

title: Verzino
description: The compilers of the Barrington Atlas indicate that evidence for ancient silver working was identified at Verzino in the present-day Italian region of Calabria. This site is located in the valley of the River Neto (the ancient Neaethus).

title: al-Husn Church
description: A ruined and now largely dispersed fifth-century CE church on the outskirts of al-Bara, Syria.

title: Church of Saint Sophia
description: The Church of Saint Sophia, also referred to as the Old Bishopric, is an Eastern Orthodox church located in Nesebar, eastern Bulgaria. The church originally dates to the sixth century.

title: Longthorpe II
description: A Pre-Roman Iron Age farmstead with a relatively short occupational history gave way to a Roman installation that was situated outside the confines of the first-century fort at Longthorpe near Peterborough. This installation was termed a "works-depot" by its excavators and shows evidence of both ceramic production and metalworking. title: Step Gate
name_variants: abul mušlālum@akk | Step Gate@en | Asakki Stairway Gate@en | Mushlalu Gate@en | Mušēṣât-šīr-asakki@akk | abul mušlālum | Step Gate | Asakki Stairway Gate | Mushlalu Gate | Mušēṣât-šīr-asakki
details: The gate is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib dating to 697-691 B.C. Most of Sennacherib’s inscriptions record that the Step Gate was the sixth of the south- and east-facing gates. One inscription, however, states that it was the fifth of those gates. The gate’s exact position is uncertain and cannot be confirmed from in situ inscriptions. Most scholarly reconstructions place the Step Gate about 3,000 m north of the southeast corner and approximately 2,000 m south of the northeast corner (coordinates: 36.3632768, 43.1724032). However, a postern gate partially excavated in 1988 about 500 m south of that spot (36.3590074, 43.1740733) could be the Step Gate, as Julian Reade (SAAB 22 [2016], 74-77) proposes. The assumed position of this city gate depends largely on where one believes Sennacherib had the Šibaniba Gate and Halahhu Gate constructed; there are four suggested locations for the former and two for the latter. Based on available textual and archaeological evidence, as well as satellite imagery, the Step Gate is tentatively located in this resource north of the Khosr River, following traditional scholarly placement of the gate.
description: Most 7th-century B.C. Assyrian inscriptions record that Nineveh had eight south- and east-facing gates: the Step Gate was the sixth of these. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it and gave it the Akkadian ceremonial name Mušēṣât-šīr-asakki, which means "The One Who Exorcises the 'Flesh' of the Asakku-demon."

description: The Temple of Zeus Lepsinos at Euromus is located southeast of the ancient settlement. The well-preserved Corinthian temple dates to the reign of Hadrian.

title: Etruscan acropolis at Volaterrae
description: The multi-phase acropolis of Etruscan Volaterrae has numerous important phases, beginning in the Archaic period. The monumental site continued to develop and grow during the Hellenistic period. It was identified archaeologically only in the nineteenth century. In the twentieth century it was the subject of major investigations under M. Cristofani and, later, M. Bonamici.

name_variants: Sanctuary of Artemis Soteira@en | Hekateion@en | Sanctuary of Artemis Soteira | Hekateion

It has often been identified as a sanctuary of Hekate, but more recent research suggests that it was dedicated to Artemis Soteira. It also contained a prophetic well associated with Paian.

title: Val d'Orcia

title: Sanctuary at San Casciano dei Bagni
name_variants: San Casciano dei Bagni@it | Monte Sacro@it | San Casciano dei Bagni | Monte Sacro
description: An ancient sanctuary located near the village of San Casciano dei Bagni, located south of Siena, Italy, has produced, following archaeological excavation, a large cache of metallic votive offerings - coins, figurines, statues, anatomical votives - dating to the late republican and early imperial periods. These votives were recovered from waterlogged mud deposits associated with the thermal springs at the site that have been frequented since at least the first millennium BCE.

title: Ad Stabulum
name_variants: Ad stabvlvm@la | Ad stabulum | Ad stabvlvm

title: Tsoungiza (Archaia Nemea)

title: Domus Faustae

At that time, the palace was known as Domus Faustae. Since the equites singulares Augusti had supported Maxentius, Constantine destroys the barracks and orders the beginnings of the construction of the Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano on the site.

title: Khorsabad ziggurat

description: The House of the Four Styles or Casa dei Quattro Stili (I.8.17) is noted for having examples of all four style of Pompeian wall paintings.

title: Mitrou

title: Tawern Roman temple complex

title: Fortifications at Civita di Artena

title: Esabad
name_variants: Esabad@sux | bīt Gula@akk | Esabad | bīt Gula
description: The temple of the goddess Gula, Esabad (“House of the Open Ear”), was located in the Tuba district of Babylon, in the western half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of three temples in that part of Babylon. Esabad was rebuilt by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal (r. 668–ca. 631 BC) and Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–652 BC). The temple survived into Arsacid times (247 BC–AD 224).

title: Ekitušgarza
name_variants: Ekitušgarza@sux | bīt Bēlet-Eanna@akk | Egarza@sux | Ekisaduga@sux | Ekitušgarza | bīt Bēlet-Eanna | Egarza | Ekisaduga
details: To differentiate the two Bēlet-Eanna temples in Babylon, inscriptions of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–652 BC) specify that Ekitušgarza, which was in the Tuba district, was built “in the recess of the city wall of Babylon” (see, for example, RIBo Babylon 7 Nebuchadnezzar II 002 iv 44–48); her other temple Ekitusgirzal, which was in the New City district, was built “on the canal bank.” As noted already by A.R. George (1992: 330), “The "recess of the city wall" rather suggests a place where the wall changed direction ( tubqu also has the meaning "corner", at the point where two walls meet), but there were no such places in the quarter Tuba, where Tintir sites E-kituš-garza. The reference may therefore be merely to a corner made by a projecting tower, such as would undoubtedly have formed part of the monumental Šamaš Gate . For this reason the temple is shown on our sketch map (fig. 4 on p. 24) as adjacent to this city gate, but the location is, of course, very tentative.”
description: The temple of the goddess Bēlet-Eanna, Ekitušgarza (“House, Abode of the Regulations”), was located in the Tuba district of Babylon, in the western half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of three temples in that part of Babylon. Ekitušgarza was rebuilt by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–652 BC).

title: Tırmıl Tepe Höyüğü
details: Kundu, a place mentioned in the inscriptions of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (r. 680-669 BC), is associated with classical Kyinda. Kundu has sometimes been identified as Tırmıl Tepe Höyüğü, a mound ca. 2 km northeast of Mersin. The association of Kundu with Tırmıl Tepe Höyüğü is uncertain since the inscriptions of Esarhaddon suggest that Kundu was located near Sissû, a place identified as modern Kozan (formerly Sis). Modern Anavarza, which is about 20 km southeast of Kozan, has been suggested as a possible location of Kundu. Since Anavarza is generally associated with classical Anazarbos/Caesarea/Ioustin(ian)oupolis, that proposed location for Kundu is also uncertain.
description: An unexcavated mound on the outskirts of modern Mersin in Turkey. Archaeological surface survey yielded pottery dating from the Calcolithic to the Medieval periods.
