title: Banditaccia necropolis, Caere
name_variants: Necropoli della Banditaccia@it | Necropoli della Banditaccia
description: The Etruscan necropolis of Caere, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Maadi
name_variants: المعادي@arz | al-Maadi | al-Ma'adi | al-Maʿadī | Maadi | Ma'adi | Maʿadi
description: A Predynastic settlement located on the eastern bank of the Nile on the outskirts of modern Cairo.

title: Tel Jatt
description: A site between the Sharon Plain and the Samarian Hills on which the modern town of Jatt is built. The site contains numerous Bronze Age burials and signs of habitation as late as the Bronze Age. The site has been proposed as a possible location for the town of Ginti-kirmil mentioned in the Amarna letters.

title: Prestatyn
details: Once thought to be the site of an early fort, that notion has now been discredited. A well-preserved civilian bath house was found at Prestatyn in 1934.
description: The modern-day site of a Romano-British settlement dating from first and second centuries A.D.

title: Arene Candide
description: A cave in Liguria with Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, and temporary Late Roman occupation.

title: Tomb of Numerius Agrestinus Equitius Pulcher
description: A schola tomb at Pompeii located near the Porta Nocera necropolis. The inscription on the tomb's hemicycle honors Numerius Agrestinus Equitius Pulcher, a Roman who had an illustrious military career, including holding the role of praefectus of the Autrigones, an Iberian tribe.

title: Ward Law
description: Ward Law, site of a temporary marching camp and hillfort on the river Nith, was identified via cropmarks.

title: Park of the Roman Villas at Carthage
name_variants: Le parc des villas romaines@fr | حديقة المنازل الرومانية@ar | Le parc des villas romaines | hadiqat almanazil alruwmania
description: An excavated section of Roman Carthage containing blocks (insulae) of townhouses organized on a grid.

title: Roman theater at Tusculum
name_variants: Roman Theatre of Tusculum@en | Roman Theatre of Tusculum
description: The Roman theater at Tusculum was first excavated in 1839.

title: Roman theater of Scythopolis
description: The Roman theater of Scythopolis.

title: Cisterns of La Maalga
description: A group of 15 large cisterns constructed during the late Punic era as a water supply for the city of Carthage.

title: Šibaniba Gate
name_variants: abul Šibaniba@akk | Šibaniba Gate@en | Dumuq-ašnan-u-lahar-qerebša-kayyān@akk | abul Šibaniba | Šibaniba Gate | Dumuq-ašnan-u-lahar-qerebša-kayyān
details: The gate is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib dating to 697-691 B.C. Most of Sennacherib’s inscriptions record that the Šibaniba Gate was the seventh of the south- and east-facing gates. One inscription, however, states that it was the sixth of those gates. The gate’s exact position is uncertain and cannot be confirmed from in-situ inscriptions. Most scholarly reconstructions place the Šibaniba Gate about 900 m or 1,450 m south of the northeast corner of Nineveh’s wall (coordinates: respectively 36.3718555, 43.1668081 and 36.3674842, 43.1700696). Julian Reade (SAAB 22 [2016], 77-80) has recently suggested two alternative locations for this gate: (1) approximately 2,000 m south of the northeast corner (coordinates: 36.3632768, 43.1724032), the spot where scholars traditionally locate the Step Gate , and (2) about 2,800 m north of the southeast corner, just south of the Khosr River, the location where most scholarly reconstructions place the Mullissu Gate (coordinates: 36.361431, 43.173201). Given the fairly regular spacing of the gates along the eastern stretch of wall, the Šibaniba Gate in this resource is tentatively located 900 m south of the northeast corner of the city.
description: Most 7th-century B.C. Assyrian inscriptions record that Nineveh had eight south- and east-facing gates: the Šibaniba Gate was the seventh of these. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it and gave it the Akkadian ceremonial name Dumuq-ašnan-u-lahar-qerebša-kayyān, which means "The Choicest of Grain and Flocks Are Constantly Inside It."

title: Halahhu Gate
name_variants: abul Halahhi@akk | Halahhu Gate@en | Bābilat-hiṣib-huršānī@akk | abul Halahhi | Halahhu Gate | Bābilat-hiṣib-huršānī
details: The gate is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib dating to 697-691 B.C. Most of Sennacherib’s inscriptions record that the Halahhu Gate was the eighth and last of the south- and east-facing gates. One inscription, however, states that it was the seventh and last of those gates. The gate’s exact position is uncertain and cannot be confirmed from in-situ inscriptions. Most scholarly reconstructions place the Halahhu Gate about 250 m south of the northeast corner of Nineveh. As Julian Reade has already pointed out, no visible evidence for an ancient gate at those coordinates be substantiated from the archaeological record and, therefore, the gate might have been located a bit further south, about 900 m south of the northeast corner of the wall (estimated coordinates: 36.3718555, 43.1668081). Because it seems more likely that the Šibaniba Gate was built by Sennacherib at the latter spot, the former spot is tentatively suggested in this resource as the location of the Halahhu Gate.
description: Most 7th-century B.C. Assyrian inscriptions record that Nineveh had eight south- and east-facing gates: the Halahhu Gate was the eighth and last of these. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it and gave it the Akkadian ceremonial name Bābilat-ḫiṣib-huršānī, which means "The Bearer of the Produce of the Mountains."

title: Adad Gate
name_variants: abul Adad@akk | Adad Gate@en | Adad-šārik-hegalli-ana-māti@akk | abul Adad | Adad Gate | Adad-šārik-hegalli-ana-māti
details: The gate is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib dating to 697-691 B.C. In those texts, the Adad Gate is listed as the first gate of the northern stretch of wall. The position of the gate is known and it was excavated/restored in 1966-68, 1973, and 1990-91. Around April 13, 2016, ISIS/ISIL demolished the Adad Gate and the adjacent wall with a bulldozer.
description: The northern city wall of Nineveh had three gates: the Adad Gate was the easternmost of the three. The Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib constructed it and gave it the Akkadian ceremonial name Adad-šārik-hegalli-ana-māti, which means "The God Adad Is the Provider of Prosperity to the Land."

title: Bolʹshoĭ Petropavlovskiĭ burial ground
name_variants: Большой Петропавловский могильник@ru | Bolʹshoĭ Petropavlovskiĭ mogilʹnik | Bolʹshoy Petropavlovskiy mogilʹnik
description: Burial complex along a stretch of over 3 km of the northern bank of the Siniukha River, a stream in the Laba River valley (Krasnodar region). The necropolis contains over 200 individual burials dated to the Middle Bronze-Early Iron Ages (3rd millennium BCE-3rd century CE).

title: Prytanikon at Athens
description: The Prytanikon was the seat of the Prytaneis and was located on the west side of the Agora in proximity to the Old Bouleuterion, with which it formed an architectural unit. This structure was supplanted by the later Tholos and its remains are referred to as "Building F". It dates to the later period of the Peisistratids, ca. 550-525 B.C.

title: Tomba dei Carri
name_variants: Tomba dei Carri@it | Tomba dei Carri
description: A mid-seventh century BCE tumulus at Populonia with a diameter of 28 meters; part of the San Cerbone necropolis.

title: Alhambra
description: Alhambra, Generalife, and Albayzín together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site that preserves elements of the medieval heritage of Granada, Spain. The Alhambra is a fortified palace complex that was begun by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, the first Nasrid emir and founder of the Emirate of Granada, in 1238.

title: Tell el-Hesi
name_variants: תל חסי@he | Tel Hesi | Tell el-Hesi | Tel Hesy | Tell el-Hesy | Tel H̱asi | Tel el H̱asi | Tell el Hasī | Tell Hasī
description: Archaeological site located in southern Palestine with signs of habitation (with gaps) from the late Neolithic through the Hellenistic period, as well as burials from Late Antiquity.

title: Mycenaean cemetery at Aidonia
description: Mycenaean burial ground located approximately 8 kilometers west of Nemea containing 20 tombs dated to the 15th century BCE. All but two of the burials were looted in the 1970s, but the illicit finds were retrieved and repatriated to Greece in 1996.

title: 'Ein-Shadud
description: Small settlement in the Jezreel Valley containing structures dated to the Early Bronze Age I. Salvage excavations were conducted on the site in 1979 prior to its destruction by construction.

title: Bouleuterion at Ietas
description: The Bouleuterion at Ietas dates to the later second century B.C.

title: "Mithraeum" at Eleusis
description: A small 1st-century AD temple south of the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis, which was identified by the original excavator as a Mithraeum. This is unlikely to be correct. Other suggestions include that it was devoted to the cult of Augustus.

title: Greater Propylaia, Eleusis
description: The outer entranceway to the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis, completed by the emperor Marcus Aurelius and modelled on the Propylaia of the Acropolis in Athens.

title: Villa di Nerone
description: Nero built a villa and a port at Antium. The villa was subsequently expanded under Domitian and other later emperors.

title: The "Auditorium site" at the Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome)
name_variants: Auditorium site@en | fattoria e la villa dell’Auditorium@it | Auditorium site | fattoria e la villa dell’Auditorium
description: An Early Republican to Middle Imperial elite complex along the Via Flaminia in the outskirts of Rome.

title: Thapedon
description: A place included on the Peutinger map.

title: So-called twin sanctuary
description: A double sanctuary on the forum of Carsulae. It is no longer clear to which gods these temples belonged.

title: Black Ball Camp
description: Black Ball Camp or Gallox hill fort is an Iron Age hill fort in Dunster, Somerset, England.

title: Grabbist Hillfort
description: Grabbist Hillfort is an Iron Age hillfort located west of Dunster in Somerset, England.

title: Abu Simbel
name_variants: Abu Simbel@en | Abou Simbel@fr | Abu Simbel | Abou Simbel
description: The site of two temples constructed by Ramesses II, one dedicated to the triad of Amun, Ra-Horakhty, and Ptah, as well as the deified Ramesses, and another dedicated to Hathor and the pharaoh's wife Nefertari. The temple was relocated between 1964 and 1968 to prevent its submersion under Lake Nasser after the construction of the Aswan High Dam.

title: Stari Grad Plain
name_variants: Stari Grad Plain@en | Stari Grad Plain
description: The Stari Grad Plain is located on the island of Hvar in the Adriatic Sea. This cultural landscape is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site due, in part, to its pristine state of preservation, which dates back to the time of Greek colonization by Paros in the fourth century BCE.

title: Porticus Vipsania
description: The Porticus Vipsania was a public complex located along the eastern side of the via Lata in the Campus Martius. This complex contained a map commissioned by Agrippa. The project was begun under Polla (Agrippa's sister) and completed under Augustus.

title: Arcus Novus
details: The Arcus Novus relied on reused sculptural reliefs ( spolia ) that likely were taken from the Ara Pietatis. Elements of the nearby Temple of the Sun were also perhaps coopted. By order of Innocent VIII, the arch was demolished in 1491. Fragments of relief sculpture were discovered in 1523 and eventually passed into the ownership of the Medici family, with some fragments making their way to the Boboli Gardens in Florence, Italy. The Diocletianic arch also reused relief sculpture from the Antonine period. These fragments also came to be owned by the Medici and were incorporated into the facade of the Villa Medici in Rome.
description: A now-lost arch on the ancient Via Lata. It was dedicated to Diocletian either in 293 CE (marking the occasion of his decennalia) or in 303-304 (joint triumph with Maximian). The present church of Santa Maria in Via Lata occupies the site of the arch.

title: Mithraeum of the Seven Gates
name_variants: Mithraeum of the Seven Gates@en | Mitreo delle Sette Porte@it | Mithraeum of the Seven Gates | Mitreo delle Sette Porte
description: The so-called Mithraeum of the Seven Gates was built at Ostia in the second century CE, repurposing rooms that originally date to the previous century.

title: Epirote League
description: A koinon (league) of Epirote tribes, which grew out of the earlier Molossian League, was established between 370 and 320 BCE. The league dissolved during the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BCE) as its constituent cities chose different sides in the conflict.

title: Tell Arpachiyah
description: A Neolithic site occupied in the Halaf and Ubaid periods.

title: Ponte Cardona
description: An aqueduct bridge near Nequinum dating ca. A.D. 24 - 33.

title: Tomba Torlonia
description: An Etruscan tumulus-type tomb in the Monte Abatone necropolis of Caere that dates ca. 320-200 BCE.

title: Eastern Outer Wall of Babylon
name_variants: Eastern Outer Wall@en | Eastern Outer Wall
details: Work on this wall began in the time of Nabopolassar (r. 625–605 BC) and completed during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–562 BC). Several Akkadian inscriptions of the latter Babylonian king record the construction of this 4,000–cubit-long wall (ca. 7,250 m) that protected the eastern half of Babylon. For example, see RIBo Babylon 7 Nebuchadnezzar II 002 and Nebuchadnezzar II 021 . According to a text that might have been drawn up as an aide-memoire for Nebuchadnezzar, the Eastern Outer Wall had 120 towers and 5 entrances ( Šūhi Canal Gate , Madānu Canal Gate , Giššu Gate , Sun of the Gods Gate , and Seashore Gate ). Only a small section of this wall has been excavated or documented). It consisted of a 7.0-meter-wide unbaked mudbrick wall, a 7.8-meter-wide baked-brick quay wall, a 3.3-meter-wide quay, and a wide moat. It has been estimated that the Eastern Outer Wall, together with its quay wall, was built from 96,600,000 mudbricks and 117,700,000 baked bricks.
description: The Neo-Babylonian ruler Nabopolassar (r. 625–605 BC) started planning and constructing an outer wall around the eastern side of Babylon. This massive mudbrick brick wall, together with its protective quay wall and a wide moat, remained unfinished at the time of Nabopolassar’s death. His son and successor Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–562 BC) finished the work started by his father. Traces of Babylon’s once-impressive eastern outer wall are still visible today.

title: Ayanis
name_variants: Ağartı Kalesi@tr | Ayanis@tr | Ayanis Kalesi@tr | Ayanıs@tr | Ağartı Kalesi | Agarti Kalesi | Ayanis | Ayanis Kalesi | Ayanıs | Ayans | Ayams
description: Ayanis (or Ayanıs, now Ağartı Kalesi) is an Urartean fortress and settlement located 35 km north of Van on a rocky outcrop 250 m above Lake Van (1867 m above sea level). It was founded in the 7th century BCE under Rusa, son of Argišti, and was named Rusahinili Eidurukai ("The City of Rusa in front of Mount Eiduru"). Here two inscriptions of Rusa, son of Argišti (7th century BCE), have been found which report that Rusa cultivated the barren land, built the fortress and the city as well as a “tower temple” (“susi temple”) and a “Gate for the God Haldi” (A 12-01 and A 12-09).

title: Casa di Pane
description: A domus in Pompeii excavated in 1818. It is linked to VIII.3.28 and VIII.3.30.

title: Santa Lucia in Selci
name_variants: Santa Lucia in Selci@it | Santa Lucia in Selci
description: The church of Santa Lucia in Selci was founded by the eighth century and perhaps as early as the sixth century.

title: Waddon Hill
description: A Roman fort in Dorset, England, that began as a temporary camp under Vespasian.

title: Roman cistern
description: A large Roman cistern at Albano Laziale.

title: Roman amphitheater at Burnum
description: A Roman amphitheater associated with the legionary establishment of Burnum.

title: Roman amphitheater at Salona
details: The Salona amphitheater is small in size, relative to its architectural peers. The outer shell measures ca. 125 by 100 meters and the arena measures 65 by 40 meters. The building accommodated an estimated 15,000 to 18,000 spectators.
description: The Roman amphitheater at Salona.

title: Acquoria
description: A basis villae near Tivoli in opus incertum on the river Aniene measuring 70 x 20 m. Two phases have been identified: second-first century B.C. and first century A.D.

title: Dragoncello
description: Dragoncello is a modern district of Rome's metropolitan area where archaeological evidence for a series of late republican villas was uncovered. At least four in number, these villa rustica sites have evidence for domestic production.

title: Egelasta
details: Pedro Barceló argues, in New Pauly , that claims that Egelasta should be taken as equivalent to Iniesta are mistaken.
description: An ancient settlement in Iberia that was part of the conventus of Carthago Nova, according to Pliny the Elder. It is noted in particular for its salt.

title: Bardsey Island
description: Bardsey Island, occupied since the Neolithic period, lies off the Llŷn Peninsula of Wales.

title: Tomb of the Shields and Chairs, Caere
description: The so-called Tomb of the Shields and Chairs at Caere dates ca. 520 - 500 B.C. The organization of this tomb is similar to that of the Tomb of the Capitals and the Tomb of the Cornice. It has a short dromos and a large vestibule. In the vestibule are two seats carved from the tuff bedrock as well as a series of hanging shields carved in relief.

title: Aristanis
description: A Byzantine site in western Sardinia, made important by the location of a bishopric there by Torcotorio in AD 1070; now the modern city of Oristano.

title: Torre di Mercurio
name_variants: Torre di Mercurio@it | Tower XI@en | Torre di Mercurio | Tower XI
description: A tower associated with Pompeii's fortification wall that is also sometimes designated as "Tower XI".

title: Fosso Marangone
description: A small stream that flows into the Tyrrhenian Sea. It now lies in the territory of the municipalities of Allumiere, Civitavecchia, and Santa Marinella and forms the geographical boundary between the latter two. The watercourse originates at Poggio Ombricolo.

title: Roman Circus at Mérida
details: Digitized in Google Earth in July 2012 at an eye altitude of 600m. The circus is included as a constituent part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site.
description: The Roman Circus at Mérida dates ca. 20 B.C.

title: Schwarzenbach
description: Celtic settlement site in eastern Austria inhabited during the 1st-2nd centuries CE.

title: Santa Maria della Libera
name_variants: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Libera@it | Chiesa di Santa Maria della Libera
description: An eleventh century church near Aquinum built largely from spolia.

title: Manoppello Roman Villa
details: The villa emerged in the second or first centuries B.C. and by the Imperial period had become an elite country estate. Remains of high quality mosaic pavement have been identified on the site; the villa also had a small bathing complex.
description: A Late Republican villa in Abruzzo that later became a productive estate. The archaeological remains of the villa are located in the locality of Piano S. Maria Arabona in Manoppello, Italy.

title: Thermi, Lesbos
details: Winifred Lamb identified the site and carried out excavations from 1929 to 1933. Additional excavation took place form 2004-2008.
description: Thermi, Lesbos, was a Bronze Age port-cum-settlement that flourished during the third millennium BCE.

title: Ponte di San Francesco
name_variants: Ponte di San Francesco@it | Ponte di San Francesco
description: The Ponte di San Francesco or Bridge of Saint Francis is a single-span medieval segmental arch bridge that crosses the River Aniene in Subiaco, Lazio, Italy. It was built in 1358.

title: Basilica of Iomnium
description: The basilica of Iomnium (Tigzirt) likely dates to the fifth and sixth centuries CE.

title: Thimara
description: A place in south Asia included in the Peutinger Map.

title: Burgus Szentendre-Dera
description: Burgus Szentendre-Dera is a late antique Roman military encampment located along the Hungarian Danube at Szentendre (St. Andrae). The fort secured the Pannonian Limes.

title: Buffa necropolis
description: One of the necropoleis of the ancient city of Selinous, on the Buffa hill in contrada Manuzza, to the NE of the ancient city

title: Tell Afis
name_variants: Hazrek@arc | Hatarikka@akk | Hadrech@hbo | تل افس@ar | Hazrek | Hazrach | Hatarikka | Hadarik | Hadrech | Tall Āfis
description: Iron Age settlement in Syria. The site has been tentatively identified as Hadarikka/Hazrek, the capital of the region of Luhuti/Luash, which became part of the kingdom of Hamath around 796 BCE.

title: Colonnes de Riez
name_variants: Temple of Apollo in Riez@en | Temple of Apollo in Riez
description: The remains of a Roman temple of the first century CE.

title: Settlement north of Buridava Roman fort and Vicus
description: A Dacian settlement, probably of indigenous origin, lying a few kilometers north of the Roman fort and vicus known as Buridava. It may have originated the toponym.

title: Basentello (river)
description: A river of southern Italy, Basentello flows near the border between Apulia and Basilicata. It flows from its source near Palazzo San Gervasio to Bradano.

title: Dema House
description: A country house in Attica dating to the fourth century BCE located near the fort and wall at Dema.

title: Pons Aurelius
description: The Pons Aurelius is known only from late Roman documents (fourth and fifth centuries CE) and is most likely the same bridge known as pons Antoninus in the early Middle Ages. The present-day Ponte Sisto (built in the fifteenth century) reused some of the ancient Roman bridge piers.

title: Ponte Sisto
description: The Ponte Sisto is a bridge that spans the Tiber River at Rome. In the present-day city, it links the Via dei Pettinari (Rione of Regola) to the Piazza Trilussa in Trastevere. The bridge was commissioned by Pope Sixtus IV and was built between 1473 and 1479. Its architect, Baccio Pontelli, reused the piers of the ancient Roman Pons Aurelius, which had come to be known as the Pons Antoninus in Late Antiquity. That bridge was at least partially destroyed in the 770s.

title: Kursi paleochristian basilica
description: An early Christian basilica was excavated at Kursi, near the Sea of Galilee in the Golan Heights.

title: Macedonia IV
description: One of four client republics created in Macedonia by the Romans after their victory in the Third Macedonian War in 166 BC. They were replaced with the province of Macedonia in 146 BC

title: Abarnani
details: The location of Abarnani is unknown. Sultan Tepe, ca. 24 km east of Ceyhan has been suggested as a possible location. Most scholars are generally sceptical about that proposal .
description: Abarnani is a fortified city in Que, probably in the eastern part of the Cilician plain. The city is mentioned with Lusanda and Kisuatni in royal inscriptions of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (r. 858-824 BC).

title: Lusanda
details: The location of Lusanda is uncertain, although it is likely to have been in the eastern part of the Cilician plain. Minareli H üyük, ca. 7 km north of Toprakkale, has been (tentatively) suggested as a possible location of Lusanda. Lusanda is often equated with Lahuzatia in Old Assyrian texts, Lawasanda in Ugaritic sources, La(hu)wasantija in Hittite texts, and Lawasantiya in Luwian sources and it has been proposed that that city is to be identified with Karah üyük, near Elbistan. The Helsinki Atlas (Map 3 and page 12) very tentatively accepts that suggested location.
description: Lusanda is a fortified city in Que, probably in the eastern part of the Cilician plain. The city is mentioned with Abarnani and Kisuatni in royal inscriptions of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (r. 858-824 BC).

title: Kisuatni
details: The location of Kisuatni is uncertain, although it is likely to have been in the eastern part of the Cilician plain. Karahüyük, ca. 15 km south of Toprakkale, has been (tentatively) suggested as a possible location of Kisuatni (see, e.g., Helsinki Atlas Map 2). That proposed location is not universally accepted.
description: Kisuatni is a fortified city in Que, probably in the eastern part of the Cilician plain. The city is mentioned with Abarnani and Lusanda in royal inscriptions of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (r. 858-824 BC).

title: Castel Lagopesole
name_variants: Castle of Lagopesole@en | Castle of Lagopesole
description: Castel Lagopesole was situated along the line of the ancient Roman Via Herculea between Melfi and Potenza in southern Italy. During the eighth through tenth centuries, the site played a strategic role in the region. The castle's construction between 1242 and 1250 is linked to Frederick II. The castle was the meeting place of Pope Innocent II and Abbot Rinaldo of Montecassino during their war against Roger the Norman. Charles I of Anjou used the castle in 1268 and 1294.

title: Zabbān
description: A city on the Diyālā River, possibly between Kifrī and Qāra.

title: Casa Matta at Kaulonia
description: The so-called "Casa Matta" at Kaulonia is an elite domestic building of the Hellenistic period that includes mosaics in the remains of its bathing rooms.

title: Theater at Arykanda
description: The Theater at Arykanda dates to the first century B.C.

title: Bur-mar'ina
name_variants: Tell Shuyukh Fawqani@ar | Būr-marʾīna@akk | Tell Shuyukh Fawqani | Būr-marʾīna
description: A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources that is identified with brmrn in Aramaic texts and the modern Tell Shuyukh Fawqani.

title: Dabigu
name_variants: Dabekon@grc | Tell Dābiq@ar | Dabigu@akk | Dabekon | Tell Dābiq | Dabigu
description: An unwalled city mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources that is identified with Tell Dābiq.

title: La Celsa
name_variants: Mausoleo La Celsa@it | Mausoleo La Celsa
description: At La Celsa (12.7 km of the Via Flaminia) are the remains of a cylindrical drum mausoleum that was likely once part of a larger funereal complex.

title: Kinneil
description: The site of a Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall. The fortlet measures ca. 21.5 x 18.5 m, covering an area of ca. 0.04 ha.

title: Delibaba Fortress
name_variants: Delibaba Fortress@en | Delibaba Fortress | Velibaba Fortress | Deli Baba | Velibaba | Dellal Fortress
description: Delibaba (or Dellal / Velibaba) Fortress is an Urartian fortress which lies to the east of the Dellal pass 17 km southeast of the city Horasan in the Horasan county of the Erzurum province between Hasankale (Pasinler) and Aleşkirt. Its name Delibaba (Velibaba) comes from the modern Turkish village Delibaba (Velibaba) which is situated in the vicinity of the fortress. A stone inscription of the Urartian king Minua, son of Išpuini (9th / 8th century BCE) which was found there reports that the fortress was built by Minua "through the protection of the god Haldi". The Urartian name of the fortress is unknown.

title: Düzceli
name_variants: Düzceli@tr | Պանանիշ@hy | Pinaşiya@ku | Düzceli | Pananish | Pinaşiya
description: Düzceli is a modern village in the Ağrı province in eastern Turkey, ca. 14 km southeast from Patnos and the Urartian fortress Aznavurtepe / Anzavurtepe. In Düzceli a reused stone block with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) was found which reports the contruction of a building called "iriduduni" (CTU A 5-78).

title: Woden Law hill fort
description: Woden Law hill fort is a multi-vallate Iron Age site in Scotland.

title: Amphitheater of Statilius Taurus
name_variants: Amphitheater of Statilius Taurus@en | Amphitheater of Statilius Taurus
description: T. Statilius Taurus dedicated the first stone amphitheater at Rome in 29 BCE. It was located at an undetermined location in the Campus Martius and was destroyed in the Great Fire of 64 CE.

title: Gymnasium at Olympia
name_variants: Gymnasium at Olympia@en | Gymnasion von Olympia@de | Gymnasium at Olympia | Gymnasion von Olympia
details: The Gymnasium was a building at Olympia (constructed ca. 250 BC) where athletes could train for the competitions at the Olympic games. It lies northwest of the Altis enclosure on flat land next to the Kladeos riverbank. The quadrilateral building has a central courtyard surrounded by colonnades in the Doric order. The west wing is occupied by a series of rooms meant for the athletes, while the east wing had a solid outer wall with an internal double Doric colonnade and another colonnade of sixty columns along the court. The outer bottom part of the wall was made of poros blocks with stone-built buttresses on the exterior; the upper elevation was in baked mudbrick. The building included a court that was used for practicing the javelin and discus, with dimensions identical to the field of competition for those events. The gymnasium is only partially preserved, as the west wing has been eroded away by the Kladeos River.
description: The Gymnasium of Olympia was a practice and training field constructed in 250 BC for male Hellenic athletes competing in the Olympic Games.

title: Library of Hadrian at Athens
name_variants: Library of Hadrian@en | Hadrian's Library@en | Library of Hadrian | Hadrian's Library
details: Located northeast of the Athenian Agora, the Library of Hadrian is a complex constructed under the Roman emperor Hadrian ca. AD 132. The columns and architecture have a distinctively Roman style, much like the buildings of the Roman Agora in Athens. The Library featured one hundred columns of Phrygian marble, had gilded roofwork, and alabaster architectural details, and was decorated with many statues and frescoes. This building, along with many others of the same style, was part of a Hadrianic building program that Hadrian himself undertook at Athens in an attempt to enhance the urban appearance of the city. It served primarily as a library and a place where the city's elite could come together to exchange ideas. It included a large room for the storage of the scrolls, as well as smaller rooms that could be used for lectures. The library was damaged in AD 267 during the Herulian sack. The complex was repaired during the early fifth century and then became the site of a paleochristian church. Subsequently a three-aisled basilica was built (seventh century) that was replaced by a single-aisle church in the eleventh century. In 2001, the library began to be used as an archaeological storeroom and was closed to the public.
description: The Library of Hadrian is located on the north side of the Athenian Acropolis, immediately to the north of the Roman Agora. The Roman emperor Hadrian built the complex in A.D. 131/2. It was subsequently destroyed during the Herulian sack of Athens in A.D. 267.

title: Temple of Apollo at Thermos
name_variants: Temple of Apollo at Thermos@en | Temple of Apollo at Thermos
details: The Temple of Apollo at Thermos is a sanctuary for the Greek God Apollo. The temple of Apollo was the focal point for the ancient Greek sanctuary of Thermos. It was used to pay honor and respect to the Greek God Apollo. The temple was built over the remains of Megaron B ca. 630 BC - ca. 610 BC. It is incredibly famous for its archaic terracotta metopes decorated with mythological scenes. This is one of the earliest records of this art form in Greece. It is also one of the oldest Doric temples in Greece.
description: A temple to the Apollo was built in the late seventh century B.C. atop the ruins of the previous megaron in Thermos.

title: Greolieres Roman Milestone
description: A Roman milestone located in France, in the town of Gréolières in the Alpes-Maritimes department in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region. The inscription on the milestone honors the Roman emperor Caracalla and is dated to 213.

title: Villa Romana de los Villaricos
name_variants: villa de Los Villaricos (Mula, Murcia)@es | villa de Los Villaricos (Mula | Murcia)
description: The site of Villaricos lies 5 km east of Mula (Murcia), Spain. The Roman villa at the site was large and well-appointed, including rich mosaics and a bathing complex. There is also an industrial area that includes a torcularium (facility for pressing of olives or grapes). The site's use ranges from the first to the fifth century CE.

title: Roman Road in Sutton Park
description: An urban park in Birmingham, England, containing a stretch of preserved Roman road.

title: Torre dei Conti
description: A fortified Medieval tower located in Rome, dating to AD 1238, and built by Richard Conti, brother of Pope Innocent III.

title: Wrekin Hill Fort
description: Wrekin Hill Fort is an Iron Age Hill fort covering ca. 8 ha located in Shropshire, England.

title: Documaci tumulus
description: An elite tomb structure constructed in the late 4th to early 3rd century BCE near the Hellenistic settlement of Callatis.

title: Roman bridge, Córdoba
description: A first century Roman bridge over the Guadalquivir river.

title: Villamassargia, Nuraghe di Santu Pauli
description: A nuragic complex situated atop a low hill near Villamassargia, Sardinia.

title: Su Carroppu
description: A Neolithic rock-shelter settlement.

title: Pisuertes
description: An ancient people of Umbria whose territory is now unlocated.

title: Locmariaquer megaliths
description: At Locmariaquer, Brittany, are the remains of a complex of Neolithic structures.

title: Ilıpınar Tumulus
description: Tumulus near İznik Lake in Anatolia with Neolithic, Late Chalcolithic, Early Bronze Age, and Early Byzantine remains.

title: Thodasa
description: An unlocated community which was close to, and eventually entered into sympolitiea with, Kildara.

title: Pleistos (River)
description: A river in Central Greece that rises near modern Arachova in Boetia. It flows west through a karst valley paralleling the Gulf of Corinth, often underground, hence one modern name (Xeropotami). Augmented by streams issuing from Mount Parnassus, the river passes the site of ancient Delphi, which overlooks the valley from the north side. Thereafter the river bed follows elevation gradients, turning south as it passes the location of modern Hrisso to enter the Gulf of Corinth on the eastern edge of the modern village of Kirra. Extensive, long-term olive irrigation and other landscape change, have likely altered the river's course throughout history. Another modern drainage, arising in the Amphissa valley to the northwest and entering the Gulf of Corinth further west, is also today labeled as the Pleistos, but this seems to be a modern application of the name.

title: Vebar
name_variants: Vebar@es | Huévar de Aljarafe@es | Vebar | Huevar de Aljarafe
description: The modern Huévar de Aljarafe, a Spanish village located near Huelva in the western part of the province of Sevilla, that once belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.

title: South Stoa I
name_variants: South Stoa I@en | South Stoa I
description: South Stoa I is the modern name for the stoa that bounded the southern edge of the Agora of Athens from the late 5th century BC until the mid-2nd century BC, when it was demolished and replaced with South Stoa II. It contained rooms for communal dining and was probably the headquarters of the metronomoi and other officials.

title: Temple of Minerva at Theveste
description: The Temple of Minerva at Theveste dates to the third century A.D.

title: Alguazila
name_variants: Alguazila@es | Sietmalos@es | El Alguacil@es | Alguazila | Sietmalos | El Alguacil
description: Known as Sietmalos in Muslim Spain, Alguazila was a small village located south of what is now Carmona, Spain. Alfonso X, King of Castile, León and Galicia, delivered some lands of this village to Pedro Blasco el Adalid in the thirteenth century.

title: Punjeri
description: Modern location in the vicinity of Mamallapuram that may have been the site of a port or harbor facility for the ancient city.

title: Wall0048, Christian house church (Dura-Europos)
description: Wall portion on the south-facing exterior side of the baptismal font from the Baptistery, Christian House Church, Dura-Europos.

title: Kermario alignments
description: A complex comprised of 1029 megaliths arranged in 10 rows.

title: Tomb of Gaius Calventius Quietus
details: The tomb's inscription reads: "To Gaius Calventius Quietus, member of the Augustal Brotherhood, The honor of a double seat was given to him because of his generosity by a decree of the town-councilors and the approval of the people."
description: An altar tomb enclosed by a peribolos in the Porta Ercolano necropolis of Pompeii.

title: Platia Magoula Zarkou
description: Tell site in western Thessaly containing the remains of a settlement and necropolis dated to the early 6th millennium BCE.

title: Veliki Preslav
description: Veliki Preslav was a fortified site that served as the capital of the Tsar Simeon I of the Bulgarian Empire. The site flourished during the ninth and tenth centuries CE. The site includes both 'inner' and 'outer' fortified areas.

title: Sykeon Roman bath (Thessaly)
description: The remains of a Roman bath complex that included mosaic pavements and marble statuary were documented during rescue excavations in 2004 to the west of Sykeon in Thessaly.

title: Nuraghe Domu Beccia
name_variants: Nuraghe Domu Beccia@it | Nuraghe Domu Beccia⁠
description: A nuragic complex near Uras, Sardinia.

title: Christian Basilica, Ostia
name_variants: Basilica Cristiana@it | Domus dei Tigriniani@it | Basilica Cristiana | Domus dei Tigriniani
description: The so-called Christian Basilica, located in Regio III of ancient Ostia, was discovered by Guido Calza in 1939. The structure likely dates to the fourth and fifth centuries CE. The interpretation of the structure and its remains has proven difficult, resulting in numerous theories that are often at odds with one another. One possibility is that the complex functioned as a xenodochium (a guest house for pilgrims).

title: Sarapieion C at Delos
description: One of three shrines sacred to Serapis identified by archaeologists working at Delos in the nineteenth century.

title: Sarapieion A
description: The earliest of the three shrines sacred to Serapis identified by archaeologists working at Delos in the nineteenth century.

title: tomb of C. Sulpicius Platorinus
details: C. Sulpicius Platorinus served as triumvir monetalis in 18 B.C.
description: A monumental family tomb dating to the late Augustan period was discovered in 1880 on the embankments of the Tiber River. This tomb was situated in the transtiberim at the head of the Pons Agrippae. It is associated with the gens of the Sulpicii Platorini. The tomb was reconstructed in 1911 at the Museo Nazionale Romano in 1911.

title: Monumenti Funerari Romani
description: An archaeological area at Avella includes a sector of the ancient monumental necropolis that was in use between the late Hellenistic period and the early imperial period. It lies along an extra-urban road axis. Remains of four Roman mausolea are presently visible.

title: Porta Aurelia
name_variants: Porta San Pancrazio@it | Porta San Pancrazio
details: The modern Porta S. Pancrazio replaced the Porta Aurelia in 1644, under the patronage of Urban VIII. That structure was subsequently damaged and removed during the 1849 siege of Rome, at which time the present gate was erected.
description: A gate in the Aurelian Wall at the summit of the Ianiculum through which the Via Aurelia passes.

title: A Ponte da Xira
name_variants: A Ponte da Xira@es | A Ponte da Xira
description: A Roman bridge in the northwestern Iberian peninsula that crosses the río Valiñas.

title: oppidum Noeta
description: Pliny the Elder mentions the oppidum Noeta as part of his discussion of tribes in Iberia.

title: Tapah Khībr
description: Large mound and site for Iron Age fortress. Possibly ancient Ḫarḫar.

title: Quarries at Molara (Grottaferrata)
description: Stone quarries at Molara (Grottaferrata, Italy). Caves produced by quarry activity were also sites of paleochristian activity.

title: Santa Susanna
name_variants: Chiesa di Santa Susanna alle Terme di Diocleziano@it | Chiesa di Santa Susanna alle Terme di Diocleziano
description: The current Church of Saint Susanna at the Baths of Diocletian located on the Quirinal Hill in Rome dates from 1585. A titular church has existed on the site since ca. A.D. 280. The remains of an elite house (domus) are preserved beneath the church.

title: Meturant
description: Hamrin basin site named Tall al-Sīb.

title: Malazgirt
name_variants: Malāẕcürd@ota | Malāẕgird@ota | Malazgirt@tr | Malāẕcürd | Malāẕgird | Malazgirt
description: Find place for Urartian stone inscriptions.

title: Jemdet Nasr
name_variants: جمدة نصر‎‎@ar | Jemdet Nasr | Jamdat Nasr
description: An ancient site in Iraq's Babil Governorate (Iraq) that lends its name to the Jemdet Nasr period (ca. 3100–2900 B.C.).

title: Dhaskalio (settlement)
description: An Early Cycladic settlement identified on the island of Daskalio in the Cyclades. This settlement is the most substantial yet known for the Early Bronze Age in the Cyclades.

title: Casteddu de Fanaris
description: A Late Bronze Age nuragic site.

title: Gerasa Nymphaeum
description: A monumental fountain dating to the second century CE at Gerasa (modern Jerash in Jordan).

title: La Spezia
description: The modern city of La Spezia, Italy, is located what was in antiquity the territory of the city of Luni. The area of La Spezia has been surveyed by archaeologists.

title: Bryn Celli Ddu
name_variants: Bryn Celli Ddu@cy | Bryn Celli Ddu
description: A Neolithic mound site on the island of Anglesey.

title: Acharnes ancient theater
description: The deme theater of Acharnai was discovered in 2007.

title: Castle Rock (Edinburgh)
description: Castle Rock is a volcanic formation in Edinburgh, Scotland, upon which Edinburgh Castle was founded in the eleventh century.

title: Ionian League
name_variants: τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Ἰώνων@grc | The Koinon of the Ionians | τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Ἰώνων
description: An Ancient Greek confederation originally formed in the sixth century BCE by twelve Ionian cities, with religious festivals celebrated at Panionia.

title: Aldborough Studforth Hill
details: Remains of an earthwork at Isurium that have been described as perhaps those of a Roman amphitheater or stadium.
description: Archaeological remains at 'Aldborough Studforth Hill' site may be the location of possible Roman amphitheater.

title: Cardiff Castle
description: Cardiff Castle incorporates remains of the antecedent Roman fort.

title: Constantine's Bridge (Mysia)
description: A Roman bridge crossing the Rhyndakos river that was built after AD 258.

title: Süngütaşı
description: Find place for cuneiform inscription.

title: Anaktoron at Pantalika
name_variants: Anaktoron di Pantalica@it | Anaktoron di Pantalica
details: 0 0 1 171 976 University of Texas 8 2 1145 14.0 Normal 0 false false false EN-US JA X-NONE /* Style Definitions */ table.MsoNormalTable {mso-style-name:"Table Normal"; mso-tstyle-rowband-size:0; mso-tstyle-colband-size:0; mso-style-noshow:yes; mso-style-priority:99; mso-style-parent:""; mso-padding-alt:0in 5.4pt 0in 5.4pt; mso-para-margin:0in; mso-para-margin-bottom:.0001pt; mso-pagination:widow-orphan; font-size:12.0pt; font-family:Cambria; mso-ascii-font-family:Cambria; mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-hansi-font-family:Cambria; mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin;} 0 0 1 276 1577 University of Texas 13 3 1850 14.0 Normal 0 false false false EN-US JA X-NONE /* Style Definitions */ table.MsoNormalTable {mso-style-name:"Table Normal"; mso-tstyle-rowband-size:0; mso-tstyle-colband-size:0; mso-style-noshow:yes; mso-style-priority:99; mso-style-parent:""; mso-padding-alt:0in 5.4pt 0in 5.4pt; mso-para-margin:0in; mso-para-margin-bottom:.0001pt; mso-pagination:widow-orphan; font-size:12.0pt; font-family:Cambria; mso-ascii-font-family:Cambria; mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-hansi-font-family:Cambria; mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin;} This building was first investigated by Paolo Orsi, who found Bronze Age material in the vicinity and identified the megalithic, polygonal masonry of one end as the remains of a major Bronze Age structure, which he dubbed the "Anaktoron" (Prince's Palace). If it can indeed be associated with the 12th-11th centuries BC, it is one of the earliest structures at Pantalica. Orsi suggested that the form of the building showed Mycenaean influences, since Mycenaean settlements were established along Sicily's Ionian coast in this period. It has been compared to buildings A and B of the Mycenaean settlement at Thapsos. On the other hand, most of the remains of the building and the objects associated with the final phase of its use date to the Byzantine period (6th-11th c. AD), and more recent interpretations insist that the entire structure should be associated with Byzantine rather than prehistoric settlement at the site.
description: The Anaktoron is an enigmatic megalithic building associated with the prehistoric Sicilian settlement of Pantalica; its polygonal blocks may date to the 12-11th c. B.C., but the current form of the building seems to be the result of Byzantine reconstruction.

title: Al-Maqsha
description: Village in Bahrain, find place for cuneiform inscribed stele.

title: Īwān Kisrā
name_variants: Īwān Kisrā@arb | Īwān Kisrā | Iwan Kisra | Iwan Kesra | Iwān Kisrā
details: GANE OBJECT 30257
description: A place from the TAVO Index

title: Piazza d'Armi
description: The site of the arx of ancient Veii located on the southern spur of the volcanic plateau on which the city is located. There is archaeological evidence for an initial occupation phase of the ninth century B.C. By the seventh century B.C., the area shows evidence for adoption of rectilinear huts and assumes an orthogonal street grid.

title: Diogeneion
description: Gymnasium and centre of the ephebate at Athens from the late 2nd century BC until at least the mid-3rd century AD. It is thought to have been located to the east of the Tower of the Winds.

title: Ea temple (Khorsabad)
details: Six inscribed paving slabs were found in a wing of Sargon II’s palace that was mistakenly identified as a harem and those in-situ texts helped identify that part of the building as the palace’s religious quarter. The temple sector of Dūr-Šarrukīn (modern Khorsabad) comprised temples dedicated to the deities Adad, Ea (Ninšiku), Ningal, Ninurta, Sîn, and Šamaš. The single-room temple of the god Ea, which was accessed from Courtyard XXVII, was identified from the eight-line Akkadian inscription (Frame, RINAP 2 online Sargon II 17 ) discovered in the doorway of Room 192. The ancient name of the temple is not known.
description: As part of the palatial complex of Dūr-Šarrukīn (modern Khorsabad), the eighth-century-BC Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) constructed six temples, including one to the god Ea.

title: Fonteblanda
description: A planned Etruscan settlement in the Albegna valley along the line of the Via Aurelia founded, perhaps, ca. 570 B.C. The site offers evidence for iron working.

title: Via Clodia
details: R. J. A. Talbert notes that the name 'Via Clodia" is included on the Tabula Peutingeriana on segment 4B4.
description: An ancient Roman road.

title: Baths of the Old Convent, Tharros
description: Roman baths at Tharros known as the "Baths of the Old Convent".

title: Tell ej-Judeideh
details: Frederick Jones Bliss and R.A.S. Macalister excavated the site in 1898–1900.
description: A tell located southeast of Gath in Israel that has been identified with the biblical Moresheth-Gath.

title: Villa di via della Magliana
description: The remains of a Roman villa on land that is now mostly consumed by a golf course connected to a hotel resort.

title: balneum Abascantis et Mamertini
name_variants: balneum Abascantis et Mamertini@la | balneum Abascantis et Mamertini
description: The balneum Abascanti were baths near the Porta Capena that were possibly built by T. Flavius Abascantus, the freedman of Domitian. Also near the Porta Capena were the balneum Mamertini, possibly dedicated by Sex. Petronius Mamertinus, praetorian prefect in 139-143 CE.

title: Per-Sopdu
description: Ancient Egyptian town that was the capital of the 20th nome of Lower Egypt and was a major cult site, dedicated to Sopdu, the god of the eastern borders of Egypt. The site is now under the modern town of Saft el-Hinna.

title: Ansignan aqueduct
description: The remains of a Roman aqueduct bridge over the Agly River.

title: Patriarchal Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta of Aquileia
details: The Patriarchal Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta of Aquileia originated in the fourth century AD. The current edifice dates to the eleventh and thirteenth centuries AD.
description: The Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta, Aquileia dates originally to the fourth century.

title: Assur Archive 34
name_variants: Assur Archive 34@en | N 19 Archive@en | Assur Archive 34 | N 19 Archive
details: The archive is located in a private house.
description: 4 clay tablets were found in dA6IV in a private house. These tablets were found near House 12 (Assur Archive 33) and House 9 (Assur Archive 32). The archive dates to the 7th century BC. The group consists of 2 loan documents concerning silver, a list of oxen and textiles, and a purchase document concerning a slave.

title: Assur Archive 35
name_variants: Assur Archive 35@en | N 20 Archive@en | Assur Archive 35 | N 20 Archive
details: The archive is located in a private house.
description: Scattered around House 15 and the adjacent House 15a in eE6IV, excavators found an archive of more than 40 clay tablets. The available datings range from 687 BC to the years shortly before the fall of the city of Assur. The archive, belonging to Šarru-iqbi and others, consists of documents dealing with loans, a purchase document, a document concerning the adoption of a girl, and a fragmentary list.

title: Throne Room in Palace of Minos
details: The Throne Room at the palace at Knossos is a small intimate room, able to hold no more than thirty people at a time, with a grand stone throne built against one wall. Theories of the purpose of the room range from religious to political to astronomical. Various scholars have noticed that at different times of the day, and at different times of the year (perhaps equinoxes and solstices), the light from the sun would highlight different elements throughout the room. In the mid-15th c. BCE, there was a moment of significant political change on the island, during which all the palaces other than Knossos were damaged or destroyed. After this period, Mycenaean culture seems to have had much greater influence on Crete, especially at Knossos, and some archaeologists believe that the stone throne and the other decorative features in the room should be dated to this phase of the palace's use.
description: The Throne Room in the "Palace of Minos" at Knossos, a room with ritual features located on the west side of the central courtyard of the palace. The room takes its name from the masonry throne, flanked by frescoes depicting griffins, that occupies one of its walls.

title: Esterzili
description: The Domu de Orgia at Esterzili is the largest nuragic "megaron" structure thus far discovered in Sardinia.

title: Statua Valeriana
description: A statue included in the Regionary Catalogue for Regio XIV, the Statua Valeriana evidently honored some members of the gens Valeria. It is possible that this statue in the Transtiberim replaced a bronze equestrian statue that depicted Cloelia or perhaps Valeria, the daughter of Valerius Poplicola, that had stood in summa Sacra Via until it was destroyed by fire prior to the time of Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Based on a Trajanic inscription (CIL 6, 975), the statue lent its name to a vicus.

title: Apollo, Aedes
name_variants: Temple of Apollo Sosianus@en | Temple of Apollo Sosianus
description: The likely site of the original sanctuary to Apollo at Rome. The visible remains belong to the Augustan phase.

title: San Salvatore monastery
description: A monastery founded in A.D. 753 by Desiderius, future king of the Lombards. Located in modern Brescia, Italy.

title: Gallo-Roman amphitheater at Montbouy
description: The Gallo-Roman amphitheater at Montbouy dates to the early Imperial period.

title: Agia Paraskevi
description: A barren, uninhabited island in the Nikasiai islands (Naxos).

title: Kazane Höyük
description: Mound with remains of fortification, close to modern city Şanlıurfa.

title: Trapeza/Koumari temple (Achaia)
description: A temple in the Doric order that begins in the sixth century BCE and continues in use until the Hellenistic period. The temple may be associated with ancient Rhypai, at Trapeza near Koumari, Aigio, Achaia.

title: tribus Palatina
details: The tribus Palatina was one of the four, large, urban tribes of Rome ( Palatina , Collina , Esquilina , Suburana ), which corresponded to the four urban regions that Servius Tullius created.
description: An urban tribe of Rome created under the reign of Servius Tullius.

title: Qaryat al-Lak
name_variants: Tulul al-Lak@ar | Qaryat al-Lak@ar | تلول اللك@ar | Tulul al-Lak | Qaryat al-Lak | Tulūl al-Lak
details: In the mid-nineteenth century, Austen Henry Layard discovered inscribed bricks "bearing the name of the Kouyunjik-king" at Tulul al-Lak. The "Kouyunjik-king" is probably to be identified with the 7th-century B.C. Assyrian king Sennacherib.
description: Qaryat al-Lak (formerly called Tulul al-Lak) is a small village in northern Iraq that is located between the Assyrian cities Nimrud and Mosul. The modern village is built on top of the ruin mound. The ancient name of the settlement is not known.

title: Assur Archive 24
name_variants: Assur Archive 24@en | N 9 Archive@en | Assur Archive 24 | N 9 Archive
details: The archive is located in a private house in Assur.
description: In the northern corner, along the northwest town wall of Assur (bE4V, bD/E5I), researchers unearthed House 66 with an archive belonging to a family with the title ḫunduraya, a gentilic meaning "from Ḫundur". Another archive belonging to a related family of ḫunduraya was found nearby (Assur Archive 25). In House 66, a total of 86 clay tablets were found, including one docket. Of these, 64 tablets were found in Room k near the inner courtyard, while others were found in the courtyard and in the rooms to its southwest. Available datings range from 681 BC to the last years of the Assyrian Empire. The archive includes legal documents, such as loan documents concerning silver, textiles and straw, purchase documents, receipts, work contracts and juridical settlements.

title: Fortino di Mazzallakkar
name_variants: Fortino di Mazzallakkar@it | Fortino di Mazzallakkar
description: A ruined ninth-century Arabic fort on the shores of Sicily's Lago Arancio.

title: Via Cornelia
description: The Via Cornelia was an ancient road that ran along the north side of the circus Gai et Neronis. The road diverged from the Via Triumphalis west of the pons Neronianus, near a large tomb known as the Meta Romuli.

title: Temple of Artemis (Aulis)
name_variants: Temple of Artemis in Aulis@en | Temple of Artemis in Aulis
description: Archaic temple to Artemis at Aulis, Boeotia. In mythology, said to be the place of death of Iphigenia. Mentioned in Euripides' 'Iphigenia at Aulis.'

title: Basilica of Lucus Feroniae
description: The Basilica of Lucus Feroniae communicates with the forum and is linked to the apsidal space identified as the Augusteum.

title: Pyla-Kokkinokremos
description: A late Bronze Age settlement on Cyprus, abandoned after a brief occupation.

title: Torre del Berrueco
name_variants: Torre del Berrueco@es | El Berrueco@es | Torre del Berrueco | El Berrueco
description: A Spanish village and castle located in the west of Jaén that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X (thirteenth century). The site is now known as El Berrueco, in the municipality of Torredelcampo.

title: Domus Romana
description: West corner of the museum built on the site of a Roman Villa. Time periods following the Barrington Atlas (BAtlas 47 inset Melita).

title: Great Dolmen of Comenda da Igreja
description: A megalithic dolmen of the fourth to third millennia BC.

title: Hagi/Aği/Kocapınar
name_variants: Hagi@hy | Aği@tr | Kocapınar@tr | Hagi | Aği | Kocapınar
description: Kocapınar (known as Hagi/Aği until officially renamed in 1959) is a modern town in the administrative district of Erciş in the Van Province in eastern Turkey. Here a stela with an inscription of Argišti II., son of Rusa (8th / 7th century BCE) was found which reports the creation of an artificial lake in front of Mount Quria.

title: Palaiosouda (island)
description: An islet also known as Marathi.

title: Domus rustica
description: The ruins of a Republican-period 'domus rustica' located on the via Alexandre Gustave Eiffel in Rome, Italy, near Ponte Galeria.

title: Oldberry Castle
description: Oldberry Castle is an Iron Age hill fort in Somerset, England.

title: Western necropolis at Egnatia/Gnathia
description: The western necropolis at Egnatia/Gnathia includes some tombs of the Messapian culture dating from the middle of the fourth to the second centuries B.C.

title: Tall-e Bakun B
description: The second of the two mounds comprising the Tall-e Bakun site.

title: Santalla de Bóveda
description: The Roman sanctuary of Santalla de Bóveda dates to the second through fourth centuries A.D. It is located in the parish of Santalla de Bóveda de Meralocated near Lugo. Discovered in 1926, the site is a protected national monument.

title: Catacombe di San Sebastiano
name_variants: ad Catacumbas@la | Catacombe di San Sebastiano@it | memoria apostolorum@la | ad Catacumbas | Catacombe di San Sebastiano | memoria apostolorum | ad Catacumbas | memoria apostolorum
description: The catacombs of San Sebastiano located on the Via Appia are located near the church of the same name. These hypogeal tombs emerged in the third century CE and were linked initially to the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul.

title: Kānī Shāyah
name_variants: كاني شاية@ar | Kani Shaie@en | Kānī Shāyah | Kani Shaie
description: A small site in Kurdistan, Iraq, consisting of a high and low mound with remains from the fourth and early third millennium BCE.

title: Petras Minoan Settlement
description: Minoan palatial settlement located on a hill 1.5km from Seteia, Crete.

title: Madhukeshwara temple
description: A Shiva temple at Banavasi in India whose foundation may date as early as the 7th century CE.

title: Shop with dwelling (VII.4.22)
description: The ruins of VII.4.22 at Pompeii are identified as a shop with an associated dwelling and are linked to VII.4.21. The site was excavated in 1822 and again in 1833 and was bombed during the Second World War (13 September 1943). Among the themes depicted in the wall paintings of the structure are those to do with Adonis and his tomb at Byblos.

title: Solenyĭ Dol
description: Burial complex in the southern Ural Mountains region containing a number of Late Antique burials.

title: Area archeologica di Satricum
description: The remains of an extensive Roman villa have been documented (amongst other phases) in the village of Le Ferriere, on the grounds of the Casale del Giglio winery. This multi-period, multi-phase settlement demonstrates continuity of human activity, albeit with varying loci of focused activity.

title: Strata Diocletiana
description: A Roman road built in the third century A.D. under the emperor Diocletian that ran along the limes Arabicus of the eastern Roman empire.

title: Polygonal wall of Roman castrum
description: The polygonal masonry wall of the Roman castrum at Pyrgi encloses an area of ca. 5.7 ha.

title: Pianello di Genga
name_variants: Pianello di Genga@it | Pianello di Genga
description: Pianello di Genga, located in Italy's Ancona province, was the site of a Final Bronze Age settlement, as attested by an extensive necropolis.

title: Basilica of St. Crispinus
description: The fourth-century Basilica of St. Crispinus is one of the largest known in Africa.

title: Fines exercitus Syriaticae
name_variants: Fines exercitvs syriatic(a)e et conmertivm Barbaror(vm)@la | Fines exercitus Syriatice et conmertium Barbarorum | Fines exercitvs syriatic(a)e et conmertivm Barbaror(vm)
description: An area of the Syrian desert marked on the Peutinger Table that may indicate the boundary between the Roman province of Syria and a client state, possibly Palmyra.

title: Suburbium Toletanum
description: The location of the Late Roman and Visigothic suburbium beyond the Roman circus. Transition from suburban villas to a large-scale Visigothic expansion, which included various churches and the Praetorium, or Royal Palace. Destroyed during the ninth century. Excavations carried out in the early 2000s.

title: Marlik
name_variants: مارلىک@fa | Cheragh-Ali Tepe@fa | Mārlik | Marlik | Cheragh-Ali Tepe | Čerāḡ-ʿAli Teppa
description: Burial site in northern Iran containing over fifty burials dated to the mid-2nd millennium BCE.

title: Acamantis
description: Acamantis, named for the hero Acamas, was an Attic tribe or phyle created by Cleisthenes' reforms. It included the demes of Cholargos, Eiresidai, Hermos, Iphistiadai, Kerameis, Kephale, Poros, Thorikos, Eitea, Hagnous, Kikynna, Prospalta, and Sphettos.

title: Ziggurat at Nippur
description: A Ziggurat in the city of Nippur that was constructed under Ur-Nammu during the 21st century BCE and renovated under Esarhaddon and Assurbanipal during the 7th century BCE.

title: Cape Themisteas
name_variants: promunturium Themisteas@la | promunturium Themisteas | Themisteas (promuntorium) | promunturium Themisteas
description: Pliny the Elder describes Cape Themisteas as lying near the boundary of Farsistan and Elymais.

title: Çine Tepecik Höyük
description: Human occupation at Çine-Tepecik begins in the Chalcolithic period. The site is located in a fertile alluvial plain near the Meander River in western Anatolia. In the Late Bronze Age, this place was located in the Arzawa lands.

title: Doune
description: A Roman fort of Flavian date located near modern Stirling, Scotland under and around the Doune Primary School. The Latin name "Voran", preserved in the Ravenna Cosmography, may be identifiable with this site. The fortifications seem to have been demolished and abandoned in the Roman era. Slight evidence (postholes) of possible prehistoric date have also been identified.

title: Theater at Madauros
description: The Roman theater at Madauros in Africa Proconsularis.

title: Porta Romana
description: The so-called Porta Romana of Saturnia was once part of the Roman wall of the second century B.C.

title: Velletri-Stimmate
description: At Velletri the remains of a Late Archaic sanctuary (ca. 530 BCE) were discovered beneath the church of the SS. Stimmate di S. Francesco. The site is often referred to as "Tempio delle Stimmate"; Cardinal Stefano Borgia discovered it in 1784. The architectural terracottas from the sanctuary are part of the so-called "Veio-Roma-Velletri" decorative system.

title: villa del Cavalcavia di Salone
name_variants: villa del Cavalcavia di Salone@it | Villa del Giurista a Salone@it | villa del Cavalcavia di Salone | Villa del Giurista a Salone
description: The so-called "Villa of the Jurist" was discovered in 2013 during salvage excavations connected with the expansion of Italy's A24 motorway. A significant villa of the Late Republican period was documented and attributed to the jurist Quintus Mucius Scaevola.

title: Basawakkulama Tank
name_variants: අභය වැව@si | අභයවාපි@si | அபயவாவி@ta | බසවක්කුලම වැව@si | Abhaya Wewa | Abhaya Væva | Abhayavāpi | Abhayavapi | Apayavāvi | Apayavavi | Basavakkulama Væva
description: A reservoir at Anurādhapura in north-central Sri Lanka, originally built in the 4th century BCE and still in use today.

title: Kanakia
name_variants: Mycenaean acropolis of Kanakia@en | Mycenaean acropolis of Kanakia
description: The Mycenaean acropolis of Kanakia is located on the island of Salamis.

title: Ponte di Traiano
description: A Trajanic bridge along the Via Appia that crosses the fosso Striscia.

title: Great pit
name_variants: Great Pit@en | Grand puits@fr | Great Pit | Grand puits
description: A great pit dug to the north-east of the village of Deir el-Medina, where hundreds of objects, particularly ostraca, were found.

title: House of the Painters at Work
name_variants: House of the Painters at Work@en | Casa del Pittori al Lavoro@it | House of the Painters at Work | Casa del Pittori al Lavoro
details: The house takes its name from the fact that wall decorators were at work at the time of the building's destruction. The house is of an unusual plan and may represent a mixed-use space, combining domestic and commercial concerns.
description: The House of the Painters at Work or Casa dei pittori al lavoro is a ruined domus at Pompeii that was undergoing renovations and repairs at the time of the city's final destruction.

title: Nineveh Archive 5
details: This archive is located in the North Palace, near the Nabû temple (Ezida) .
description: In the Palace of Ashurbanipal (North Palace), in the southwest corner nineteenth-century British excavators unearthed the remains of a library, including many clay tablets inscribed with literary texts. During the reign of Ashurbanipal (r. 668–ca. 631 BC), the last great king of Assyria, the tablets found in this archive repository were probably part of his tablet collection. Because these tablets were excavated very close to the Nabû temple (Ezida), which also had its own archival repository, some of the tablets thought to have come from the so-called “Library of Ashurbanipal” might have actually belonged to the neighboring Nabû temple. Today, the North Palace library material is not clearly differentiated from that of Ezida, due to the fact that the excavators did not provide detailed information about the exact findspots of the tablets.

title: Building IV on the Athenian Acropolis
name_variants: Southeast Building@en | Building IV@en | ἱερὸν τοῦ Πανδίονος@grc | Southeast Building | Building IV | hieròn toû Pandíonos | ἱερὸν τοῦ Πανδίονος
description: A building at the southeast end of the Acropolis of Athens, built perhaps in the 440s BC. Suggested identifications include the workshop for construction of the Parthenon, the hero shrine of Pandion (the eponymous hero of the tribe Pandionis), and the Chalkotheke. It is now covered by the Old Acropolis Museum.

title: Military compound in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona
name_variants: Military compound in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona@en | Military compound in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona
details: Based on inscriptional evidence, the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona was likely damaged by an earthquake in 160 CE and rebuilt shortly after. In the period after the earthquake (i.e., Phase 2), the area formerly belonging to the temple in Phase 1 was reorganized to include both the temple and an adjacent complex of rooms used for military storage and record keeping.
description: A complex of rooms requisitioned for military record keeping and administration, formerly belonging to the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona.

title: Caerau Hillfort
description: Caerau Hillfort is a multivallate Iron Age hillfort in the western suburbs of Cardiff, Wales. The fort covers an area of ca. 51,000 m².

title: Gallo-Roman sites at Érome, France
description: A pair of archaeological sites in Gallia Narbonensis. The site of Les Orpaillots shows traces of a sanctuary and a group of tombs while Notre-Dame-de-la-Mure showed traces of a late third century Gallo-Roman villa.

title: Saint-Romain-en-Gal
description: An urban quarter of Roman Vienne, now presented as an archaeological museum.

title: Ponte Tufaro
description: A bridge of Roman origins located near Montesarchio.

title: Lamington
description: Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall, Scotland

title: Roman amphitheater of Martigny
name_variants: Amphithéâtre de Martigny@fr | Amphitheatre de Martigny
description: The Roman amphitheater of Martigny likely dates to the reign of Trajan.

title: Theopetra Cave
description: Located in Thessaly, the Theopetra Cave is an important archaeological site with evidence of multi-phase prehistoric human occupation. Radiocarbon dates indicate human activity beginning at least 50,000 years ago. Archaeogenetics have focused on evidence related to Mesolithic inhabitants of the cave site.

title: Alyscamps
description: Alyscamps is a necropolis located outside the walls of Arles, France.

title: Coastal Tower 16b (Old Mawbray)
description: Coastal Tower 16b, part of the Hadrian's Wall Coastal defences

details: The Erechtheion is a small, unusual temple on the Athenian Acropolis dedicated to Athena Polias and Erechtheus. The structure's foundations rest in part on the Mycenaean fortification walls of the Acropolis, on a slope that raises the south and east sides higher than the rest of the building. The temple consists of a central rectangular structure divided into several cellas, the largest of which is on the east side of the building. Several platforms and porches are also attached to the temple. On the east side, the porch has a row of Ionic columns and a frieze of white marble figures on a background of black Eleusinian limestone. The porch that projects from the temple's south side is the famous caryatid porch or "Porch of the Maidens", marked by six columns in the shape of young women in elaborate drapery. In addition to cult facilities for Athena Polias and the archaic wooden cult statue of the goddess, parts of the building housed other tokens of the mythic past of Athens, including the tomb of a local hero and the olive tree and salt spring created by Athena and Poseidon during their competition to be patron divinity of Athens. Like the rest of the Acropolis, the Erechtheion had a long post-antique history, during which it served as a church and, for a time, as the home of an Ottoman harem. At the beginning of the 19th century, one of the caryatids was brought to England with the rest of the Elgin marbles, around the same time, the porch served as inspiration for a similar porch on St. Pancras Church in London. The remaining caryatids, damaged by time, pollution, and old restoration efforts, have now been transferred to the new Acropolis Museum, and modern copies have taken their place on the monument.

details: The Stoa of Attalos, built ca. 150 BCE, was commissioned by King Attalos II of Pergamon as a gift to the city of Athens and its inhabitants. The structure was a two-story stoa, or colonnaded hall, built on the eastern side of the ancient Athenian agora. Its external colonnade was in the Doric order on the ground floor and Ionic on the upper floor, while the internal colonnade was Ionic on the ground floor and Pergamene on the upper floor. It served as a commercial and cultural center for several hundreds of years. Attalos’ monument was destroyed during the Herulian sack in 267 CE and its materials were subsequently reused in a fortification wall. Excavations on the site began in the 1930s, and the structure was then entirely reconstructed by the American School of Classical Studies in the 1950s to serve as a museum.
